title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat - BBC
summary:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the USA is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."

The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.

It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.

Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.

This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?

The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.

title: Turkmenistan Nears Major Milestone in $10 Billion TAPI Gas Pipeline - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: Turkmenistan expects a key section of a pipeline to begin supplying gas to Afghanistan’s third-largest city in early 2027, despite years of delays and hurdles in the $10-billion Turkmenistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan–India TAPI project, Turkmen officials have told Reuters. Turkmenistan is estimated to be the world’s fifth-largest holder of natural gas reserves, after Russia, Iran, Qatar, and the United States. The Central Asian country holds an estimated 5.3% of global gas reserves, with 146 years of production at current rates. At the Turkmen Energy Forum last month, Turkmenistan said that the Serhetabat–Herat section of the TAPI pipeline had reached the outskirts of Herat, in Afghanistan, with commissioning on track by the end of this year. Downstream projects identified for Herat include a pipeline to the Herat Industrial Park, gas distribution stations, industrial zone gasification, and a compressed natural gas complex. A private investor has also proposed a gas-fired power plant near the city, Turkmenistan said in October. However, the Serhetabat–Herat section is just around 150 kilometers 93 miles long, or less than a tenth of the planned 1,800-km 1,118-mile TAPI pipeline. The TAPI project has faced political and financing hurdles in recent years. The return of the Taliban to power in Afghanistan in the early 2020s and the historical hostility and distrust between Pakistan and India have been major risks to the execution and international funding for the project, estimated to cost $10 billion. Turkmen officials are optimistic that the imminent startup of the first leg of the pipeline between Serhetabat, a Turkmen city on the border with Afghanistan, and Afghanistan’s third-biggest city, Herat, could raise confidence among international investors and creditors. The section to Herat is expected to “provide early revenue streams and increase confidence among lenders,” Muhammetmyrat Amanov, head of the Turkmen state company responsible for the pipeline project, told Reuters. By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

summary:
US markets remained closed for the Thanksgiving holiday, and in the Forex space, the Australian Dollar and the Greenback posted modest gains. The Swiss Franc reversed course and was the weakest within the G8 FX space, while traders brace for inflation data in Japan, France and Spain, along with speeches by European Central Bank (ECB) Officials.

The table below shows the percentage change of US Dollar (USD) against listed major currencies today. US Dollar was the strongest against the Swiss Franc.

The heat map shows percentage changes of major currencies against each other. The base currency is picked from the left column, while the quote currency is picked from the top row. For example, if you pick the US Dollar from the left column and move along the horizontal line to the Japanese Yen, the percentage change displayed in the box will represent USD (base)/JPY (quote).

The US Dollar Index (DXY), which tracks the value of six currencies against the buck, was flat at 103.77, snapping two consecutive days of losses amid a light economic docket. Expectations that the Federal Reserve (Fed) will raise rates in December, following the release of strong US GDP data and high inflation on Wednesday, keep the Greenback underpinned, along with hawkish comments by Fed policymakers. On Friday the docket features Wholesale Inventories and the Goods Trade Balance.

EUR/USD was flattish near 1.0970, with the main catalyst being the announcement that the former Bank of Spain Chief, Pablo Hernandez de Cos, would become the next President of the European Central Bank (ECB), succeeding Christine Lagarde since February 7, 2027. ECB Minutes said interest rates were within staff estimates of the neutral rate and weren’t restraining the economy. Up next, Germany’s Unemployment Rate and inflation data in France and Spain, to be keenly followed by traders.

GBP/USD consolidated within 1.3100 with no clear catalyst or economic data release on either side of the Atlantic. However, Pound buyers had stepped in after the pair lost over 3.50% since peaking at 1.3500 early in November, as Bank of England (BoE) policymakers signal that further tightening is needed.

USD/JPY floats around 159.20, virtually unchanged as the pair consolidates, with buyers wary that a test of 160.00 could trigger another round of intervention. On Friday, the Tokyo Consumer Price Index (CPI) for November is eyed, with the core reading expected to rise from 2.4% to 3% YoY.

AUD/USD barely moved after Wednesday’s hot inflation report. The RBA faces a choice: raise rates to curb inflation and risk further labour-market damage after two consecutive monthly declines.

Despite bouncing, Gold prices finished the session with a loss of 0.47% but are poised to end Thursday’s session above $3,550, opening the door for a recovery, as a hammer candle on the daily chart implies further upside. As US markets remained close, Bullion I poised to consolidate further, ahead of next week’s US employment data, which would be the last jobs report ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.

The Japanese Yen (JPY) is one of the world’s most traded currencies. Its value is broadly determined by the performance of the Japanese economy, but more specifically by the Bank of Japan’s policy, the differential between Japanese and US bond yields, or risk sentiment among traders, among other factors.

One of the Bank of Japan’s mandates is currency control, so its moves are key for the Yen. The BoJ has directly intervened in currency markets sometimes, generally to lower the value of the Yen, although it refrains from doing it often due to political concerns of its main trading partners. The BoJ ultra-loose monetary policy between 2013 and 2024 caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks. More recently, the gradually unwinding of this ultra-loose policy has given some support to the Yen.

Over the last decade, the BoJ’s stance of sticking to ultra-loose monetary policy has led to a widening policy divergence with other central banks, particularly with the US Federal Reserve. This supported a widening of the differential between the 10-year US and Japanese bonds, which favored the US Dollar against the Japanese Yen. The BoJ decision in 2024 to gradually abandon the ultra-loose policy, coupled with interest-rate cuts in other major central banks, is narrowing this differential.

The Japanese Yen is often seen as a safe-haven investment. This means that in times of market stress, investors are more likely to put their money in the Japanese currency due to its supposed reliability and stability. Turbulent times are likely to strengthen the Yen’s value against other currencies seen as more risky to invest in.

title: Governments Cut Fuel Taxes as Oil Prices Surge - Wisevoter
summary:
An International Transport Forum review finds most of 47 member countries chose tax cuts and subsidies over measures to reduce road dependence.

Updated on Nov. 26, 2026 in Economic Policy

Live Poll

Should the government cut fuel taxes when gas prices spike?

An International Transport Forum analysis of 47 member countries found that 36 have introduced at least one fuel-related tax measure, with 27 cutting fuel taxes or excise duties. Governments favoured price relief over helping people reduce their reliance on road transport.

Sharply rising oil prices have pushed governments toward tax cuts, price controls and subsidies, which ease costs for drivers and freight operators in the short term. Whether these measures outlast the price spike remains an open question for transport and energy policy.

Brent crude exceeded USD 100 per barrel in September 2026, and by 5 October average EU petrol and diesel prices reached EUR 2.01 and EUR 2.15 per litre, up 23.9% and 39.7% year over year. The analysis does not address how long these price levels will persist.

International Transport Forum

The International Transport Forum is an intergovernmental organisation within the OECD framework that brings together transport ministers from its member countries to analyse transport policy.

Eight countries have set maximum retail fuel prices and six have capped retail profit margins, with Poland applying both price caps and margin caps. The IEA coordinated a release of 400 million barrels from strategic reserves, and the United States cut fuel taxes while releasing Strategic Petroleum Reserve oil.

September 2026: Brent crude exceeded USD 100 per barrel.

5 October 2026: EU petrol and diesel prices reached record-level increases year over year.

October 2026: EU finance ministers agreed to establish a working group on energy profit taxation.

The current response echoes the emergency fuel-tax cuts and price controls many governments adopted after the 1973 oil embargo. Unlike that episode, the EU's October 2026 move toward taxing energy profits signals a shift toward recouping windfall gains.

For drivers, tax cuts and price caps may offset some of the 23.9% year-over-year rise in EU petrol prices, though the reduction depends on each country's measures. Households that rely on road transport for commuting or goods delivery face higher costs wherever such relief is absent.

Short-term relief from tax cuts and subsidies can cushion households, but the ITF analysis highlights that few governments paired them with measures to reduce dependence on road transport. Readers should watch whether these measures are extended or withdrawn as prices change.

For related coverage of how governments set and adjust these policy tools, see Economic Policy .

Read the ITF factsheet on fuel price spikes and road transport for the full country-by-country comparison.

title: Cold Snap Squeezes UK Spare Power Capacity - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: The UK faces a system margin shortfall of more than 2.7 gigawatts GW between noon and 8 p.m. local time on Thursday, as the cold snap is reducing the margin of spare capacity for the third day in a row.  The UK’s National Energy System Operator NESO issued early on Thursday an electricity margin notice, which encourages market actions to increase system margins.   Electricity Margin Notices are used to send a signal to the electricity market. It highlights that, in the short term, NESO would like a greater safety cushion, or margin, between power demand and available supply. Such notices do not signal that blackouts are imminent or that there is not enough generation to meet current demand, the grid operator said.  The notice of a reduced system margin comes as the UK’s wind power generation has slumped in recent days while electricity demand has jumped due to below-normal temperatures in most of Europe.  According to data from market operator Elexon, early on November 26, wind power generation was about 2.5 GW below the latest forecast.  Over the past months, NESO has issued several Electricity Margin Notices to warn that the margins were tightened during periods of low wind power generation.   Wind power supplied nearly 30% of the UK’s electricity last year, and regularly provides about this share of total power generation when wind speeds are favorable.   Reduced system margins this week pushed Britain’s day-ahead electricity prices higher, just as the energy regulator, Ofgem, on Wednesday announced that energy prices for UK households would surge by 26% from January 1 as the Middle East war is pushing wholesale gas prices higher.  The regulator’s decision on Wednesday was widely expected by analysts and forecasters, who projected that UK household energy bills would jump by between 25% and 30% in the first quarter of 2027 amid surging natural gas prices as the Middle East crisis drags on. “The reason wholesale gas prices are still high is due to the ongoing war in the Middle East,” Ofgem said on Wednesday.   By Michael Kern for Oilprice.com

The energy needs of planned data centers outstrip planned energy additions in many places where hyperscalers are developing massive campuses. As a result, the private and public sector alike are increasingly and urgently adopting an all-of-the-above approach to energy development, increasing the scale and lifespan of fossil fuels and renewable energies alike, while also pouring funding into the research and development of next-gen energy alternatives. One of those promising energy alternatives is enhanced geothermal. Geothermal energy itself is nothing new about 85 percent of all houses in Iceland have been heated with geothermal energy for years now. But that kind of geothermal energy is only viable in geologically anomalous places like Iceland, where the heat from the Earth's core naturally breaks through to the surface in the form of hot springs, geysers, or other forms of heat vents. But the emerging field of enhanced geothermal seeks to make geothermal energy viable anywhere on Earth by digging deep enough to access that heat and pump it to the surface. In order to do that, geothermal startups and research projects are borrowing technology from a sector that knows a whole lot about drilling Big Oil. That's right, the next big thing in clean and green energy may come in the form of none other than fracking. Hydraulic fracturing could allow geothermal initiatives to cost-effectively drill to extreme depths where thermal heat is naturally abundant in order to provide a source of zero-emissions energy 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "If you drill down deep enough three, four, even six kilometers you reach the point where the crust is uniformly hot," University of California Irvine engineer Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi was quoted in a recent article from the UC Newsroom. "Then you can drill horizontally, create fractures, and pipe in water." The rock heats the water, turning it to steam that can run turbines that generate electricity. However, we still have a long way to go before that can be achieved at a commercially viable scale. "There is more than enough potential geothermal energy underground to power the entire United States, but unlocking it safely and economically is still a major challenge," Qomi went on to say. Scientists at the University of California are one of many groups trying to find a pathway toward bringing enhanced geothermal out of lab-based modeling and into the market. Some private companies are likewise working on employing hydraulic fracturing technology to unlock commercial enhanced geothermal. Meanwhile, others are employing techniques from the field of nuclear fusion, using a vacuum-tube gyrotron to vaporize rock molecules with high-frequency electromagnetic waves down a borehole. The round-the-clock energy potential of enhanced geothermal is just one of the sector's benefits. Another critical advantage of the sector is its broad, bipartisan appeal as one of the vanishingly few forms of clean energy to receive equally enthusiastic policy support under the Biden and Trump administrations. The UC project is backed by the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission as part of this push. The Department of Energy is bullish about the potential of geothermal in the future of the United States' energy mix. Projections from the agency state that enhanced geothermal projects could provide about 90 gigawatts of carbon-free energy in the U.S. by 2050, or approximately enough to power at least 65 million homes. Big Tech is also throwing its weight behind enhanced geothermal research and development. Quaise Energy, a startup employing the fusion-derived gyrotron approach, just signed a major power purchase agreement with Google to supply 50 megawatts MW of superhot geothermal power, beginning as soon as 2030. The deal stands as a major vote of confidence in the nascent sector. By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

title: Something Strange Just Happened in the Ukraine War: Russia, with Its Vast Crude Oil, Is Importing Fuel and Rationing Gasoline and Diesel - National Security Journal
summary: Ukraine launched further large-scale drone attacks on Russian infrastructure overnight Wednesday into Thursday, hitting an oil pumping station in Bashkortostan and reportedly attacking a key power plant. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that its air defense systems had intercepted and destroyed 343 Ukrainian drones overnight, according to state news agency TASS. Tu-22M3 Bomber from Russia. Image Credit: Creative Commons. The attacks followed a threat from Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to respond to Kyiv’s escalating attacks on Russia’s oil sector. Ukraine Says it Hit Oil Supply Center The Ukrainian General Staff confirmed on Thursday that its armed forces had attacked the Subkhankulovo oil supply and pumping center in Bashkortostan–part of Russian state-owned oil pipeline company Transneft. “Each such hit means less oil for refining and fewer oil rubles for which Russia is waging war,” the General Staff said in a Telegram statement, as quoted by The Kyiv Independent. Bulat Musin, head of the Tuymazinsky district administration, said drone debris had fallen in the industrial area and started a fire, according to local Russian news outlet Bashinform. No casualties have been reported. Independent Russian news website Astra was able to pinpoint the target based on video footage provided by witnesses. “The extent of the damage is still being assessed,” the Ukrainian open-source intelligence monitoring channel Exilenova+ said in a Thursday social media post. On Thursday, Ukraine’s General Staff reported that an oil storage tank had been hit and that a fire had broken out at the facility. While the center had been targeted in July, there was no immediate information that oil flow at the center had been disrupted. T-90M. Image Credit: Creative Commons. Second Samara Refinery Ablaze Further video footage apparently showed a fire at the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, owned by the Russian state-controlled oil company Rosneft. Ukraine’s military said on Wednesday that it had targeted and damaged both the Kuibyshev and Syzran oil refineries. It said it had hit oil refining and storage units. Each refinery had already undergone about two months of repairs after Ukrainian attacks in September, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said. It was not immediately clear whether Thursday’s fire was caused by another attack, Hromadske said. Nevinnomyssk Power Plant Likely Targeted Stavropol Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said on Thursday on Telegram that “the industrial zone of Nevinnomyssk” had been subjected to a “massive drone attack.” Falling debris had fallen near “industrial and energy facilities,” according to The Kyiv Independent’s English translation of the governor’s post. Two people were taken to a medical facility. The governor also said that educational institutions had been damaged. Astra concluded that the Nevinnomyssk thermal power plant was likely to have been the target, based on analysis of video. The plant provides power for local industry, including a large chemical firm owned by the EuroChem group. Ukrainian officials have previously referred to the chemical firm as “a critical component” of Russia’s defense production sector. Tu-95 Bomber from Russia. Image Credit: Creative Commons. Kyiv has not claimed responsibility for the Nevinnomyssk attack. Russian Oil Refining in Crisis Russian oil refining activity has plummeted to its lowest level for over 20 years, Bloomberg has said. Russian oil refineries were operating at between 2.6 million and 2.7 million barrels per day-roughly half the output seen on October 30, said Viktor Kurilov, senior oil analyst at Rystad Energy. However, these data did not include Wednesday’s attacks on Samara’s refineries. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak acknowledged on Wednesday that Russia’s domestic fuel market was “quite tense.” Putin acknowledged during a Kremlin meeting on Russia’s fuel and energy sector on Tuesday that the market for oil products “remains challenging.” In addition, several Russian regions have introduced controls on the sale of gasoline and diesel, and Moscow has had to import oil products as, despite Russia’s vast crude oil resources, the domestic market is struggling. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said in an analysis on November 15 that its actions were exerting “sustained pressure on an entire production and logistics chain.” Moscow Braces Itself for Winter Drone Attacks Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin told legislators on Wednesday that ensuring Russia’s energy infrastructure survived the winter was a top state concern. Tu-95. Image Credit: Creative Commons. “This is now the most important question: how we’ll get through the winter, especially given drone attacks,” Khusnullin was quoted by Reuters as saying. His statement was made as Russia itself was continuing with its large-scale attacks on Ukrainian civilian energy infrastructure. At a meeting at the Kremlin on Tuesday, Putin said: “Retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable.” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha hit back at Putin’s remarks via X on Tuesday. “If Putin doesn’t like Ukraine’s strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war,” Sybiha said, adding: “Stop complaining. End the war.” About the Author: Georgia Gilholy Georgia Gilholy is a journalist based in the United Kingdom who has been published in Newsweek, The Times of Israel, and the Spectator. Gilholy writes about international politics, culture, and education.

Businesses use the software to coordinate complex logistics activities, making technology an important component of freight operations. Disruptions across global shipping routes have also increased operational complexity for logistics companies. Port congestion, changing trade routes, shipping diversions and tighter customs requirements have created additional administrative demands across the freight industry.Geopolitical tensions can intensify these challenges when maritime operators need to avoid strategically sensitive shipping routes. Longer transit times and changes to transportation arrangements can increase documentation and coordination requirements. Higher oil prices present a separate challenge for the logistics industry because fuel expenses contribute to transportation costs. At the same time, the market analysis highlights how greater operational complexity can increase the importance of automation and logistics management software.For technology investors, the distinction between company performance and broader market movements remains relevant. Changes in sector valuations can reflect shifts in capital allocation and investor sentiment rather than developments within an individual company's operations. Higher energy costs can also influence freight expenses, business input costs and the valuation of companies whose expected earnings extend further into the future. These factors can weigh on technology shares even when their underlying business operations have not experienced an equivalent change.The market session also featured developments in Australia's banking sector. Bank of Queensland Ltd (ASX:BOQ) reported lower cash earnings year on year alongside higher revenue during its fiscal first half, according to the source report.The combination highlights different pressures facing regional lenders, including funding expenses, margin conditions and investment in business transformation. Revenue growth and cash earnings therefore presented contrasting indicators of the bank's financial performance. Banking developments also provide context for Australia's broader financial sector, where technology investment remains relevant to operational efficiency and digital infrastructure.Financial institutions are significant users of enterprise software as they continue to manage their technology requirements. Australia's share market remains heavily represented by financial services and resources companies, although internationally focused software businesses have gradually increased their presence. WiseTech's position within the ASX 200 reflects the growing importance of technology companies in the domestic equity market.

title: U.S. Rig Count Holds Steady as Oil Production Hits Fifth Straight Record - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: The total number of active drilling rigs for oil and gas in the United States stayed the same this week, according to new data that Baker Hughes published on Wednesday ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The total rig count in the US remains at 607, up 63 from this same time last year. The number of active oil rigs rose by 1 to 470 during the latest reporting period, according to the data. This is 63 above this same time last year. The number of gas rigs fell by 1, which is 3 fewer than this time last year. Miscellaneous rigs stayed the same at 10. The latest EIA data showed that weekly U.S. crude oil production hit a record for the fifth week in a row, rising during the week ending November 20 to 14.065 million bpd, up from 14.032 million bpd last week and up 251,000 bpd from a year ago. Primary Vision's Frac Spread Count, an estimate of the number of crews completing wells, rose during the week ending November 20, regaining 3 of the 4 crews it lost last week, settling at 194, which is up 15 year-over-year. The number of active drilling rigs in the Permian Basin was unchanged during the reporting period, at 277. This is 26 rigs above year-ago levels. The count in the Eagle Ford stayed at 50, which is 11 more than this same time last year. Oil prices were up on Friday prior to the data release, with Brent now trading at $94.28 3.15% per barrel. WTI was also trading up on the day at $83.89 2.28%. By Julianne Geiger for Oilprice.com

title: Oil prices fall amid forecasts of global oversupply - Inspenet
summary:
The oil prices retreated on Wednesday, November 25, amid expectations of a global crude oil surplus, forecasts of supply exceeding demand weighed more heavily on prices than fears of potential supply disruptions in the Middle East.

The Brent crude futures they fell 0.5% to $90.96 per barrel, while the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) it registered a drop of 0.8%, to $81.43 per barrel, according to quotes at 10:35 GMT.

This pullback comes after both oil benchmarks registered gains of more than 2% during the previous session.

The forecasts of the International Energy Agency (IEA) they point to a global crude oil surplus, a scenario that is keeping prices under pressure. This is compounded by the increase in oil inventories in the United States.

According to data from American Petroleum Institute (API) , US crude oil inventories increased by 126,000 barrels during the week ending November 20.

Furthermore, the reactivation of the Sharara oil pipeline in Libya allowed the resumption of crude oil transport to the Akakus storage facilities in Zawiya.

Oil market operators are also keeping a close eye on the meetings of the OPEC+ scheduled for November 29, in which the ministers will address the crude oil production policy for 2027.

Ahead of these meetings, Iraq is seeking an upward revision of the alliance’s estimate of its extraction capacity. This revision will be crucial in determining member countries’ production quotas for the coming year.

Despite the prospects of oversupply, the situation in the Middle East continues to generate uncertainty among energy market participants.

The Houthis in Yemen claimed to have attacked the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia, a facility that is part of a strategic complex for processing and exporting Saudi oil.

Added to this situation are the recent maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, which maintain concerns about the safety of international hydrocarbon transport.

For now, expectations of a global crude oil surplus outweigh geopolitical risks and are keeping oil prices down throughout the day.

title: Standard Chartered Oil Needs a New Shock to Fall Further - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: Oil prices continued to recover from their recent slump, with renewed Middle East supply threats outweighing earlier global surplus concerns. Brent crude for January delivery climbed 1.3% to trade at $95.90 per barrel at 12.00 pm ET on Thursday, a sharp rise after closing at $89.37/bbl on Monday while the corresponding WTI crude contract was up 1.2% to change hands at $84.65/ bbl. Yemen's Houthi forces claimed on Wednesday that their strikes on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and export complex caused fires, with satellite imagery from NASA and Planet Labs revealing thick black smoke over the site. The Houthis also claimed multiple strikes on Riyadh's financial district, where Saudi civil defense reported 11 people were injured on Tuesday after a strike hit a tower housing the Public Investment Fund for the second time in under a week. U.S. commercial crude oil inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, marking a third consecutive weekly build as higher net imports and domestic output outweighed increased refinery runs while crude exports dropped to their lowest level since early August amid higher freight costs and softer Asian demand. Traders will be watching the November 29 OPEC ministerial meeting, where members are set to discuss 2027 production policy amid competing views on potential supply surpluses and internal quota disputes. And now, oil and commodity experts at Standard Chartered have weighed in, saying that oil prices are unlikely to sink below recent lows, with further downside needing clearer evidence of sustained inventory builds or a faster recovery in physical supply, even as the geopolitical uncertainty continues to complicate the outlook. Brent crude spent much of the past week consolidating around the low $90s/bbl, following a sharp correction from the late-October highs, before slipping below $90/bbl on Monday with the $89.37/bbl settlement the lowest in nearly three months. Related Goldman Sachs Sees U.S. Natural Gas Demand Surging on Data Center Boom According to the analysts, the price action reflects the increasingly entrenched bearish fundamental narrative, which was reinforced by the IEA's substantial upward revision to Q4 supply. The IEA raised its Q4 supply estimate by 3.3mb/d in its November Oil Market Report, reflecting a faster recovery in Gulf production and exports than previously expected. This has reinforced expectations of a return to surplus by the end of the year, coupled with a more substantial build in 2027. However, StanChart says that the recent price correction has already discounted much of the anticipated supply surplus, implying that a sustained move lower may require evidence that the surplus will emerge sooner, be larger, or persist for longer than currently expected, rather than simply confirming existing forecasts. That said, there's an ongoing broad decline across refined product prices, refining margins and freight rates, suggesting that some of the exceptional tightness associated with geopolitical disruptions is beginning to unwind. According to StanChart, European jet fuel NWE Jet CIF cargo balance of month and Asian fuel oil Singapore 380 M1 prices declined 24% and 31% MTD, respectively, while the European diesel crack ICE gasoil/Brent spread has fallen 21%, indicating that the adjustment extends beyond falling crude prices. Refining economics have also weakened, with both Asian FCC margins and NWE hydrocracking margins down 25% MTD. Meanwhile, Middle East-to-China TD3C clean product freight rates have declined 27%, while dirty VLCC freight rates on the Gulf-to-China route have fallen 55% MTD. These developments provide increasingly broad evidence of easing market stress, although absolute prices and transportation costs remain elevated. However, the gradual easing of physical market tightness continues against a backdrop of uncertain diplomatic progress between Washington and Tehran, with the latest spate of attacks on regional energy infrastructure and shipping underscoring the vulnerability of the physical supply recovery. The muted price response suggests that the market is increasingly discounting persistent hostilities in the absence of material additional supply losses. StanChart has predicted that a diplomatic breakthrough could accelerate the resumption of physical flows and reinforce downward price pressure, while renewed disruptions to export infrastructure or maritime routes could quickly challenge expectations of a surplus. Continued attacks on Russian energy infrastructure also constrain the recovery in middle distillate availability, even as broader crude supply conditions improve. Meanwhile, OPEC meets on Sunday, three months after it completed the rollback of 1.65 million bpd of voluntary cuts with a final 188,000 bpd increase in September. The group then agreed to hold September targets through December, according to Rystad Energy. StanChart says members now have to decide whether to add barrels, hold steady or cut again as surplus forecasts grow. They also have to settle their 2027 production baselines without splitting the group. Iraq's weight in the group grew when the UAE left in May, "although not necessarily its formal influence," the bank says. Baghdad has a long record of producing above its quota and wants OPEC to recognize its higher production capacity. Recent OPEC meetings have barely moved prices. StanChart says Sunday's could, particularly if members agree to act together on supply again. The analysts note that the UAE's departure in May has increased the relative importance of Iraq, although not necessarily its formal influence. Iraq has historically been among the group's least compliant members on quotas and is seeking recognition of its higher production capacity. StanChart says that whereas recent OPEC meetings have elicited little market reaction, the Sunday meeting could prove more consequential for near-term crude prices, particularly if it signals a renewed and collective willingness to manage supply in response to an increasingly bearish balance. By Alex Kimani for Oilprice.com

The latest measures have also drawn criticism within the United States. Democratic Senator Ron Wyden condemned Trump's tariff policy as an attempt to impose unilateral global duties, pledging to use available legislative tools to challenge the measures. title: Gold steadies as investors return to precious metals despite mounting US rate hike fears - Proactive financial news
summary: Gold prices recovered as investors returned to precious metals following a sharp sell-off earlier in the week, although mounting expectations of further US interest rate increases continue to cloud the outlook. Spot gold climbed 1.70% to US$3,627.43 an ounce, while silver outperformed with a gain of 4.98%. Platinum advanced 3.01% and palladium rose 2.72%. The recovery follows a volatile period for bullion, which briefly dropped below US$3,500 on Wednesday and remains under pressure after suffering a 9.4% decline last week, its steepest weekly loss in eight months. Gold has traded below US$4,000 an ounce since November 11 and remains on course for a third monthly decline exceeding 6%. Inflation strengthens case for US rate hikes The latest US inflation figures have complicated gold's recovery prospects, strengthening expectations that the Federal Reserve will tighten monetary policy further. Core personal consumption expenditures inflation, the Fed's preferred measure of underlying price pressures, accelerated to 3.3% in October, its highest annual reading since 2023. Interest rate futures are now pricing in a 96.2% probability of a 25-basis-point increase at the Fed's December 9 meeting. Markets also assign a 64.3% probability that the federal funds rate will reach a target range of 4.25% to 4.50% by the January 27 meeting. Higher interest rates generally work against gold by increasing the opportunity cost of holding an asset that generates no income. Rising energy costs stemming from Middle East tensions have added to inflationary pressures, weakening expectations of monetary policy relief heading into 2027. Precious metals join broader market recovery Gold's rebound coincided with gains across European and Asian equity markets on Thursday, as investors returned to technology stocks following recent heavy selling. US equity markets remained closed for Thanksgiving, limiting trading activity and potentially contributing to volatility across commodity markets. Silver's stronger recovery points to renewed buying across metals with industrial applications, although concerns about global economic growth remain. Australian gold miners face uncertain outlook For Australian gold producers, the recovery offers some relief after several weeks of falling bullion prices and heightened share market volatility. However, rising diesel, labour and financing costs could squeeze operating margins if gold prices remain subdued. A weaker Australian dollar could provide some protection for domestic producers by supporting local currency gold prices. With US inflation proving stubborn and financial markets increasingly anticipating successive interest rate increases, gold's latest rebound faces a difficult test before investors can declare an end to the recent sell-off.

title: (BOJ Review) Developments in JGB Market-Making Business by Securities Companies
summary:
November 27, 2026 ASAMATSU Hiroki, AIDA Eri * , HORIKAWA Takumi, OGAWA Yoshiya Financial System and Bank Examination Department

* Previously at the Financial System and Bank Examination Department

Securities companies function as market makers in the Japanese government bond (JGB) market by intermediating the trading needs of investors. They manage the interest rate risk they bear and earn profits from their intermediation. In this paper we analyze the developments in factors that are internally considered by securities companies, such as balance sheet size, interest rate risk, and profits, as they undertake the role of market makers, and we examine the impact of these factors on liquidity in the government bond market, including through case studies. Generally, under stable market conditions, the risk management factors of securities companies rarely have a significant impact on the liquidity of the government bond market. However, during the market turmoil in April 2025, the cautious stance of securities companies toward taking on additional risks may have contributed to the widening of bid-ask spreads. Moving forward, it remains important to deepen our understanding of the developments in market-making business.

title: What are tariffs, how do they work and why is Trump using them? - BBC
summary:
Tariffs have been one of US President Donald Trump's favourite economic tools since he returned to the White House.

He argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs. But critics say they have put up prices for American consumers and disrupted and damaged the global economy.

Tariffs are taxes on imported goods.

Typically, the charge is a percentage of a good's value.

For example, a 10% tariff on a $10 product would mean a $1 tax on top - taking the total cost to $11.

The tax is paid to the government by companies bringing in the foreign products.

These firms may pass some or all of the extra cost on to their customers, which in this case means American consumers and other US businesses.

Companies may also decide to import fewer goods.

Trump argues tariffs increase the amount of tax raised by the government, encourage consumers to buy American-made goods and boost investment in the US from foreign companies.

Parts of the US were hollowed out economically when free trade deals resulted in industrial jobs heading overseas.

Trump also wants to reduce the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

The president argues that countries that sell more products to the US than they buy from it are cheating the US and that tariffs correct this imbalance.

In February 2026, the US Supreme Court said that Trump had exceeded his authority when he used emergency powers to introduce tariffs on specific countries without approval from Congress.

That ruling affected all tariffs Trump brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

That includes the first tariffs Trump announced in early 2025 which targeted Mexico, Canada and China.

The ruling also covers those announced on Trump's so-called "Liberation Day" in April 2025, when the president set out tariff rates of up to 50% for dozens countries, including Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

About $100bn (£74bn) has since been refunded to companies that paid those "Liberation Day" tariffs.

This represents roughly 60% of the roughly $166bn collected under the government policy, according to a court filing.

Around $29bn in potential refunds are still being reviewed by trade authorities, while a further $1.6bn remains unpaid because importers have not provided the banking details needed to process payments.

No. The White House has been looking at alternative ways.

After the Supreme Court ruling, Trump used different legislation - Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 - to impose temporary 10% tariffs on all global imports.

Those tariffs expired on 24 July, but have been replaced by tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on all goods from the top 60 US trade partners, including the UK, the EU and China.

In late November, Trump announced new duties against 14 partners, including China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, which follows other similar moves made in the wake of the SCOTUS ruling against the administration.

The actions have been taken under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices.

The Trump administration has begun arguing that the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" or that some countries are making more goods than they need and then selling them cheaply in the US, which makes it difficult for American companies to compete.

Over the summer, 25 US states - all Democrat-controlled - launched legal action that calls these tariffs "arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law". The lawsuit accuses the administration of using forced labour as a pretext to continue tariffs.

Trump also used Section 301 to levy a 25% tax on certain goods from Brazil, claiming that Brazilian policies have harmed US trade.

In August, he announced a 50% tariff on a wide range of goods imported from Canada, in retaliation for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

Those tariffs cover about $20bn (C$28bn; £14bn) of Canadian imports, or about 5% of all goods Canada sends south.

The UK had already negotiated a 10% tariff with the US on most goods in June 2025.

The latest announcement does not change that, but tariffs have been removed on whisky imports, something Trump had said he would do after the King's state visit to the US earlier this year .

In 2024, the UK exported about £58bn of goods to the US - mainly cars, machinery and pharmaceuticals.

Under the terms of the 2025 deal, the 10% rate applied to the first 100,000 UK vehicles exported every year - roughly the number sold in 2024. Additional cars face the standard 25% tariff.

UK steel exports to the US are also subject to 25% duty, compared to the 50% rate which applies to steel and aluminium products from the rest of the world.

Many firms said they would pass on the cost of tariffs to US customers, including Target, Walmart and Adidas.

Some products have become more expensive - including toys, appliances and furniture as well as certain foodstuffs.

The cost of some goods manufactured in the US using imported components has also gone up.

In October 2025, a study by Goldman Sachs estimated that about 55% of the tariff charges were passed on to US consumers.

And in April, a Federal Reserve study said Trump's sweeping 2025 tariffs had caused a surge in inflation this year.

The White House has always maintained that it will take time for the tariffs to pay off, pointing to promises by firms and countries to make big investments in the US.

Despite the new barriers to trade, US imports actually increased by 4% in 2025.

Trump was accused of throwing the global economy into turmoil when he announced the first tariffs of his second presidential term in early 2025.

Share prices around the world fell sharply, as did the value of the dollar.

Although the US currency and global financial markets have since largely recovered, the ongoing uncertainty around Trump's tariff policy has continued to destabilise international trade.

Some US allies have looked to alternative markets, causing what some economists describe as a "re-wiring" of global trade.

In January 2026, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said the tariffs had "definitely [slowed] down global activity", and warned further trade tensions could threaten economic growth.

Since then the Iran war has restricted the global supply of oil and fertiliser, pushing up prices.

title: Navy Uncovers Suspected Stolen Crude Oil, Illegal Refinery In Rivers - New National Star
summary:
By Joy Onu

The Nigerian Navy has uncovered 112,525 litres of suspected stolen crude oil and illegally refined petroleum products at four illegal refining sites in Rivers State.

According to a statement issued by the Director of Naval Information, Navy Captain Abiodun Folorunsho, the discoveries were made on November 25 during separate operations in Ogbogolo Community, Ahoada West Local Government Area, and George Pepple Community, Bonny Local Government Area, as part of the Navy’s sustained efforts to combat crude oil theft, illegal bunkering and related criminal activities.

At Ogbogolo, personnel of Nigerian Navy Ship (NNS) SOROH identified two illegal refining sites containing approximately 15,000 litres of suspected stolen crude oil and 525 litres of suspected illegally refined Automotive Gas Oil (AGO). The sites also contained three cooking drum ovens, two dugout pits and other equipment used for illegal refining.

In George Pepple Community, personnel of Forward Operating Base (FOB) BONNY identified two additional refining sites with 13 dugout pits. Seven of the pits held approximately 97,000 litres of suspected stolen crude oil, while four contained water and two were freshly excavated. The Nigerian Navy said the facilities and petroleum products found during the operations were handled in accordance with established procedures.

The findings indicate continued attempts by oil thieves to establish new locations and resume illegal refining activities despite previous disruptions. It said the operations would focus on protecting critical oil and gas infrastructure, safeguarding the country’s energy resources and preventing activities that undermine the national economy.

title: Japanese Yen flat lines as BoJ uncertainty offsets hot Tokyo CPI and USD downtick - www.tmgm.com
summary:
The USD/JPY pair lacks a firm intraday directional bias on Friday, trading in a narrow 20-25 pips band above the 159.00 mark through the Asian session amid mixed cues. Moreover, spot prices remain confined in a multi-day-old range, warranting caution for aggressive traders heading into the weekend.

Data released earlier today showed that the headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) in Tokyo – Japan's capital city – rose 2.8% year-on-year (YoY) in November, up from October's downwardly revised print of 2.7%. Meanwhile, the core gauge, which excludes volatile fresh food prices, climbed from 2.6% to 2.9% YoY, or a 16-month high. This, along with Bank of Japan (BoJ) board member Naoki Tamura's hawkish comments on Thursday, reaffirms bets for an imminent rate hike at the December 17–18 policy meeting. The Japanese Yen (JPY), however, struggles to attract any meaningful buyers amid the uncertainty over the BoJ's future policy path.

Furthermore, the wide interest rate differential between Japan and other major economies, including the US, contributes to the JPY's relative underperformance. Bearish traders, however, remain on high alert amid speculation that Japanese authorities might step in again to prop up the domestic currency. Apart from this, the emergence of some US Dollar (USD) selling caps the upside for the USD/JPY pair. Meanwhile, firming Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hike expectations, along with a further escalation of tensions in the Middle East, favor USD bulls, suggesting that any corrective pullback in the currency pair is more likely to be bought into.

The USD/JPY pair retains a modest bullish bias above the 200-period Simple Moving Average (SMA) on the 4-hour chart and the 50.0% Fibonacci retracement confluence, around 158.50. On the topside, immediate resistance is located at the 61.8% Fibo. retracement at 159.79, followed by a stronger barrier at the 78.6% retracement near 161.66.

On the downside, initial support is seen at the 200-period SMA at 158.47, reinforced by the nearby 50.0% retracement at 158.48, ahead of deeper Fibonacci floors at 157.17 (38.2%) and 155.55 (23.6%). A sustained break above 159.79 would open the way toward the 161.66 region, while a drop back below the 158.50 area would signal fading bullish pressure and a potential rotation toward the lower retracement supports.

(The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool. Know more. )

The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is the Japanese central bank, which sets monetary policy in the country. Its mandate is to issue banknotes and carry out currency and monetary control to ensure price stability, which means an inflation target of around 2%.

The Bank of Japan embarked in an ultra-loose monetary policy in 2013 in order to stimulate the economy and fuel inflation amid a low-inflationary environment. The bank’s policy is based on Quantitative and Qualitative Easing (QQE), or printing notes to buy assets such as government or corporate bonds to provide liquidity. In 2016, the bank doubled down on its strategy and further loosened policy by first introducing negative interest rates and then directly controlling the yield of its 10-year government bonds. In March 2024, the BoJ lifted interest rates, effectively retreating from the ultra-loose monetary policy stance.

The Bank’s massive stimulus caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers. This process exacerbated in 2022 and 2023 due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks, which opted to increase interest rates sharply to fight decades-high levels of inflation. The BoJ’s policy led to a widening differential with other currencies, dragging down the value of the Yen. This trend partly reversed in 2024, when the BoJ decided to abandon its ultra-loose policy stance.

A weaker Yen and the spike in global energy prices led to an increase in Japanese inflation, which exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target. The prospect of rising salaries in the country – a key element fuelling inflation – also contributed to the move.

title: As Trump targets 14 major economies with new tariffs, China’s $203 billion export surge into Africa presents a new economic dilemma - Business Insider Africa
summary:
US President Donald Trump’s renewed offensive against China’s manufacturing dominance could have consequences far beyond America’s borders, leaving Africa increasingly exposed to the economic fallout of a competition between the world’s two largest economies.

As Washington seeks to protect its industries from cheaper foreign competition, African economies face a difficult balancing act: benefiting from affordable Chinese products and industrial investment without undermining their own manufacturing ambitions.

The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, India, Japan, South Korea and the European Union, following an eight-month investigation into industrial overcapacity.

According to the Office of the US Trade Representative, Washington concluded that industrial policies and other practices in the affected economies had encouraged excess manufacturing capacity at the expense of American commercial interests.

China faces proposed tariffs of up to 20% on many products, alongside existing duties dating back to Trump’s first administration. The measures remain subject to public consultation and have not yet taken effect.

The announcement comes despite recent efforts by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to stabilise relations ahead of the January 10 expiration of their existing trade truce.

Beijing has rejected Washington’s accusations, arguing that the competitiveness of Chinese exports reflects its industrial strengths rather than unfair trading practices.

Reuters reported that Washington’s latest measures also place pressure on China’s trading partners, particularly economies where Chinese manufacturers have established production facilities.

Although no African country is directly targeted by the latest proposals, the continent’s growing commercial relationship with Beijing leaves it vulnerable to shifts in global trade flows.

Data from China’s General Administration of Customs, compiled by the University of International Business and Economics, showed that Chinese exports to Africa increased by 24.5% to $202.98 billion between January and September 2026.

Chinese imports from Africa rose by 18.5% to $109.13 billion, bringing bilateral trade to $312.11 billion, an increase of 22.3% compared with the corresponding period of 2025.

The continent’s trade deficit with China stood at approximately $93.84 billion during the period.

The trend builds on a record-breaking year in 2025, when China-Africa trade reached $348 billion and the continent recorded a $102 billion trade deficit with Beijing.

The latest figures predate Trump’s November tariff proposals, but they illustrate an existing imbalance that could become more pronounced if Chinese manufacturers encounter greater restrictions in Western markets.

China’s economic challenges are also contributing to the shift. Weak domestic consumption and a prolonged property market downturn have increased the importance of overseas markets to Chinese manufacturers.

Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America offer alternative destinations for products facing intensifying competition and trade restrictions elsewhere.

China’s commercial influence across Africa has already surpassed that of the United States.

An August 2026 report by the US Congressional Research Service showed that China’s goods trade with sub-Saharan Africa was worth four times that of the United States in 2025.

However, the composition of that trade remains heavily uneven. While Africa predominantly supplies China with minerals, crude oil and other commodities, Beijing exports machinery, vehicles, electronics and other manufactured products to the continent.

This imbalance has implications beyond trade statistics. African countries that export raw materials but import higher-value finished products capture a smaller share of the economic benefits associated with manufacturing, including skilled employment, technological development and industrial investment.

South Africa, Africa’s most industrialised economy, provides an important example of the competing interests at play.

The country recorded $53.6 billion in bilateral goods trade with China in 2025, compared with $22.7 billion with the United States.

Unlike several African economies that rely predominantly on commodity exports, South Africa has an established industrial base, including automotive manufacturing, steel production and engineering.

Its automotive industry is particularly exposed to changes in international trade policy because it relies on both domestic vehicle sales and access to overseas markets.

An expansion of competitively priced Chinese vehicle imports could benefit South African consumers while placing additional pressure on established manufacturers and their local suppliers.

The steel industry faces similar challenges.

September 2026 research by Rhodium Group found that China’s economic slowdown and excess steel production were weighing on global ferrous metal prices, affecting South Africa’s earnings from iron and chromium ore.

However, the consequences of China’s changing economy are not uniform across Africa.

While weaker demand for traditional commodities presents challenges for oil exporters such as Angola, the expansion of China’s clean energy industries is supporting demand for copper and cobalt from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Chinese machinery, solar panels and other industrial equipment also offer potential benefits to African businesses by reducing the cost of production and improving access to technology.

For countries struggling with electricity shortages and expensive industrial infrastructure, affordable renewable energy equipment could strengthen manufacturing competitiveness rather than weaken it.

The policy challenge is therefore not simply whether African governments should restrict Chinese imports, but whether they can distinguish between products that support domestic production and those that threaten the viability of local industries.

Sweeping import restrictions could increase costs for consumers and businesses, while unrestricted competition could make it harder for emerging manufacturers to establish themselves.

While South Africa illustrates the competitive pressure facing established industries, Morocco offers an example of how African economies could capitalise on the restructuring of global manufacturing supply chains.

The North African kingdom has positioned itself as an automotive manufacturing hub, using its proximity to Europe, industrial infrastructure and preferential trade arrangements with major Western markets to attract international investors.

Chinese interest in Morocco’s electric vehicle and battery industries reflects a broader effort by manufacturers to diversify production beyond their home market.

For African economies, attracting manufacturers seeking alternative production locations could create employment, encourage technology transfer and increase exports of higher-value products.

However, establishing factories in Africa does not automatically guarantee unrestricted access to American or European markets.

Washington’s latest trade investigations extend beyond China to economies that have attracted Chinese manufacturing investment, highlighting the growing scrutiny of international supply chains.

Rules governing the origin of products could become increasingly important, particularly where factories rely heavily on imported Chinese components or undertake limited processing before exporting finished goods.

African countries seeking to benefit from manufacturing relocation would therefore need to develop local supply chains rather than simply serve as assembly or transit points for Chinese products.

Beijing, meanwhile, has taken steps to strengthen its commercial relationship with the continent.

In May 2026, China extended its zero-tariff policy to all 53 African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations, offering African exporters broader access to the world’s second-largest economy.

The policy could support agricultural exports, including South African citrus fruits and wine, Kenyan coffee and avocados, and cocoa products from West Africa.

But removing tariffs addresses only one of the barriers limiting African exports.

Unreliable electricity, expensive financing, insufficient processing facilities and transport bottlenecks continue to constrain the ability of many African businesses to compete internationally.

The African Continental Free Trade Area ( AfCFTA ) provides another potential opportunity. By reducing barriers to trade within the continent, it could allow manufacturers to serve larger markets, develop regional supply chains and reduce dependence on imported finished goods.

Ultimately, Africa’s economic interests extend beyond whether Washington or Beijing gains an advantage in the global trade confrontation.

The more consequential question is whether African economies can use intensifying international competition to expand their own productive capacity.

Without significant investment in manufacturing, infrastructure and regional supply chains, the continent risks remaining a major destination for the very industrial output that the United States is seeking to keep out of its market.

title: US tariffs on China could rise to 40%, but trade truce likely to hold - ThinkChina
summary:
The Trump administration’s proposed tariffs on Chinese goods could rise to 40% if the bilateral trade truce is not extended in January. However, analysts expect any tariff escalation to remain contained, with advanced AI chips and technology restrictions emerging as the real battleground in US-China competition. Lianhe Zaobao associate China news editor Sim Tze Wei explains.

27 Nov 2026

Politics

​​(This is an edited version of an article first published on Lianhe Zaobao (English edition) .)

The Trump administration is proposing additional tariffs on 14 economies , including China, on the grounds of “structural excess capacity” in manufacturing. Most Chinese goods exported to the US would be subject to tariffs of up to 20%, while certain products, including smartphones and laptops, would face tariffs of up to 10%, with exemptions on some other goods.

Under the proposal released by the Office of the US Trade Representative on 25 November, the relevant tariffs on Chinese goods could rise to 40% if the US-China trade truce is not extended before it expires on 10 January next year. The proposed measures are still subject to public consultation, with written submissions due by 5 January next year and a public hearing scheduled for 25 January. The effective date has yet to be announced.

Analysts interviewed noted that after the US Supreme Court ruled in February this year that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorise the president to impose tariffs, the Trump administration turned to alternative legal grounds, including Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, to rebuild tariff barriers and continue using tariffs as bargaining chips in trade and economic negotiations.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded to questions on the matter for two consecutive days, while the Ministry of Commerce also voiced its opposition on 26 November. The commerce ministry accused the US of engaging in typical unilateralist behaviour by launching investigations and proposing additional tariffs on the grounds of excess capacity, saying that such actions seriously violated World Trade Organization rules. It urged the US to return to dialogue and consultation, adding that China would closely monitor developments and reserved the right to take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.

Reuters reported that the latest US tariff proposal and lingering concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) kept investors on the sidelines, with Chinese A-shares fluctuating on Thursday. The CSI 300 Index closed marginally higher by 0.06%, while the Shanghai Composite Index edged up 0.01%. The STAR 50 Index, however, fell 1.36%.

In a report, Nomura Securities noted that the new tariff on China is capped at 20%, in line with the one-year truce agreed upon at the Kuala Lumpur trade talks on 30 October 2025.

In July this year, the US imposed a 12.5% forced-labour tariff to replace part of the IEFPA tariffs. Nomura estimated that, after accounting for this existing tariff, the incremental tariff would be around 7.5 percentage points, rather than 20 percentage points.

Responding to the US warning that tariffs could double to 40% if the current truce unravels, Nomura said the truce is very likely to be extended again when it expires, especially considering China’s ongoing progress on soybean and aircraft purchases. “We expect any tariff escalation to be contained, and the 7.5 percentage points tariff increase to have a limited impact.”

Nomura expected the US effective tariff rate on Chinese goods to rise from the current level of roughly 22% to around 27%, after including﻿ some exemptions and US$30 billion in US-China mutual tariff treatment. Nomura also believed that “the real battleground for the US-China rivalry is AI”, with bilateral tensions to centre mainly on the US ban of advanced AI chips and remote access to China.

Xu Tianchen, senior China analyst at the Economist Intelligence Unit, told Lianhe Zaobao that the proposed 20% tariff did not materially violate the consensus reached between China and the US in Kuala Lumpur last year, and that Beijing was unlikely to respond with retaliatory tariffs or other countermeasures. However, the US move to impose a 10% tariff on certain previously exempt products, including smartphones and computers, amounted to “making small moves without upending the negotiating table”, and Beijing was unlikely to be satisfied.

Xu said that US arms sales to Taiwan, sanctions against major mainland Chinese companies, tariffs on Chinese goods exceeding the agreed ceiling, or further tightening of technology export controls — such as restricting mainland China’s access to critical equipment including lithography machines — could all cross Beijing’s red lines. Should that happen, Beijing could adopt tougher countermeasures, including restrictions on rare earth exports.

Looking at recent interactions between China and the US, Xu felt that engagement would remain the predominant approach in bilateral relations, and that the trade truce due to expire in January next year stood a good chance of being extended. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami next month, with the trade truce and tariffs likely to be key topics of discussion.

Among the 14 economies targeted by the proposed additional US tariffs, Taiwan faces a proposed tariff rate of 15%, although the measures have similarly yet to be finalised.

According to Taiwanese media reports, Taiwan’s Vice-Premier Cheng Li-chiun said on Thursday that Taiwan and the US had previously agreed on a tariff rate of 15%, which would not be stacked on top of other tariffs, putting Taiwan on a par with Japan, South Korea and the European Union. She expressed confidence that the latest investigation would not alter the existing agreement.

Cheng also said that the Taiwan-US investment memorandum of understanding had secured separate preferential tariff treatment under Section 232 for Taiwan’s semiconductors and derivative products, including zero tariffs on imports within agreed quotas and a maximum tariff rate of 15% on imports exceeding those quotas, without any additional tariffs. The Taiwanese government would also assist companies investing in the US in negotiations with the US Department of Commerce to seek exemptions for raw materials, equipment and components required for the construction and operation of manufacturing facilities.

title: Tokyo inflation backs a Bank of Japan hike that may not rescue the yen - Startup Fortune
summary:
Economists polled by Reuters overwhelmingly expect Japan's policy rate to reach 1.50% on December 18, yet the Federal Reserve looks set to raise its own rate nine days earlier. Matching moves would leave the US-Japan rate gap, a weight on the yen, just as wide.

Two central bank meetings in December could decide how calm your year end is. A sudden jump in the yen can hit AI shares and bitcoin even if you've never traded a currency.

Tokyo's electricity prices jumped 14.2% in a single month, helping push core inflation in the Japanese capital to a 16-month high of 2.9% in November. The reading, published on Friday, November 27, was up from 2.6% in October and just under the 3.0% median forecast reported by Reuters. This measure leaves out fresh food but keeps energy, and it has now topped the Bank of Japan's 2% target for three months running.

Headline inflation edged up to 2.8% from 2.7%, according to Japan's Statistics Bureau, while the gauge that strips out both fresh food and energy eased to 2.5% from 2.6% and rose only 0.1% on the month after seasonal adjustment. Energy did a lot of the lifting, up 9.5% on the year against 2.2% in October, and investingLive noted that the end of utility subsidies fed into the jump.

Very probably. In a Reuters poll taken from November 11 to 18, 61 of 71 economists, or 86%, expected the policy rate to move from 1.25% to 1.50% at the December 17-18 meeting. A large majority also doubted that this month's slide in the Nikkei would derail the move, although investingLive still flags turmoil in AI and chip shares as the main risk to it. Board member Naoki Tamura, one of the bank's hawks, said on Thursday that it must respond swiftly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by raising rates faster.

Traders can read all of that too, which is bad news if you're counting on a hike to rescue the yen. The currency traded around 159.3 per dollar early Friday, close to the 160 mark that has drawn official action before. Frankly, recent history doesn't help. When the bank lifted its rate to 0.75% on December 19, 2025, the dollar climbed to about 157 yen, the Associated Press reported. On September 18 this year the rate went to 1.25%, two board members dissented, and the dollar rose 1.2% to 157.897 yen as Governor Kazuo Ueda spoke to reporters, according to Reuters.

Reuters surveyed 78 economists; 54 expect a December hike to 1.50%, Japan's third straight quarterly move. The BOJ's October 2025 and January 2026 shutdowns, by contrast, have left the Fed working off permanently damaged jobs and inflation data. - bank of japan interest rate hike december 2024 - federal reserve economic uncertainty december meeting outlook

Then there's Washington. The Federal Reserve raised its target range to between 3.75% and 4% in September, and CME's FedWatch tool put the chance of another quarter point on December 9 at roughly 97% to 98%, TheStreet reported on Thursday. If both central banks move by that much, the gap between their rates doesn't narrow at all. Dollars would still pay far more than yen.

Tokyo has a blunter tool. It spent a record ¥15.4 trillion, about $96 billion, between July 30 and August 26, a run that included the first joint operation with the US in 28 years after the yen had sunk to almost 164, AFP reported. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama warned against one-sided moves on November 13, after the currency briefly slipped past 160. Nobody has promised to step in at that number, so don't trade as if they had.

Borrowing cheaply in yen to buy higher-returning assets elsewhere works nicely until the yen leaps. On July 24, 2024, AI and tech stocks shed around $1 trillion in a sell-off that showed early signs of an unwind. A Bank of Japan hike that markets read as hawkish and soft US jobs data followed, and on August 5 Japan's TOPIX index lost 12% in a day. The Bank for International Settlements later put yen carry positions going into the turmoil at a rough ¥40 trillion, or $250 billion, and said that estimate was probably low if anything.

The part you can measure looks much less crowded now. Commodity Futures Trading Commission data for November 17 show hedge funds and similar traders net short about 23,800 yen futures contracts. At the end of June they were net short almost 138,000, Hedgeweek reported, on a count that included options, so the comparison isn't exact. Across the broader non-commercial group, the futures market was actually net long the yen by about 116,000 contracts. That's only one window. The BIS has noted that carry trades are often built with forwards, swaps and options, much of which these futures figures won't show you.

Risk assets are already bruised. The Nasdaq 100 fell 10.4% in the week to November 20, and StoneX analyst David Scutt noted that the yen reached two-week highs as the gap between US and Japanese bond yields narrowed. Bitcoin traded near $61,400 early Friday after dipping under $60,000 within the previous day. US spot bitcoin funds had lost a net $5.39 billion in November through Wednesday, according to SoSoValue data cited by crypto.news.

Those moves don't prove a carry unwind has started, but if one does, it'll hit portfolios that are already hurting.

When the decision comes, listen for anything Ueda says about speed. Nearly 60% of economists in the Reuters poll already expect 1.75% by the end of March, so a governor who sounds slower than that could easily send the yen lower and hand the problem back to the finance ministry. One who opens the door to faster tightening could set off the sharp currency move that carry traders dread, especially if the Fed surprises everyone by holding first. The Bank of Japan finishes meeting on December 18, the same day nationwide November inflation figures arrive.

Japan's two-year bond yield hit a 31-year high this week, raising the cost of yen-funded carry trades that help prop up Bitcoin, just as the Fed under Kevin Warsh meets a day ahead of the Bank of Japan. - bitcoin price surge from japanese bond yield hike - how yen carry trade affects bitcoin leverage positions
