title: Bank of Japan warns digital money risks extend beyond the token - finchannel
summary:
The FINANCIAL — The Bank of Japan called for stronger safeguards against digital money risks on Friday, as Executive Director Kazushige Kamiyama warned that tokenized finance and increasingly capable artificial intelligence could create new vulnerabilities across payments and markets.

In his November 27 speech at an International Monetary Fund seminar in Tokyo , Kamiyama described a financial system in which stablecoins, tokenized bank deposits and other digital assets coexist. He urged authorities to preserve trust, strengthen cybersecurity and establish clear responsibilities as new platforms develop.

Reuters reported that his warning covered both financial stability and the ability of AI to identify and exploit security weaknesses. He also highlighted legal uncertainty over whether transferring a digital token effectively transfers rights to the underlying asset. These were risks requiring safeguards, rather than a report of a newly identified loss or attack.

Tokenization changes the way an asset is recorded and transferred. The Bank of England explains it as creating a digital representation of something such as a share, bond or unit of money on a shared ledger. Authorized users can keep track of ownership, while software attached to the token can enable transactions to follow specified conditions.

The British central bank distinguishes that process from creating an unbacked cryptoasset. A token can represent an asset that already exists, rather than derive its value solely from what another buyer will pay for it. The distinction matters for the financial products under discussion: a new recordkeeping system and a new underlying investment are separate propositions.

Among the possibilities the bank describes are payments triggered by confirmed delivery, faster international transfers and more flexible movement of corporate cash. These are potential applications of programmable finance. They depend on the arrangements supporting a particular system, rather than follow automatically whenever a financial claim is represented by computer code.

The Bank of England also describes dividing assets into smaller units as a possible way to broaden access to investments. Its stated approach includes small-scale testing before wider adoption.

The Bank for International Settlements set out a broader architecture in its 2025 Annual Economic Report. Its proposal placed tokenized central bank reserves, commercial bank money and financial assets on a common programmable platform. Bringing those elements together could combine instructions, reconciliation and transfer processes that currently take place through separate stages.

The BIS assessed new monetary arrangements against three requirements: acceptance at face value, an ability to supply liquidity as payment needs change, and protection against financial crime . Its report argued that stablecoins fell short of the requirements needed to serve as the foundation of the monetary system. That was the BIS’s assessment, rather than a finding that every proposed tokenized payment arrangement has the same weaknesses.

A shared platform, in that account, need not use distributed ledger technology. The proposed benefit lies in connecting the money and assets involved in a transaction while retaining reliable settlement. The BIS emphasized central bank reserves as the final settlement asset, with commercial bank deposits continuing to perform their role in financing economic activity.

A June 2026 Federal Reserve staff paper identified a different potential weakness: safe reserve assets alone may not prevent a run on digital money. The research examined the interaction between network effects, which make a payment instrument more useful as more people adopt it, and congestion-sensitive fees, which make transactions more expensive when network demand rises.

In the authors’ model, those forces can encourage users to redeem together even when the assets backing the instrument are perfectly safe. The result concerns the incentives created by the payment network itself. It does not require the reserve portfolio to suffer the kind of credit loss that might otherwise undermine confidence in an issuer.

The paper was published in the Fed’s Finance and Economics Discussion Series, under the title “The Fragility of Perfectly Safe Digital Money.” Its conclusions represent the authors’ research, not a policy determination by the Board of Governors. The mechanism is a theoretical finding, rather than evidence that a particular issuer has experienced such a run.

AI presents a parallel set of questions about how risks spread between institutions. In November 2024, the Financial Stability Board identified dependence on outside providers, correlated market behavior, cyber threats and model governance as vulnerabilities that could become systemic. Its review also recognized benefits, including more efficient operations, improved compliance and more powerful analysis of financial data.

The board’s concern extended beyond individual software errors. Similar tools used across institutions could produce correlated responses, while dependence on a small group of service providers could create common points of failure. Generative AI could also increase financial fraud and disinformation, the report said. These were potential channels of instability, rather than a claim that all uses of AI increase overall risk.

That earlier review called for better information about adoption and an assessment of whether supervisory frameworks adequately addressed emerging vulnerabilities. Authorities themselves were using AI to improve supervision, it noted. Limited data and rapid technological change made it harder to monitor the financial system’s exposure.

The FSB moved from identifying vulnerabilities to outlining institutional controls in 12 sound practices published on October 15, 2026 . They cover oversight across an organization and management throughout an AI system’s development and deployment. Financial institutions are encouraged to consider them; the report presents practices rather than a new statute applying directly to every bank.

The practices assign a role to boards and senior management in aligning AI use with business strategy and risk appetite. They also call for clear accountability, documentation and assessment of the significance of each use case. Model selection is meant to reflect the institution’s operational needs as well as the materiality of the risks involved.

Further practices address data quality, explainability, performance evaluation and appropriate human oversight. Cyber-risk testing and information sharing sit alongside management of third-party dependencies. That last category includes the performance and transparency of outside suppliers, concentration in the supply chain and continuity of operations if a provider fails.

The European Central Bank’s November 2026 Financial Stability Review analysis of AI describes the same issue across banks, asset managers and the wider economy. It says financial firms are using AI for activities including fraud detection, credit scoring and portfolio management, while reliance on a concentrated group of technology providers can create shared operational exposures.

The ECB distinguishes broader adoption from the deployment of more autonomous systems. Its review says advanced uses in credit assessment, trading and portfolio management remain less widespread, with agentic AI largely at the pilot stage. It warns that greater automation could increase operational risk and contribute to correlated behavior in investment markets.

Financial exposure also reaches beyond the institutions using the software. The review describes potential transmission through equity and credit holdings in companies affected by AI, including firms financing infrastructure expansion. Its conclusion calls for governance, better monitoring and international cooperation, reflecting the cross-border reach of the technology and its suppliers.

The ECB also identifies potential gains from lower information and transaction costs, better investment analysis and more efficient financial intermediation when adoption is properly managed.

In Japan, Kamiyama said the central bank was pursuing experimentation alongside improvements to existing infrastructure. Its work includes a distributed-ledger sandbox and a retail central bank digital currency pilot. No decision to issue a retail digital currency has been made, he said.

No. Kamiyama said work on a pilot continues, but no issuance decision has been made.

The October report describes practices financial institutions are encouraged to consider; it does not present them as a new statute.

title: Oil Prices Reflect US Pressure on OPEC Members on November 27 - Demokratis.co.id
summary: Uncertainty over global oil supply coordination intensified on November 27, 2026, as crude prices remained elevated amid reports that the Trump administration had encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to leave OPEC. The reported pressure has raised questions about the organization's stability ahead of its November 29 production policy meeting.Brent crude traded in the low-to-mid $90s per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) hovered in the mid-$80s, according to market indications reported by Commodity Board. Both benchmarks recovered from early-week losses after a rally on November 25 pushed Brent above $94 and WTI back into the low $80s.Ten people familiar with the matter told Finance BigGo that US officials had encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to reconsider their OPEC membership earlier this year. Washington reportedly argued that production restrictions could complicate efforts to increase crude output and attract foreign investment.Venezuela faced additional financial pressure when US authorities blocked the payment of its annual OPEC membership dues using funds under American oversight. The fees amount to approximately €2.8 million, or $3.1 million, and are generally paid during the first quarter.The pressure eased after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened during the summer. Two people familiar with the discussions said he persuaded the Trump administration not to pursue the withdrawal issue further.Following the removal of former Venezuelan President Maduro in January, the US State Department discussed the country's OPEC membership with Venezuelan officials. President Trump has sought greater involvement from major American oil companies in restoring Venezuelan production as part of his Western Hemisphere energy strategy.Venezuela is currently exempt from OPEC+ production quotas. OPEC data showed that its crude output reached approximately 1.2 million barrels per day in September, while state-owned Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) aims to increase production to 1.5 million barrels per day by the end of 2027.OPEC sources said the organization could waive unpaid membership fees and had no current intention of expelling Venezuela. Trump also said in August that the decision to leave the organization should belong to Venezuela itself.Iraq has taken a different approach. During the summer, US officials reportedly encouraged Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi to consider withdrawal as Exxon Mobil and Chevron planned expanded investments in the country.Al-Zaidi subsequently raised the possibility during a government meeting, but Iraq's oil ministry opposed the proposal. Officials instead favored negotiating a higher production allocation within OPEC.Iraq is also challenging a preliminary capacity assessment that placed its crude production capability at 4.9 million barrels per day. Baghdad wants a higher recognized figure to strengthen its position in negotiations over 2027 production quotas.The US State Department said it could not rule out discussions between lower-level officials and Venezuela about leaving OPEC, but maintained that senior officials had not raised the issue. Regarding Iraq, Washington said discussions primarily concerned energy infrastructure, production and transportation capacity.Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro, highlighted the growing organizational risk."The risk of OPEC fracturing is rising," said Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro.OPEC membership has declined to 11 countries following the departures of Qatar, Ecuador, Angola and the United Arab Emirates since 2019. The UAE left OPEC and OPEC+ in May 2026, seeking greater freedom from production restrictions.Venezuela and Iraq together produce more than 5 million barrels of crude oil per day. Their potential departure or reduced compliance with production agreements could affect the group's ability to coordinate supply, particularly as global oil consumption growth is expected to slow in 2026 compared with 2025.OPEC+ is scheduled to meet on November 29 to discuss production policy for 2027. According to Rapidan, uncertainty surrounding infrastructure damage, the duration of the ongoing Middle East conflict and disruptions to crude exports could encourage the alliance to postpone major quota adjustments until 2027.

title: Two oil tankers explode in Strait of Hormuz - Mehr News Agency
summary:
TEHRAN, Nov. 26 (MNA) – The IRGC Navy said two violating tankers exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines north of Khosab port in the Strait of Hormuz, including a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude.

Two violating tankers exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines north of Khasab port in the Strait of Hormuz, the IRGC Navy said.

One of the vessels is a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil and has been left burning.

The IRGC Navy said the tankers had unknown identities and their navigation systems switched off, and were attempting a covert passage relying on U.S. military fighter jets. Naval mines stopped them with fire and explosion on the unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Trump admin targets Spanish olive oil exports to the US with new shipping penalties over Israeli weapons ban at Algeciras port - Olive Press News Spain
summary:
SPAIN’s olive oil giants face an unprecedented blow as the US mulls a multi-billion-euro ban on Spanish imports.

The US Federal Maritime Commission proposed on October 14 slapping Spanish-flagged ships with $200,000 fees when they dock at US ports, as well as restricting imports including cosmetics, ceramics and olive oil.

The latter alone accounted for more than $830 million worth of Spanish exports to the US last year, according to the US body, while the total value of goods potentially facing restrictions is estimated at a staggering €2.8 billion.

READ MORE: Spain celebrates four months of no border with Gibraltar – but warns it will have to be rebuilt if the treaty fails

The measure is a tit-for-tat response to a row dating back to 2024, when Spain refused to allow three US-flagged ships carrying cargo to or from Israel to dock at Algeciras port, in Andalucia.

Malaga-based Dcoop, the world’s largest producer of olive oil and table olives, said it was ‘very concerned’ about the measure, which could be finalised in the coming weeks following a public consultation in the US.

The US is Spain’s second-biggest market for olive oil after Italy, accounting for about 15% of Spanish exports last year, according to figures from the International Olive Council (IOC).

A ban on olive oil would deal Spanish producers a crippling blow, industry experts have warned, as dozens of local firms rely on the US market for their livelihood.

READ MORE: Moroccans fear Vox, Venezuelans reject the left: How Spain’s three-million strong immigrant populations plan to vote in this Sunday’s election

Spanish olive oil exports to the US have faced tariffs of at least 10% since US President Donald Trump launched his global trade war in April 2025.

After the tariffs were introduced, the value of Spanish olive oil exports to the US fell from approximately €1 billion in 2024 to €730 million in 2025, according to Spain’s ministry of economy.

Dcoop president Antonio Luque said he was ‘very concerned’ and that the threatened ban represented a ‘great risk’ for the industry, adding that he hoped it would ultimately not be approved.

The controversy is the latest escalation in mounting tensions between Spain and the US after prime minister Pedro Sanchez refused to raise defence spending to 5% of GDP, as demanded by Trump, at a NATO summit in June 2025.

Trump then threatened to punish Spain with trade penalties, including tariffs, and vowed to make Madrid pay twice as much for a trade deal.

The two leaders clashed again over the war in Gaza, after Spain formally recognised a Palestinian state in May 2024 and later imposed restrictions on weapons shipments to Israel.

Washington condemned Madrid’s position, accusing it of potentially limiting US military operations and turning its back on Israel.

Spain, meanwhile, recalled its ambassador to Israel amid the escalating diplomatic row.

Tensions reached another flashpoint following the outbreak of war between the US, Israel and Iran in February 2026.

READ MORE: Spain’s centre-right PP raise spectre of ‘vote rigging’ as Pedro Sanchez’s PSOE closes in during final polling of election

Sanchez refused to allow American forces to use the jointly operated Rota and Moron military bases in Andalucia for strikes against Iran, describing the conflict as ‘illegal’ and contrary to international law.

Trump responded by threatening to cut off all trade with Spain and instructing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to end dealings with Madrid.

Spain then went further by closing its airspace to US military aircraft involved in the Iran war, prompting further criticism from Washington.

title: Stockpiling Will Support Oil Prices in 2027, Energy Aspects Says - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: Depleted inventories are setting the stage for a major stockpiling push next year, which will support oil prices despite an expected market surplus, Energy Aspect’s founder and director Amrita Sen told Bloomberg TV in an interview on Friday. China will lead the global stockpiling in the coming months, as it typically does when oil prices fall. Beijing is also expanding its storage capacity, which could accelerate buying for storage, assuming that no escalation hikes oil prices again, according to the analyst. “Inventory refilling is a multiyear story, with 2028 being the bigger one than 2027 especially as the conflict continues for the first half at least,” Energy Aspect’s Sen told Bloomberg. “From a geopolitical point of view, we think this current status quo is the new reality,” Sen told Bloomberg. Oil prices have been below $100 per barrel over the past three weeks, but traders may have become “very complacent”, seeking to short oil. In reality, risks to supply have not eased much, according to Sen. The world is nearly out of buffers to cushion the supply shock of the Iran war, which raises the floor under oil prices each time re-escalation threatens oil supply from the Middle East. Despite numerous estimates that the Middle East’s crude oil supply is back to – and even exceeding – pre-war levels, the fundamentals show increasingly tighter markets because shipping, trade routes, and tanker costs are anything but normal. Crude oil is flowing in greater amounts, but fuel exports from the region remain severely constrained. The world entered this crisis with nearly 10 billion barrels of global oil stocks, Saudi Aramco’s CEO Amin Nasser said last month. Since then, nearly 3 billion barrels of gross oil supply were lost, or roughly half the crude and products that would normally have moved through Hormuz over the same period. “So the system is already straining. And, with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin,” Nasser warned. By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

title: AI, jobs and prices: what euro area consumers expect - European Central Bank
summary:
27 November 2026

By Dimitris Georgarakos, Geoff Kenny and Justus Meyer

Artificial intelligence could significantly boost productivity, but its effects on prices will depend on how quickly it is adopted and how consumers respond. New evidence from the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey sheds light on consumers’ views on jobs, prices and AI regulation. [ 1 ]

Overall adoption rates of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace have increased substantially, as AI has moved rapidly from experimentation to regular use. More than 50% of workers reported using AI at work in May 2026. [ 2 ] In August 2026, 44% of employed euro area consumers reported using AI at least weekly at work, and around 18% used it daily. Many AI users report that the technology already helps them produce more or higher-quality work, and workers expect its use to broaden substantially over the next five years.

However, widespread adoption does not automatically translate into economy-wide productivity gains. Firms also need to invest in skills, data, computing capacity and organisational change, while consumers need to adapt their behaviour. New evidence from the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) [ 3 ] shows how consumers see this transition in real time, and what they expect it to mean for productivity, jobs and prices.

Daily AI use has increased steadily over the past year (Chart 1, panel a). Overall, AI adoption in the euro area is similar to that in the United States. Strikingly, a larger share of consumers in the euro area report using AI daily, although this gap is narrowing.

AI adoption is rising, but barriers remain

a) AI adoption in the euro area and the United States

b) Barriers to AI use

(percentage of consumers, by region)

(percentage of employed consumers not using AI)

Sources: CES, authors’ calculations and Gallup.

Notes: Panel a): euro area estimates are population-weighted CES estimates among employed consumers aged 18-64, latest data from August 2026. United States estimates are from Gallup (latest data: August 2026). Importantly, CES and Gallup use different survey questions and samples, so comparisons across regions should be interpreted as indicative of trends rather than fully harmonised estimates. In Gallup, total AI users includes employees who say they use AI daily, a few times a week, a few times a month or a few times a year. In the CES, every May, as part of a special module on labour market topics employed consumers are asked if they personally use artificial intelligence (AI) in their work. Daily use of AI is collected in the CES at irregular frequency since June 2025 (latest data: August 2025) by asking respondents about the frequency of their AI use for tasks related to their job. Panel b): population-weighted shares among employed respondents aged 18-64 who reported not using AI at work in June 2025. Respondents could select multiple barriers. EA-11 denotes the population-weighted average across the 11 euro area countries covered by the CES.

Rapid adoption, however, does not necessarily translate into domestic investment. A recent estimate projects that investments by firms will rise by around 40% in the United States between 2021 and the end of 2027, compared with about 12% in the euro area, with AI-related investment contributing significantly to US growth. [ 4 ] Combined with high and rising AI adoption, weaker domestic investment could also increase Europe’s dependence on foreign AI-related technologies and infrastructure.

At the same time, many workers still face barriers to using AI at work, and daily use remains limited. These barriers are similar across the largest euro area economies (Chart 1, panel b). Skills and knowledge gaps, together with privacy and security concerns, are among the most frequently reported obstacles. By contrast, social norms and existing regulations are less frequently identified as direct barriers.

For policymakers, the similarity of barriers across the euro area suggests that euro area wide measures could support wider AI adoption, including training to address skills gaps, clear employer policies on safe AI use and better access to approved tools. The prominence of privacy concerns also indicates that trusted, appropriately governed AI tools, such as European solutions, could encourage wider workplace adoption.

Policy efforts can support AI diffusion in several ways. Safeguards can build confidence among workers and consumers, while clear and predictable rules can make it easier for firms to invest in and deploy AI. The challenge for Europe is to combine these objectives by supporting trusted use without creating unnecessary complexity or uncertainty that could deter investment.

According to recent CES findings , consumers report that AI helps them save time. But time savings alone do not necessarily increase productivity. For AI to expand effective capacity, workers need to translate faster task completion into more or better-quality output.

The CES shows that workplace AI users report perceived gains in both the quantity and quality of their work (Chart 2, panel a). Around 56% say that AI increases the amount of work they complete, while 47% report producing higher-quality output. Among those indicating that they complete more work, 62% cite AI’s ability to help them find or process information, and 51% say that it reduces the effort required to perform their work. Other frequently reported benefits include generating new ideas, automating repetitive tasks and handling larger workloads.

However, these perceived gains are not universal. Among users who reported no increase in output, the most commonly cited reason is the time needed to check or correct AI-generated results (Chart 2, panel b). Other reported obstacles include AI not being suitable for the task and concerns about retaining control. This points to remaining workplace frictions at the task-level and suggests that productivity gains depend on the tasks for which AI is used and the degree of verification and human oversight required. [ 5 ]

As workers learn where AI can be used most effectively and firms adapt their workflows, some of the constraints currently limiting productivity gains may diminish. Translating AI use into higher productivity is likely to be a gradual process of experimentation and adjustment.

Perceived effects of AI on productivity

a) Effects on work quantity and quality

b) How AI affects the amount of work completed

(percentage of AI users, employed consumers)

Sources: CES and authors’ calculations.

Notes: Panel a) shows population-weighted shares among employed respondents aged 18-64, including employees and the self-employed, who reported using AI at work in June 2026. Respondents were asked separately whether AI had changed the amount of work they completed and the quality of their work. Panel b) shows population-weighted shares among employed respondents aged 18-64 who reported using AI at work. “Helpful” refers to users who reported that AI increased the amount of work completed; “not more helpful” refers to users who reported either no change or a decrease. Respondents could select multiple reasons.

Workers increasingly expect the use of AI to become more widespread. In August 2026, employed respondents aged 18-64 expected 46% of workers in their current sector to use AI within five years, up from 34% one year earlier (Chart 3, panel a). This upward revision is visible across the distribution, not just among the most optimistic respondents.

The pace at which AI spreads also matters because households and firms often base their decisions on what they expect will happen. Higher productivity and incomes could support spending and investment. At the same time, concerns about jobs and wages could make workers more cautious about their current employment situation and more inclined to consider alternative job opportunities.

AI can therefore affect the economy through two channels: the productivity gains it eventually delivers and the expectations it creates along the way. Both can influence spending, saving, investment, labour market choices and, ultimately, prices.

The CES points to both opportunities and adjustment costs (Chart 3, panel b). Around half of respondents expect AI to save time on everyday tasks or make it easier to find the best prices for goods and services, while many also expect to gain access to better products and services.

Expected adoption and near-term effects of AI

a) Expected AI use at work over the next five years

b) Expected effects of AI over the next 12 months

(percentage of employed consumers)

Notes: Panel a) shows population-weighted estimates among employed respondents aged 18-64 of the expected share of workers in their sector who will use AI over the next five years. Dashed vertical lines indicate the survey means. Panel b) shows population-weighted shares of employed respondents aged 18-64 who expect each effect over the next 12 months, based on the June 2026 survey. Outcomes were measured separately, so the shares do not sum to 100%.

At the same time, consumers expect AI to bring not only benefits but also some costs. Learning new skills and spending more time checking information are among the challenges they anticipate. Consumers are more likely to see AI as increasing the risk of job loss than as raising household income or improving job opportunities over the next year. A sizeable share also expects AI to push up prices of goods and services over the same period. [ 6 ]

Such perceptions help show how AI may affect the economy during the transition, because households and firms often make spending, saving and investment decisions based on their expectations.

Consumers’ concerns about AI are also reflected in their views on regulation. Support for safeguards does not simply reflect unfamiliarity with the technology. For instance, demand for AI regulation is strong among both regular AI users and those who use it less often or not at all (Chart 4, panel a). Across euro area countries, support for regulation also tends to be stronger in countries where workers also perceive a greater risk of losing their jobs due to AI (Chart 4, panel b). While this relationship does not establish causality, it suggests that economic insecurity may be one factor shaping attitudes towards AI regulation.

Consumers’ demand for AI regulation

a) Consumers’ demand for AI regulation

b) Demand for regulation and perceived AI-related job loss risk

(country-level averages)

Notes: In August 2026 consumers were asked whether priority should be given to “the development of AI, even if this means accepting greater risks” or “regulating AI, even if this slows its development”. Panel a) shows the population-weighted average demand for AI regulation among employed respondents, by AI use frequency. Demand for regulation is measured on a scale from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating stronger support. Panel b) shows population-weighted averages by country among employed respondents in August 2026. The horizontal axis reports the average subjective probability of losing one’s current job because of AI, while the vertical axis reports average demand for regulation. The fitted line shows an unweighted linear relationship across countries, with each country given equal weight. The relationship is descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal.

The CES findings point to a delicate balance. Consumers see clear benefits from AI, but they also worry about jobs, privacy, security and the reliability of AI-generated information. Clear rules on data use and accountability, together with access to trusted tools and the skills needed to use them, can help build confidence. The challenge for Europe is to put those safeguards in place without unnecessarily slowing the investment and innovation needed to realise AI’s productivity potential.

The views expressed in each blog entry are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily represent the views of the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem.

Check out The ECB Blog and subscribe for future posts.

For topics relating to banking supervision, why not have a look at The Supervision Blog ?

This blog draws on ongoing research conducted as part of the ECB Research Task Force’s work on the economic effects of AI, including Workstream A on AI and the real economy. The work presented here forms part of a forthcoming working paper: Borlescu, A., Georgarakos, D., Kenny, G., Pairan, T. and Meyer, J. (2026), “AI diffusion in the euro area: Adoption, workplace effects and economic expectations”, mimeo, European Central Bank. The authors thank the ECB’s CES team for collecting and processing the data and Ipsos for carrying out the survey.

See Lane, P. R. (2026), “ AI adoption in Europe ”, keynote speech at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Research Symposium on AI and the economy, San Francisco, 30 October.

For background on the CES, see ECB (2021), “ ECB Consumer Expectations Survey: an overview and first evaluation ”, Occasional Paper Series , No 287, and Georgarakos, D. and G. Kenny (2022), “Household Spending and Fiscal Support During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Insights from a New Consumer Survey”, 129(2022), Journal of Monetary Economics, S1-S14.

See also Financial Times (2026), “US widens AI-driven investment gap with Europe”, 24 August. See also for a more comprehensive analysis Andersson, M., Jarvis, V. and Soudan, M. (2025), “Business investment: why is the euro area lagging behind the United States? ”, ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 2/2025, European Central Bank.

The aggregation problem is central to macroeconomic assessments of AI. Economy-wide productivity depends not only on how much AI improves the tasks it performs well, but also on the share of those tasks in total work, the pace of adoption and the complementary organisational changes required. See Acemoglu, D. (2025), “Institutions, Technology and Prosperity”, Economic Policy , Vol 40, No 121, and Brynjolfsson, E., Syverson, C. and Rock, D. (2021), “The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies”, American Economic Journal, Vol 13, No 1. See also Dell’Acqua, F. et al. (2026), “Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality”, Organization Science , Vol 37, No 2.

Among respondents who expect AI to increase prices, greater pricing power for firms and higher energy and material costs are the most cited reasons, according to additional CES data that will be covered in Borlescu et al. (2026).

title: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026 - European Central Bank
summary:
27 November 2026

Compared with September 2026:

In October the median rate of perceived inflation over the previous 12 months increased to 4.1% from 3.6% in September and stood at its highest level since July 2024. Median expectations for inflation over the next 12 months also rose to 3.5% from 3.1%, but remained below the level reached at the start of the conflict in March 2026 (4.0%). Median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased to 3.0% from 2.9%, returning to the March 2026 level. Median expectations for inflation five years ahead were unchanged at 2.5% for the third consecutive month, the highest level since the start of the series in August 2022. Uncertainty about expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased for the second consecutive month, remaining higher than the level prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. Respondents in the bottom income quintile continued to report higher inflation perceptions and expectations, on average, than those in the top quintile. Younger respondents (aged 18-34) continued to report lower inflation perceptions and expectations than older respondents (aged 35-54 and 55-70).

Consumers’ expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months fell to 0.6% from 1.1% in September. While expectations declined across all income quintiles, the decline was most pronounced in the bottom income quintile (by 0.7 percentage points to 0.8%) and in the top quintile (by 0.8 percentage points to 0.4%). Perceived nominal spending growth over the previous 12 months increased to 5.4% from 5.3% in September, while expected nominal spending growth over the next 12 months was unchanged at 3.7%.

Expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased in October to -1.3% from -1.5% in September. Expectations for the unemployment rate 12 months ahead decreased to 11.0% from 11.3% in September. As observed in previous months, households in the bottom income quintile expected the highest unemployment rate 12 months ahead (13.3%), while households in the top income quintile expected the lowest rate (9.5%). Consumers continued to expect the future unemployment rate to be only slightly higher than the perceived current unemployment rate (10.4%), suggesting a broadly stable labour market outlook. Quarterly data revealed a somewhat mixed labour market sentiment. Unemployed respondents reported a lower expected probability of finding a job over the next three months, at 29.6% in October compared with 30.8% in July. Employed respondents reported a lower expected probability of job loss over the next three months, at 9.4% in October compared with 9.8% in July.

Consumers expected the price of their home to increase by 3.3% over the next 12 months, lower than in September (3.5%). As in previous months expectations for home price growth over the next 12 months remained, on average, higher in the lowest income quintile (3.8%) than in the highest income quintile (3.0%). Expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged from July, at 4.9%. As in previous months, households in the top income quintile expected the lowest mortgage interest rates 12 months ahead (4.6%), while those in the bottom quintile expected the highest rates (5.4%). The net percentage of households reporting a tightening (relative to those reporting an easing) of access to credit over the previous 12 months increased compared with September. The net percentage of households expecting tighter credit conditions over the next 12 months (relative to those expecting an easing) also increased compared with September, reaching its highest value since October 2023. Quarterly data showed that the share of consumers who reported having applied for credit during the past three months increased slightly to 14.4% in October, from 14.3% in July.

The release of the Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) results for November is scheduled for 7 January 2027.

title: Meeting of 28-29 October 2026 - European Central Bank
summary:
26 November 2026

Ms Schnabel started her presentation on the latest financial market developments with the observation that higher energy prices since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 9-10 September 2026 had reinforced concerns about persistent inflationary pressures. At the same time, market attention had shifted towards fiscal dynamics and concerns about the increasingly debt-financed artificial intelligence (AI) investment cycle.

Energy price pressures had intensified substantially since the September meeting, pushing oil and gas prices above the adverse scenario of the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. In response to renewed tensions in the Middle East, the latest oil futures curve had shifted markedly higher compared with the baseline of the September projections and had also moved visibly above the adverse scenario over the short term. The repricing in gas markets had been even more pronounced, with the futures curve currently standing well above the adverse scenario over the entire horizon.

Diesel refining margins stood at a historically high level, with euro area diesel crack spreads – the differences between wholesale prices and crude oil prices – above the levels observed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Freight rates from the Gulf region to Europe had surged to record highs, while the probability of a US-Iran peace deal by the end of 2026 was at its lowest since the start of the war in the Middle East. The increase in energy prices was reflected in inflation compensation. Inflation fixings throughout 2026 and 2027 had shifted higher, peaking at 4.5% for January 2027 and remaining above 2.5% until the first quarter of 2028, while inflation fixings for 2028 were broadly unchanged. Option-implied inflation risks continued to be skewed to the upside over the next two years and five years.

Despite the sharp increase in energy prices and the deterioration in the inflation outlook, expectations for the key ECB interest rates stood near their September levels. The one-year overnight index swap (OIS) rate one year ahead had decoupled from energy prices, consistent with communication that interest rates would not move in lockstep with energy costs. Immediately after the Governing Council’s September monetary policy meeting, the OIS forward curve had shifted markedly higher, temporarily pricing in more than four additional 25 basis point hikes over the next 12 months, before investors pared back expectations to just under three additional hikes. Market pricing adjusted for term premia pointed to an expected peak in the deposit facility rate at around 3%, implying a more pronounced tightening than the median expectation of participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts, which foresaw only one more hike.

Euro area risk-free rates had stabilised and, at longer tenors, had even declined since the September meeting, while US rates had risen across maturities on the back of higher real rates. The divergence between real yields in the euro area and the United States was consistent with investors’ perceptions of a more dynamic US economy.

The rise in euro area ten-year rates relative to the average in 2024 had been driven primarily by higher real term premia, reflecting increased uncertainty about the long-run macroeconomic outlook and a growing net supply of public and private debt. Higher expected short-term real rates and higher inflation expectations accounted for around one-third of the increase in ten-year rates. Moreover, the shift in stock-bond correlations into positive territory pointed to reduced diversification benefits from bonds amid more frequent adverse supply shocks, requiring greater compensation to hold duration risk.

As higher real rates raised governments’ borrowing costs and reduced fiscal space, sovereign bond yields had become more sensitive to differences in the fiscal outlook. Sovereign bond spreads had increased notably for some countries since the previous monetary policy meeting, but they had generally remained well below earlier peaks and broadly in line with fundamentals. A greater responsiveness of euro area sovereign bond yields to market stress also reflected a shift towards more price-sensitive investors. Despite the recent widening in spreads, systemic stress indicators had remained contained, well below levels recorded in previous episodes of market strain.

Euro area bank equities had overall remained resilient and, despite a recent correction, had continued to trade in positive territory over the year to date, benefiting from the higher interest rate environment and banks’ solid profitability and strong capital positions. Euro area banks had continued to reduce their domestic exposures in total government bond holdings. This suggested that they were less exposed to domestic shocks, as portfolios had become more diversified.

Concerns about inflation, financial conditions and fiscal policy had also extended to broader equity markets, with euro area stocks underperforming. A further factor weighing on equity markets globally had been the sharp correction in tech stocks, as growing concerns about the increased debt financing of the AI build-out and the returns it would generate had caused significant volatility. The substantial increase in debt issuance by hyperscalers to finance AI investment had so far been smoothly absorbed in euro area corporate bond markets, but at a higher cost for issuers.

Weakening risk sentiment towards the euro area and diverging interest rates had been reflected in the EUR/USD exchange rate, which had depreciated noticeably since the September meeting. Overall, financial conditions had tightened recently, mainly owing to a correction in risk assets and higher sovereign yields, although partly offset by the weakening of the exchange rate.

Ms Schnabel then turned to short-term funding markets. Bank borrowing costs in overnight repo markets had continued their gradual upward trend, with the spreads between rates for French, Italian and Spanish collateral broadly stable against those using German collateral. Liquidity redistribution across banks had continued to operate smoothly, with money market conditions adjusting well to an environment with less excess liquidity. On 27 October 2026, recourse to the Eurosystem’s standard refinancing operations had risen to its highest level since the end of 2016, with short-term money market rates remaining close to the deposit facility rate. Both the seven-day main refinancing operation, which covered the October 2026 month-end, and the three-month longer-term refinancing operation, which covered the 2026 year-end, had contributed to the increase. Overall, this was a comforting sign that banks were becoming more accustomed to using standard refinancing operations in their day-to-day liquidity management as balance sheet normalisation and the reduction of excess liquidity progressed.

Mr Lane then went through the latest economic, monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area.

Starting with inflation in the euro area, Mr Lane noted that headline inflation, as measured by the Harmonised index of Consumer Prices (HICP), had risen to 3.8% in September, from 3.2% in August. This increase had been driven by energy price inflation, which had increased markedly to 18.9% from 14.3%. Diesel and petrol prices had reached new peaks in September, in part reflecting elevated refining margins. Inflation excluding energy had risen to 2.3% in September, from 2.1% in August. Food inflation had increased by 0.2 percentage points in September, to 1.3%, in part owing to the impact of the summer heatwaves on the unprocessed food component. Core inflation (HICP inflation excluding energy and food) had edged up to 2.5% in September, from 2.4% in August: a 0.1 percentage point decline in goods inflation to 1.1% had been offset by a 0.2 percentage point increase in services inflation to 3.2%.

The pass-through of the energy shock to inflation remained most visible in direct effects. Indirect effects had, overall, evolved as expected and were still limited. So far there had been no material signs of second-round effects. Indicators of underlying inflation had remained broadly stable and wage pressures remained moderate. Compensation per employee had grown by 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.6% in the first quarter, while rising productivity had helped contain the growth of unit labour costs. At the same time, the early stages of the pricing chain pointed to upward pressures. The ECB’s forward-looking wage tracker suggested that negotiated wage growth would fluctuate between 2.5% and 2.8% in the remaining months of 2026 and average 2.6% in the first three quarters of 2027, broadly in line with the September staff projections. However, in the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) input prices had picked up to 67.3 in October, from 67.0 in September and 62.8 in August. In addition, the selling price expectations of firms over the coming year had increased in the latest round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises in the euro area. These signals suggested that indirect and second-round effects would become more material over time, as anticipated in the September staff projections.

Market and survey-based inflation expectations over shorter horizons had risen, but most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stood at around 2%, supporting the stabilisation of inflation around target in the medium term. Estimates of market-implied inflation expectations (derived from measures of inflation compensation by adjusting for risk premia) averaged 3.1% for 2026, 3.3% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028. Expectations of professional forecasters for headline inflation had been revised up for 2027 but were unrevised for 2028 at 2.0%. Medium to longer-term inflation expectations of consumers were broadly stable, as were expectations of firms, according to the second quarter and third quarter rounds of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises.

Brent crude oil prices (front month – based on futures) had increased by 13% to USD 115 per barrel since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting, in an environment of heightened volatility, elevated freight rates and high global prices for refined products. Price pressures had been particularly pronounced for physical Brent contracts, which reflected prices for more immediate delivery than the front-month prices. Gas prices had increased by 22% to €97 per MWh over the same period, owing to upward pressure from the Middle East conflict. The euro had depreciated by 4.0% against the US dollar since the September meeting, and by 2.2% in nominal effective terms.

The incoming information pointed to continued global economic growth in the third quarter, with the global composite output PMI (excluding the euro area) increasing to 54.5 in September, reflecting expansion in both the manufacturing and services sectors. At the same time, stocks of finished goods had increased to well above their long-term averages, suggesting some hoarding of finished goods to insulate against persistent uncertainties. Global trade continued to grow, bolstered by AI-related demand, but had shifted from goods to services.

For the euro area, the incoming data suggested that the economy had continued to expand in the third quarter. The October figure of 51.9 for the composite output PMI remained in expansionary territory, although it was slightly lower than the readings for August (52.0) and September (53.1). Both the services and manufacturing PMIs signalled expansion. Manufacturing, digital services and exports were benefiting from AI-related business investment. Government spending on infrastructure and defence was also supporting activity. These factors should continue to underpin growth in the near term. At the same time, renewed energy price increases had hit consumer confidence and higher financing costs were likely to weigh on growth.

As regards the labour market, the unemployment rate had remained at 6.4% in August. Growth in employment and the labour force remained subdued, while productivity had gradually picked up. Indeed job postings had moved sideways in recent months, while the composite employment PMI remained just above the 50 threshold. The unemployment expectations of consumers for one year ahead had risen to the highest level since the start of the Middle East conflict, but expectations in the Survey of Professional Forecasters were little changed. While the survey pointed to a gradual moderation in the unemployment rate, to 6.3% in 2027 and 6.2% 2028, this was above the rates in the September staff projections, which saw unemployment at 6.1% in 2027 and 5.9% in 2028.

Turning to fiscal policies, the profile continued to be one of significant loosening in 2026 followed by a significant tightening in 2027 and 2028. Newly specified fiscal measures since the September staff projections reinforced that pattern, with some additional loosening this year and some additional tightening next year.

Over the medium term, a recovery in confidence and real incomes, driven by gradually declining energy prices and a robust labour market, should bolster domestic demand. Investment in AI-related activities and government spending on infrastructure and defence should also continue to support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand.

Financial conditions had tightened since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. Interest rates had broadly moved up, while stock prices had fallen. The increase in interest rates had been part of a more general trend in global financial markets, reflecting the fallout from the Middle East conflict and high debt issuance in the public and private sectors in many economies. As the rise in long-term yields had been driven in part by higher real risk premia, it constituted a tightening impulse that would contribute to restraining demand.

The cost of market-based debt for firms had risen to 4.1% in August, from 4.0% in July, while bank lending rates for firms had remained at 3.8%. Growth in bank lending to firms had slowed to an annual rate of 4.2% in August and September, from 4.4% in July, while corporate bond issuance had grown at an annual rate of 4.2% in September, up from 3.8% in August and 3.5% in July. Credit standards for loans to firms had tightened in the third quarter, with banks citing concern about the economic risks faced by their customers. The latest round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises corroborated the message of tightening credit conditions, as firms had widely reported a further net tightening in bank lending rates. Despite higher financing needs for inventories and working capital, demand for corporate loans had declined, reflecting in particular higher interest rates. Mortgage rates had risen to 3.6% in August, from 3.5% in July, while mortgage lending growth had edged down to 3.0% in September. Credit standards for mortgage lending had been unchanged in the third quarter, whereas demand for mortgages had declined substantially given higher interest rates.

Based on the assessment of the incoming information against the three elements of the Governing Council’s reaction function, Mr Lane proposed that the Governing Council keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. Energy prices had increased beyond the baseline path foreseen in the September ECB staff projections, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook. The increase was likely to raise inflation further in the near term and keep headline inflation well above target over the coming quarters. Thereafter, declining energy inflation, together with the effects of higher interest rates, should support the return of inflation to target. While the full effects of the energy shock were still unfolding, underlying inflation had remained broadly stable so far and wages did not show a material response at this stage. The interest rate hikes in June and September left the Governing Council well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty. The December projections, which would extend the forecast horizon to include 2029, would provide an updated integrated assessment of how the energy shock, AI-related dynamics, the shift in financing conditions and all other relevant developments were shaping the inflation outlook and the surrounding risks. The data that had come in by December would also help the Governing Council to assess developments in underlying inflation and the strength of monetary transmission.

Regarding the economic analysis, members agreed with the assessment provided by Mr Lane in his introduction. Starting with the external environment, the global economy was continuing to prove more resilient than expected, notwithstanding further increases in energy prices, tighter financial conditions and elevated geopolitical tensions. The incoming information pointed to steady global economic growth in the third quarter, with the global composite output PMI (excluding the euro area) increasing in September, reflecting expansion in both the manufacturing and services sectors. Global activity was being supported by AI investment, inventory accumulation and the fact that tariffs had turned out to be lower than initially announced. AI was driving an investment boom, bolstering global trade and the manufacturing cycle. Inventory accumulation was in part related to some hoarding of finished goods to insulate against persistent uncertainties.

While it was noted that the resilience of economic growth had persisted despite the headwinds of higher energy prices, geopolitical uncertainties and tighter financial conditions, concern was expressed about how far AI investment growth and inventory accumulation could be relied on to continue providing support to global activity. The Middle East conflict and geopolitical tensions had persisted much longer than initially anticipated. Uncertainty, including about a potential intensification of geopolitical tensions, remained elevated. The positive impact of AI investment on global economic activity and its broader global inflation implications needed to be monitored. On the one hand, AI investment growth was supporting economic activity and global demand via manufacturing activity, investment and trade, and was thereby increasing inflation. On the other hand, if AI raised productivity, it could be disinflationary. Specifically, it could lower employment and curtail the ability of firms to raise prices.

Turning to commodity markets, members noted that energy prices had gone above the adverse scenario of the September projections. Not only had crude oil prices risen further, but increases in energy prices had also broadened and strengthened, including for natural gas and refined products, especially diesel. This development was linked to geopolitical tensions and supply-side factors. Euro area natural gas prices had tripled since the start of the conflict in the Middle East and were now at their highest level since 2022. As for liquid fuel prices, the initial shock seemed to have been absorbed to some degree by adjustments in both supply and demand. The renewed spike appeared to be due to an anticipation of further escalations in the Middle East conflict. On the one hand, there was little indication that the conflict in the Middle East would be resolved soon, suggesting an even more prolonged energy price shock. On the other hand, the geopolitical origins of the energy shock created two-sided risks as regards the direction of energy prices. The spread between the price of refined diesel and the price of crude oil had widened, owing in large part to supply disruptions in the Middle East and in Russia, as well as a reduction in supply from China. The current high levels of prices for refined products were seen as worrying, as they could feed into transport, shipping, agricultural and production costs, spreading the impact beyond that of the direct energy component of inflation. Food commodity prices, especially in Asia, were also coming under pressure owing to adverse weather conditions linked to the “El Niño” phenomenon. While it was noted that staff had already incorporated some lagged effects from energy price increases and weather conditions into their food inflation projections, further effects could materialise next year as new contracts and price agreements were established for food production. Energy prices could ease if the current premium for diesel spurred the use of the available capacity to narrow the global supply gap, or, if the geopolitical situation were to improve, the associated risk premium could unwind relatively quickly. Conversely, gas prices could rise further if supply were disrupted further or an unusually cold winter coincided with low storage levels, amid global competition for liquified natural gas.

With regard to domestic economic activity, members concurred with the assessment presented by Mr Lane. Despite higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions, euro area economic growth had continued to display some resilience and had performed better than expected so far. The incoming data suggested that the euro area economy had continued to expand in the third quarter of the year. Services had recovered, after weakening at the start of the Middle East conflict. Manufacturing, digital services and exports were benefiting from AI-related business investment. Government spending on infrastructure and defence was also supporting activity. These factors should continue to underpin growth in the near term. At the same time, renewed energy price increases had hit consumer confidence, and higher financing costs were likely to weigh on growth.

Despite higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions, the October PMI still signalled expansion in the manufacturing and services sectors. There was some indication of positive, albeit not strong, growth momentum in some sectors, particularly those linked to AI and to defence and infrastructure spending in Germany. The euro area had benefited from AI-related activity in the first two quarters of the year, with the services most involved in the digitalisation process accounting for about one-third of growth in value added, which was a good sign for the future.

While growth had held up at around 0.2-0.3% per quarter, there were some signs that economic activity might be slowing, particularly as the PMI had declined markedly in October and consumer confidence and private consumption had weakened. The short-term growth outlook was considered to be gloomier than previously expected and downside signals were more visible, although it was noted that near-term growth expectations reported in the Survey of Monetary Analysts had been revised up.

Looking ahead, members generally agreed that tightening financial conditions and the renewed spike in energy prices would have a negative effect on growth, although its magnitude remained to be seen. The decline in demand for loans suggested a stronger adverse effect on activity than had been seen so far, although some of the effect from higher rates on private investment spending, housing and consumption might be attenuated by the weaker exchange rate. The more recent surge in energy prices since August was creating a stronger headwind and, overall, higher energy prices still had to feed through to euro area activity and become visible in GDP data.

Private consumption, having previously developed in line with the projected recovery, had begun to weaken. There were a number of factors at play. Higher energy prices were having an impact on real incomes and were weakening consumer confidence. Higher interest rates had increased incentives to save and to reduce consumption. The sharp decline in demand for housing loans and rising mortgage rates could start to weigh on housing investment. One area of support was strong demand for tourism services. Over the medium term, recovering confidence and real incomes, supported by gradually declining energy prices and a robust labour market, were expected to strengthen domestic demand.

Business investment was being supported by AI-related activity, but there were increasingly questions as to how long this factor (alongside lower than initially announced tariffs) might continue to provide support. Higher borrowing costs and tighter credit standards were expected to constrain investment more broadly.

The euro area labour market had remained largely resilient, although there were some signs of softening. The unemployment rate had remained near historical lows in August. Employment and the labour force continued to grow, albeit at a subdued pace, while productivity had gradually picked up. Job postings had remained stable in recent months and the composite employment PMI remained just above the threshold of 50. The unemployment rate expectations of professional forecasters as reported in the Survey of Professional Forecasters were little changed and continued to point to a gradual decline in the unemployment rate from the current level. However, consumers’ expectations for unemployment one year ahead had risen to the highest level seen since the start of the Middle East conflict. An additional factor to consider was the potential impact of AI on productivity and jobs.

The fiscal stance, while providing support to growth in 2026 through defence and infrastructure spending, was likely to be tighter in 2027. At the same time, upcoming elections could result in more spending than currently envisaged. By contrast, elevated fiscal and political uncertainty could weigh on growth.

Members considered that, over the medium term, a recovery in confidence and real incomes, driven by gradually declining energy prices and a robust labour market, should bolster domestic demand. Investment in AI-related activities and government spending on infrastructure and defence should also continue to support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand.

Concerning structural and fiscal policies, members reiterated that higher potential growth required structural reform and had to be underpinned by sound public finances. Fiscal sustainability was a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. Governments needed to be proactive in enhancing fiscal sustainability. To this end, fiscal responses to the energy shock should be temporary, targeted and tailored.

Increasing the euro area’s growth potential required structural reform: simplifying and harmonising rules across the EU’s Single Market, accelerating the energy transition and completing the savings and investments union. These were key building blocks for making the euro area economy more dynamic and resilient. As the process for agreeing on the legal framework for the digital euro moved into its final stage, members reiterated the importance of reaching agreement on the European Commission’s Single Currency Package as quickly as possible.

Against this background, members assessed that the risks to the growth outlook were to the downside. This was due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and recent developments in Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. Continued disruption of energy supplies could cause energy prices to rise further and for longer than currently expected. This would weigh on real incomes, spending and investment. A worsening of global financial market sentiment or intensifying spillovers in global bond markets could tighten financing conditions and thereby dampen demand. Fiscal uncertainty might also further tighten financing conditions and weaken confidence, thereby lowering consumption and investment. A resurgence of trade tensions between major economies could further disrupt supply chains, reduce exports and weaken consumption and investment. By contrast, growth could turn out to be higher if the economy and energy markets were to adapt more quickly than expected to the disruption caused by the ongoing conflicts or if these were resolved sustainably. Moreover, the adoption of new technologies by euro area firms and government spending on infrastructure and defence, as well as reforms to enhance productivity and complete the EU’s Single Market, might drive up growth by more than expected.

With regard to price developments, members concurred with the assessment presented by Mr Lane in his introduction, noting that, on the one hand, energy prices had increased beyond the baseline path foreseen in the September ECB staff projections, which was likely to raise inflation further in the near term and keep headline inflation well above target over the coming year. On the other hand, underlying inflation had remained broadly stable in recent months and wage growth data had moderated further.

With the further and broader rise in energy prices, headline inflation had increased by more than expected, rising to 3.8% in September, from 3.2% in August. Energy price inflation had increased markedly, to 18.9%, from 14.3% in August. Other components of consumer price inflation, however, including food, non-energy goods and services, were either in line with or slightly lower than what had been previously expected. title: Trump embraced Xi, then slapped new tariffs on China: What’s his game plan? - Al Jazeera
summary:
In February 2025, US President Donald Trump marked his return to office by kick-starting a trade war with China.

New tariffs, amid accusations that China was failing to prevent the flow of drugs into the United States, set the stage for an escalating economic confrontation between the world’s two largest economies, which stands to reshape global trade.

While Trump’s new trade tariffs regime hit allies and rivals alike, China took the fight head-on.

Washington first put a 10 percent duty on Chinese goods, citing fentanyl and immigration concerns, and Beijing responded by curbing exports of five rare earth metals key to defence, clean energy and tech products.

Then it came to a showdown with Trump’s “ Liberation Day ” tariffs in April, including 34 percent for Chinese products. A tit-for-tat exercise ensued as headline US tariffs on China climbed to 145 percent, while US goods entering China were slapped with tariffs of 125 percent, alongside restrictions on rare earth exports.

The tariff war seesawed for much of that year before the two leaders sat at a table in October, on the sidelines of the 2025 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in South Korea, to call a truce.

The limited-time pause in hostilities paved the way for a diplomatic thaw.

Trump then travelled to Beijing last May for talks with Xi, who then visited Washington in September for the first time in more than a decade. Trump embraced the Chinese president when he arrived in Shenzhen, China’s technology hub, earlier this month for this year’s APEC summit.

But then Trump returned to Washington and, in less than a week, his administration had announced a new tariff regime – its second attempt at reshaping its trade war after the Supreme Court declared his Liberation Day tariffs of April last year illegal.

“The practical purpose is simple: rebuild [the] tariff leverage the Supreme Court stripped away and force Beijing to the table before the next summit,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, the chief economist for Asia Pacific at investment bank Natixis.

This time, the Trump administration has announced plans to impose new tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods through unfair government subsidies, policies and suppressed wages.

China is subject to the highest rates – a new 20 percent levy that is still within the bounds of the trade truce that is set to expire in January. Washington has, however, threatened a 40 percent levy if trade talks break down .

Instead of the emergency powers it used the first time – and which the Supreme Court struck down – the Trump administration is using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, alleging that targeted countries are making use of “structural excess capacity”. It has identified these 14 specific economies during an investigation it launched in March, but views China as the biggest offender, particularly in its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, a trade policy think tank in Singapore, said the “original intention” of the investigation “was to provide a more durable way to get back to the tariff levels” announced on Liberation Day.

“Over that time, I think the purpose changed somewhat,” she told Al Jazeera.

“Originally a means to apply tariffs, it seems clear that the White House wants a more sweeping use of Section 301, which allows a broad range of activities to be subject to possible negotiations and future punishment like tariffs,” she added.

Elms argued that Trump’s announcement coming in “now is rather interesting”, given he is due to meet with Xi next month, in Miami, at the G20 Leaders’ Summit. “This announcement adds another layer of possible tensions,” she said.

Just before Trump landed in Shenzhen, where he was greeted by Xi on the tarmac, earlier this month, the Chinese leader had opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting with a call to “reduce barriers to trade and investment”.

Xi also portrayed Beijing as a stable trade partner in contrast with the US, where Trump’s tariff war had already rattled global economic equations.

Responding to the latest round of tariffs this week, Beijing warned that it “reserves the right” to retaliate with steeper tariffs.

“China urges the US to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said, adding that Beijing “will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.

Referring to the eight-month investigation into “structural excess capacity” practices undertaken by Jamieson Greer, Trump’s trade representative, China said it was “a typical act of unilateralism that severely disrupts the international economic order and seriously violates WTO rules”.

Under the latest measures, Washington is seeking to take its economic confrontation with Beijing beyond bilateral trade, targeting the industrial policies of countries emerging as alternative manufacturing hubs but whose supply chains remain closely intertwined with China’s.

Hinrich Foundation’s Elms told Al Jazeera that while Beijing “is probably ok with a 20 percent tariff, they are undoubtedly less comfortable with the attempt to hold all other trade partners accountable to the US for engagement with China”.

Investment bank Natixis’s Herrero said that Trump’s latest tariffs “are less a grand strategy than a familiar negotiating ploy: keep the pressure on after a friendly photo-op”, referring to the meeting in Shenzhen.

“The stated rationale is Chinese overcapacity,” she said, adding that, however, the aim is to “rebuild tariff leverage” and “force Beijing to the table before the next summit”.

Chen Bo, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore (NUS), said the new measures are a substitute for the struck-down reciprocal tariffs, with “the same kind of inherent reasons or motivations”.

Bo argued that the US government “needs to raise money to keep its many activities going, including the war on Iran”. Furthermore, “it cannot rely on the bond market due to high interest rates – and consumer inflation already hit them hard in midterm election results”.

“Tariff money is one of the easiest ways to finance itself, rather than asking for more from Congress,” Bo told Al Jazeera.

Despite nearly a decade of the ongoing trade tensions between the US and China, Beijing’s global goods trade surplus reached a record $1.19 trillion last year, underscoring the scale of its export dominance. By comparison, the US ran a $1.24 trillion goods trade deficit over the same period.

“Nothing has changed substantially over the years,” he said, adding that “no new tariff will be effective to reduce the Chinese overcapacity at all, or in a significant way.”

Bo said he believes both China and the US are “working hard on the trade negotiations to de-escalate or mitigate” before the two leaders meet again next month, where they want to discuss issues like AI, nuclear weapons and the wars in Iran and Ukraine. “That’s a much bigger picture for them than a trade relationship,” Bo said.

For Beijing’s part, Herrero said that “China can still blunt” these new measures by the US.

“Rare earths remain its sharpest tool,” she added.

“The risk for Trump is the same as always: higher prices land on American consumers, and the wider trade system frays further,” Herrero said. “Whether that counts as a feature or a bug depends on how much pain Washington is willing to absorb.”

title: Gold rebounds after sharp sell-off as brighter stock market sentiment supports precious metals - MarketPulse
summary:
27 November 2026 at 13:27 UTC

Referenced assets

Gold prices rose on Friday, recovering some of the losses from a sharp sell-off that had pushed the metal to a 15-month low. Sentiment improved across global stock markets, and selling pressure eased as investors had less need to raise cash. Despite the gains, the outlook for precious metals remains uncertain, mainly because investors expect tighter US monetary policy.

Gold rose as much as 3.3% during Friday’s session, increasing its chances of ending the week higher. US stock index futures also gained, while Chinese stocks rallied after the government reaffirmed its readiness to provide further support for the country’s capital markets.

Daily chart of gold, source: OANDA TradingView

Although investors have traditionally viewed gold as a safe haven in times of heightened volatility, its price has largely tracked the stock market in recent months. One reason is that when stocks fall sharply, investors often sell precious metals to raise cash and meet margin calls on other positions.

The recent rebound in gold and silver prices illustrates how precious metals can serve as a kind of ATM for investors during market turmoil. A recovery in AI-related technology stocks and a growing appetite for risk have reduced the need to raise cash, easing pressure to sell precious metals.

Despite the recovery, the gold market remains unsettled. Gold has traded below $4,000 an ounce since November 11, and November looks set to be the third consecutive month in which the price falls by more than 5%.

The sell-off that began after January’s record high accelerated when war broke out between the United States and Iran, sending energy prices sharply higher. Expectations of tighter monetary policy from the US Federal Reserve and persistent uncertainty in global stock markets are also weighing on precious metals.

October figures for the core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, were released on Wednesday and reinforced expectations that the central bank would raise interest rates at its December meeting.

United States Core PCE Price Index Annual Change, source: TradingEconomics

Higher interest rates typically weigh on gold prices because they increase the opportunity cost of holding assets that pay no interest. Markets have probably already priced in a December rate increase in full. For precious metals, what may matter far more is what the Fed signals about the size and pace of any further monetary tightening in 2027.

summary:

"We're assuming that in 2027 we could remain durably above 3%," Nagel, who heads Germany's Bundesbank, told an event. "This means that, on the monetary policy side, we might have to do even more. We'll be meeting again in December."
