title: Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates)
summary:
27 November 2026

Agreement for Sweden to join T2

On 25 November 2026 the ECB announced that it had concluded an agreement with Sveriges Riksbank for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. More information is available in the press release issued at the occasion of the signing ceremony with ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen of the T2 currency participation agreement.

Acceptance of marketable assets issued on distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime as Eurosystem collateral

On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation (EU) 2022/858 and reachable via TARGET2-Securities (T2S) as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This decision is part of a roadmap exploring ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks. The decision is due to take effect in June 2027 and is explained in a press release available on the ECB’s website. It follows the ECB announcement of 27 January 2026 that marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using DLT will be accepted as collateral. These decisions testify to the Eurosystem’s commitment to aligning its collateral framework with advances in technology, while upholding the principles of adequacy of collateral, safety, efficiency and a level-playing field.

Financial Stability Review – November 2026

On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council held an exchange of views on the basis of the November 2026 edition of the Financial Stability Review and authorised its publication on the ECB’s website. In addition to providing an overview of key financial stability vulnerabilities in the euro area, this edition includes three special features. The first discusses the financial stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy and the financial industry. The second explores the complex interplay between AI and cybersecurity. The third assesses the financial stability implications of large initial public offerings and equity issuance in general, as well as how they both interact with the trend towards passive investing. The Financial Stability Review was published on 18 November 2026 on the ECB’s website, together with a related press release .

2026 study on payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area

On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council took note of the results of the 2026 study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area and approved its publication on the ECB’s website. The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. Moreover, while payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences nonetheless remain stable. The results of the study , together with a related press release , are available on the ECB’s website.

ECB Opinion on the supervisory independence of the Bank of Greece and prevention of conflicts of interest of its members of staff and governance body

On 4 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/33 at the request of the Greek Ministry of Economy and Finance.

ECB Opinion on designating the Deutsche Bundesbank as a recipient of administrative data for statistical purposes

On 10 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/34 at the request of the Deutsche Bundesbank on behalf of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy.

ECB Opinion on the competences of the Supervisory Board of the Magyar Nemzeti Bank

On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/35 at the request of the Hungarian Ministry of Finance.

ECB Opinion on a tax on excess profits of credit institutions and other specified companies

On 25 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/36 at the request of the Bulgarian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance.

ECB Recommendation on the external auditors of the Bank of Greece

On 5 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Recommendation ECB/2026/29 to the Council of the European Union on the external auditors of the Bank of Greece.

Eurosystem participation in Phase II of Project Agorá

On 18 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the participation of the Eurosystem – represented by the Banque de France – in Phase II of the BIS Innovation Hub’s Project Agorá which is due to run until December 2027. This ongoing Eurosystem participation in Agorá is without prejudice to any future policy decisions the Eurosystem may take on the possibility of providing central bank money on external or shared DLT platforms. At the invitation of the Banque de France and the ECB, other interested Eurosystem national central banks may join a newly established Eurosystem technical group to operationalise this participation in Project Agorá Phase II.

Disclosure of Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) methodologies

On 3 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish: the SREP 2026 methodology applied to significant institutions under the direct supervision of the ECB, the more detailed SREP methodology for operational risk and ICT risk, the more detailed SREP methodology for assessing capital adequacy, and the internal governance and risk management SREP methodology. The related press release, together with these four documents, is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

Results of the SREP 2026 exercise

On 9 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish the SREP 2026 aggregated results. Overall, these results show that the euro area banking sector has continued to be resilient in the face of the heightened uncertainty clouding the economic and geopolitical environment. The publication is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

Outcome of the 2026 risks and priorities exercise

On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish the outcome of the 2026 risks and priorities exercise, listing the supervisory priorities for the next three years (2027-29). The publication is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

2027 Supervisory Examination Programme (SEP) for on-site inspections and internal model investigations at significant institutions

On 16 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board concerning the 2027 SEP for on-site inspections and internal model investigations at significant institutions under European banking supervision. The on-site SEP is based on the SSM supervisory priorities for 2027-29 published on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

Less significant institution (LSI) supervision report 2026

On 23 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish a report on the supervision of LSIs in 2026. The report , which examines the structural features of the LSI sector, its key developments and major supervisory activities, is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

The streaming company also advanced its growth pipeline and repaid a significant portion of its credit facility .

For readers who follow Gold Stocks , Wheaton Precious Metals is a leading precious metals streaming company that provides upfront financing to miners in exchange for the right to purchase a portion of their gold and silver production at low fixed prices. The company is listed on the NYSE Composite .

Revenue grew strongly from a year earlier, driven by higher realized gold equivalent prices and more ounces sold. Net earnings and operating cash flow also rose. Earnings per share and revenue were slightly below some analyst estimates.

For the first nine months of the year, Wheaton reported record revenue, net earnings and operating cash flow.

In a streaming deal, Wheaton pays a mining company an upfront sum to help fund mine development or other needs. In return, it receives the right to purchase a share of the mines gold or silver production at a low, fixed cost per ounce. When metal prices rise, Wheatons margins expand significantly because its costs are fixed.

Unlike traditional miners, streaming companies do not operate mines, so they avoid direct exposure to rising labor, energy and equipment costs. This model provides high margins and steady cash flow, though it depends on partners operating their mines successfully.

Production grew strongly from a year earlier, helped by a new agreement with BHP for silver from the Antamina mine in Peru. Peasquito in Mexico produced record silver during the quarter. Contributions from newer assets also supported growth.

Wheaton highlighted progress across its growth pipeline, including first gold pour at Montage Golds Kon project in Cte dIvoire, construction approval at Hudbays Copper World project and first deliveries from Ivanhoes Platreef project in South Africa. The company has a large portfolio of operating mines, development projects and exploration-stage assets.

Wheaton repaid a substantial portion of its revolving credit facility during the quarter, reducing debt taken on to fund recent acquisitions. It continues to pay a quarterly dividend linked to its cash flow .

Silver makes up a large share of Wheatons revenue , nearly equal to gold. Silver prices have risen sharply this year, boosting Wheatons results. The new Antamina agreement with BHP adds significant silver production, increasing Wheatons exposure to silver at a time of strong prices.

Wheatons cash costs per ounce remain low because they are fixed by contract. With higher realized prices, its cash operating margin per gold equivalent ounce rose substantially from a year earlier.

Wheaton expects meaningful production growth over the coming years as development projects enter production. Its strong financial position allows it to pursue new streaming deals with miners seeking funding.

Wheaton offers exposure to gold and silver prices with high margins and lower operational risk than traditional miners. Its diversified portfolio and growth pipeline support long-term production growth.

When gold and silver prices rise, Wheatons fixed-cost structure allows its margins to expand more predictably than those of mining companies facing rising costs. This has made streaming companies popular with investors seeking precious metals exposure.

Risks include lower metal prices, operational problems at partner mines, project delays, geopolitical risk and counterparty risk.

Key indicators include gold and silver prices, production from new assets , growth project progress, debt reduction and new streaming deals.

Wheatons streaming model is delivering record results as precious metal prices rise. Its growth pipeline supports continued production expansion.

title: Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates) - European Central Bank
summary:
27 November 2026

Agreement for Sweden to join T2

On 25 November 2026 the ECB announced that it had concluded an agreement with Sveriges Riksbank for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. More information is available in the press release issued at the occasion of the signing ceremony with ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen of the T2 currency participation agreement.

Acceptance of marketable assets issued on distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime as Eurosystem collateral

On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation (EU) 2022/858 and reachable via TARGET2-Securities (T2S) as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This decision is part of a roadmap exploring ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks. The decision is due to take effect in June 2027 and is explained in a press release available on the ECB’s website. It follows the ECB announcement of 27 January 2026 that marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using DLT will be accepted as collateral. These decisions testify to the Eurosystem’s commitment to aligning its collateral framework with advances in technology, while upholding the principles of adequacy of collateral, safety, efficiency and a level-playing field.

Financial Stability Review – November 2026

On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council held an exchange of views on the basis of the November 2026 edition of the Financial Stability Review and authorised its publication on the ECB’s website. In addition to providing an overview of key financial stability vulnerabilities in the euro area, this edition includes three special features. The first discusses the financial stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy and the financial industry. The second explores the complex interplay between AI and cybersecurity. The third assesses the financial stability implications of large initial public offerings and equity issuance in general, as well as how they both interact with the trend towards passive investing. The Financial Stability Review was published on 18 November 2026 on the ECB’s website, together with a related press release .

2026 study on payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area

On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council took note of the results of the 2026 study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area and approved its publication on the ECB’s website. The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. Moreover, while payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences nonetheless remain stable. The results of the study , together with a related press release , are available on the ECB’s website.

ECB Opinion on the supervisory independence of the Bank of Greece and prevention of conflicts of interest of its members of staff and governance body

On 4 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/33 at the request of the Greek Ministry of Economy and Finance.

ECB Opinion on designating the Deutsche Bundesbank as a recipient of administrative data for statistical purposes

On 10 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/34 at the request of the Deutsche Bundesbank on behalf of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy.

ECB Opinion on the competences of the Supervisory Board of the Magyar Nemzeti Bank

On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/35 at the request of the Hungarian Ministry of Finance.

ECB Opinion on a tax on excess profits of credit institutions and other specified companies

On 25 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/36 at the request of the Bulgarian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance.

ECB Recommendation on the external auditors of the Bank of Greece

On 5 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Recommendation ECB/2026/29 to the Council of the European Union on the external auditors of the Bank of Greece.

Eurosystem participation in Phase II of Project Agorá

On 18 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the participation of the Eurosystem – represented by the Banque de France – in Phase II of the BIS Innovation Hub’s Project Agorá which is due to run until December 2027. This ongoing Eurosystem participation in Agorá is without prejudice to any future policy decisions the Eurosystem may take on the possibility of providing central bank money on external or shared DLT platforms. At the invitation of the Banque de France and the ECB, other interested Eurosystem national central banks may join a newly established Eurosystem technical group to operationalise this participation in Project Agorá Phase II.

Disclosure of Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) methodologies

On 3 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish: the SREP 2026 methodology applied to significant institutions under the direct supervision of the ECB, the more detailed SREP methodology for operational risk and ICT risk, the more detailed SREP methodology for assessing capital adequacy, and the internal governance and risk management SREP methodology. The related press release, together with these four documents, is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

Results of the SREP 2026 exercise

On 9 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish the SREP 2026 aggregated results. Overall, these results show that the euro area banking sector has continued to be resilient in the face of the heightened uncertainty clouding the economic and geopolitical environment. The publication is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

Outcome of the 2026 risks and priorities exercise

On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish the outcome of the 2026 risks and priorities exercise, listing the supervisory priorities for the next three years (2027-29). The publication is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

2027 Supervisory Examination Programme (SEP) for on-site inspections and internal model investigations at significant institutions

On 16 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board concerning the 2027 SEP for on-site inspections and internal model investigations at significant institutions under European banking supervision. The on-site SEP is based on the SSM supervisory priorities for 2027-29 published on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

Less significant institution (LSI) supervision report 2026

On 23 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish a report on the supervision of LSIs in 2026. The report , which examines the structural features of the LSI sector, its key developments and major supervisory activities, is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

title: Financial Stability in Focus: Outcomes of the FPC’s review of the bank capital framework - Bank of England
summary:
We use necessary cookies to make our site work. We’d also like to use some non-essential cookies (including third-party cookies) to help us improve the site. By clicking ‘Accept recommended settings’ on this banner, you accept our use of analytics cookies. For more information on how these cookies work please see our Cookie policy .

The FPC has completed its review of the bank capital framework – looking at how much capital the UK banking system needs and how the framework delivers it.

In recent years, the UK’s capital framework has helped banks meet the everyday needs of households and businesses and continue supporting the economy through material shocks. It has also underpinned investor confidence in the banking sector, as reflected in a fall in the premium investors require on bank equity relative to debt.

It is important that the capital framework adapts to reflect how the banking system has evolved and that it is adjusted where it can be made more efficient, effective and proportionate. The FPC’s capital review has sought and taken account of stakeholder feedback, evaluated how the UK compares to other major jurisdictions, and considered carefully and critically how the framework best serves the needs of the UK economy.

The FPC and the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) have proposed changes to capital requirements. And they are taking steps to enhance banks’ confidence in using their capital to support the economy.

Changes proposed as part of the review will make capital requirements for the banking system more proportionate, better targeted and – as a result – lower.

A series of policy changes have been put forward as part of the review over the past 12 months:

Taken together, the changes announced across the review as a whole will make the capital framework more proportionate by making requirements more evenly distributed across UK and international activity, and more targeted, for example by making the calibration of leverage requirements more closely linked to the financial market activity for which it is a key prudential constraint.

As a result of being more proportionate and better targeted, capital requirements will also be lower. While the reduced benchmark will give banks certainty that reductions in requirements that were already in train will endure, the further changes to leverage and risk-weighted requirements that have been proposed over the course of the review will reduce Tier 1 capital requirements for major UK banks by an amount equivalent to around 50 basis points of risk-weighted assets in normal times. There would be additional reductions in capital banks need to maintain through stress scenarios. The impact will vary by bank, depending on their business model. These measures will free up further capacity to lend to UK households and businesses.

The changes will maintain a level of resilience that balances the costs and benefits of bank capital to support sustainable growth. Capital requirements will also remain consistent with international standards and with international peers.

The FPC and PRA intend to enhance banks’ confidence in using their capital resources to support the economy.

Banks currently maintain capital in excess of UK regulatory requirements – sometimes worth several percentage points of risk weighted assets – driven by a range of factors including impediments to the use of regulatory capital buffers.

Regulatory capital buffers are intended to be used to absorb losses and to help maintain the provision of services to the real economy by reducing the need for banks to reduce lending to preserve capital during a stress event. But a range of interrelated factors can impede the usability of regulatory capital buffers in practice. These factors can also contribute to banks maintaining capital in excess of regulatory requirements.

To address these factors:

The changes announced as part of the review will allow the banking system to continue to support the economy in both good times and bad.

The FPC’s assessment of the appropriate level of capital requirements is set to maximise sustainable economic growth by balancing the macroeconomic benefits of fewer and less severe financial crises and the macroeconomic costs that can come about through higher borrowing costs. As such, it allows the banking system to support the economy in good times, while retaining the resilience to support the economy in bad times.

Taken together, the changes proposed in this review will deliver that resilience in a way which is more effective, efficient and proportionate and better calibrated to the risks in today’s financial system. The framework will retain key desirable features, including systemically important banks holding more capital than non-systemic banks and the ability to build and release capital requirements as the economic cycle evolves.

Lowering capital requirements much further would put financial stability, and hence sustainable economic growth, at risk.

Capital requirements will be reduced as a result of the changes set out in this review, but will remain consistent with the FPC’s benchmark of around 13%. That benchmark itself is towards the lower end of the range of capital requirements likely to maximise sustainable growth. It is also towards the lower end of the range of academic estimates of the optimal level of capital, in part because it takes into account other post-crisis reforms, such as the existence of an effective resolution regime and the FPC’s active use of the CCyB.

Were capital requirements to be reduced much further, that would put financial stability, and hence sustainable economic growth, at risk. Banks could lose market confidence more quickly when losses did arise, with consequences for their (and hence household and business) borrowing costs. Lower capital could also reduce the credibility of the resolution regime by reducing the overall capacity for losses to be absorbed without putting depositors or public finances at risk.

Materially lower capital requirements would also risk undermining international standards intended to promote financial stability and a level playing field. Since the UK is a global financial centre, and is therefore exposed to shocks from abroad, the UK depends upon other jurisdictions implementing robust standards. Were the UK to reduce capital requirements in a way that was significantly below those standards it would undermine UK authorities’ ability to promote a robust implementation of standards by others, and hence the competitiveness of UK financial services.

With this review complete, the FPC and PRA have begun to consult on the changes outlined above, with a view to implementing them as soon as possible.

As well as the consultation already launched to clarify that systemic buffers on domestic banks are releasable and explain its proposed release and rebuild approach, the FPC and PRA will launch further consultations on proposals to implement changes to the leverage ratio and Pillar 2A requirements in early 2027 and the first half of 2027 respectively. The FPC will consider the implications of the policy measures proposed as part of this review for the hurdle rate in the 2027 Bank Capital Stress Test ahead of its launch in Q1.

Prompt implementation of these changes will provide clarity and certainty to firms about the capital framework in the years to come. The updated capital framework will provide a strong core to support ongoing evolution in the prudential framework as part of the PRA’s strategic priorities of resilience, growth, innovation and transparency.

The reforms delivered through this review deliver meaningful change, remain consistent with international standards, and balance the costs and benefits of bank capital to support sustainable growth for the UK economy.

The UK banking system plays a vital role in the economy by providing lending and financial services to households and businesses.

In recent years, the UK’s capital framework has helped banks meet the everyday needs of households and businesses and be able to continue supporting the economy through material shocks – such as those related to Covid, the energy and supply shocks caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the turbulence associated with the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse. This is in contrast to the experience of the global financial crisis, when bank deleveraging significantly worsened the economic shock.

The capital framework has also underpinned investor confidence in the banking sector. Higher returns on equity – major UK banks have returned around £100 billion footnote [2] to shareholders through buybacks and dividends over the past three years – have supported a material increase in UK banks’ valuations. There has been a decline in the premium investors require on bank equity relative to debt funding, and major UK banks’ average price to tangible book (PtTB) ratio is well above 1.

In turn, high returns relative to the cost of capital has helped reinforce banks’ incentives to support the economy, including through periods of heightened economic uncertainty. For example, as set out in the November 2026 Financial Stability Report , bank lending to large and small businesses grew by 12% and 5% respectively in the year to Q3.

Ensuring an appropriately resilient financial system is the most important contribution the FPC can make to support economic growth. Financial stability underpins the continued provision of vital financial services and contributes to a stable and predictable economic environment. This in turn supports consumer and business confidence, facilitates investment that drives long-term productivity growth, makes the UK an attractive place to do business for international investors, and supports UK firms’ ability to compete abroad.

An appropriate level of capital helps ensure that the banking system is resilient – able to absorb rather than amplify shocks – so that it can continue to support UK growth, in good and bad times. Holders of bank capital are the first to bear the costs when a bank’s assets decline in value. This provides protection from losses to holders of some other types of liabilities, including depositors.

It is important that the level of capital requirements adapts to how the banking system has evolved, and that the capital framework is adjusted where it can be made more proportionate and better targeted. In July 2025, the FPC committed to reviewing the bank capital framework since it had been 10 years since the FPC’s initial assessment of the appropriate system-wide level of capital, and five years since it was last revisited. The review has sought and taken account of a wide range of stakeholder feedback, evaluated how the UK compares to other major jurisdictions, and considered carefully and critically how the framework best serves the needs of the UK economy.

The findings of the FPC’s capital review have been published in a series of Financial Stability in Focus (FSiF) publications.

This FSiF summarises the final area identified for review: capital requirements related to domestic exposures (Section 2). With the review now complete, the remainder of this section sets out the conclusions of the review overall, as well as plans for implementation of its proposals.

This review sits alongside other wider steps already being taken by the Bank and the PRA to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the prudential framework. In 2027, the PRA will set out its long-term strategy for delivering greater resilience, growth, innovation and transparency.

In December 2025, the FPC updated its benchmark for the system-wide level of Tier 1 capital requirements to around 13% of risk-weighted assets (RWAs). This is 1 percentage point lower than the previous benchmark of around 14%.

The 13% benchmark comprises a judgement on the underlying optimal level of 11% based on the range of capital requirements likely to maximise sustainable economic growth, and additional capital to account for outstanding gaps and shortcomings in the measurement of RWAs (of around 2% based on expectations for the level of Pillar 2A requirements after improvements in risk measurement from the implementation of Basel 3.1). It is equivalent to a Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio of around 11%. System-wide requirements include aggregate capital requirements and buffers for the major UK banks but exclude firm-specific PRA buffers and requirements set by overseas authorities, such as the international component of the CCyB. Within the banking system, in practice, there will be a distribution of capital requirements reflecting individual banks’ business models, their level of systemic importance, the degree of gaps and mismeasurement in their RWAs, and the PRA’s view of firm-specific risks.

The FPC’s assessment of an appropriate benchmark balances the macroeconomic costs and benefits of bank capital. Macroeconomic costs arise because loss-absorbing capital is a more expensive way for banks to fund lending than debt liabilities, which could mean higher capital requirements increase the cost of credit to the real economy and reduce household spending and business investment. Macroeconomic benefits arise as the likelihood and costs of financial crises, which tend to have very large and long-lasting negative effects on economic growth, are reduced.

The FPC’s assessment takes account of this trade-off, reflecting the level of capital it believes would be best for the wider economy by maximising sustainable economic growth. The FPC’s updated benchmark for systemwide Tier 1 capital requirements is towards the lower end of the 12%–16% range for optimal Tier 1 capital set out in previous Bank analysis. footnote [3]

The FPC’s updated judgement is consistent with the evolution in the financial system since its first assessment, including a reduction in the systemic importance of some banks and improvements in risk measurement.

In updating its benchmark, the FPC took account of how the banking system and the capital framework had evolved since previous assessments.

The FPC reviewed judgements underpinning past assessments about the effectiveness of post crisis reforms in capital requirements and the broader prudential framework. It continues to judge that they have reduced the probability and costs of future crises. Credible and effective resolution arrangements are expected to reduce materially both the probability of future financial crises and the economic costs of any future firm failure. Active use of the UK CCyB also continues to facilitate lower capital requirements outside periods of elevated risk. And forward-looking, judgement-led prudential supervision by the PRA helps ensure the safety and soundness of UK banks. Without the combined benefits of these elements, the FPC’s benchmark would be higher.

The FPC also took into account how the banking sector and capital framework has evolved. Some UK banks have become less systemically important over the past decade, meaning that systemic buffers are lower than envisaged at the time of the FPC’s initial assessment in 2015, contributing less to overall capital requirements than had been expected. The implementation of Basel 3.1 on 1 January 2027 will improve risk measurement, allowing the PRA to reduce minimum requirements for major UK banks by around ½ percentage point. Average risk weights had fallen since the beginning of 2016, such that the nominal level of capital consistent with the previous benchmark was around £60 billion less than would have been the case absent the fall in risk weights.

The FPC judged that these changes to capital requirements reflected the intended and desirable responsiveness of the capital framework to the evolution of the banking system, and that it was therefore desirable to update its benchmark rather than take action to restore actual capital requirements towards the previous benchmark. The change in the benchmark should therefore give banks the certainty that reductions in capital requirements that were already in train – arising from a reduction in systemic importance of some banks and improvements in risk measurement – will endure. In turn that should enhance banks’ confidence in using their capital resources to support the economy.

The FPC evaluated how UK capital requirements compared to international peers.

The Basel Committee sets a common baseline level of capital standards for internationally active banks. This enhances financial stability, especially for banks whose failure could have cross-border effects. It also helps maintain a level playing field for banks to be competitive internationally and aids comparability across banks in different jurisdictions.

Individual jurisdictions retain flexibility to tailor their implementation to reflect the nature of their banking systems and the risks they face. The existence of differences in capital requirements between the UK and other jurisdictions is therefore not reason for change in and of itself, but those differences should be well understood and justified by differences in risk.

Comparisons of capital requirements across jurisdictions is challenging. Analysis outlined in the December 2025 FSiF, based on requirements at the time, concluded that risk-based capital requirements for large banks in the UK were broadly similar to that in the euro area, and lower than in the US after adjusting for key differences in the way that risks are captured. However, leverage ratio requirements for large domestically focused banks were higher than in some other jurisdictions, which in turn informed the proposed changes to the leverage ratio.

The July 2026 FSiF considered stakeholder feedback received on comparing international capital requirements. It noted that while there were different ways of comparing regulatory frameworks, further consideration of how risks are captured in the US framework continued to suggest a sizeable adjustment for differences in approach to capturing these risks in capital requirements is appropriate when making comparisons between the two jurisdictions. It also noted that the PRA’s decision to maintain the requirement for full deduction of software assets from capital was based on evidence that the realisable or recoverable value of software assets could not absorb losses effectively in liquidation or stress. In addition, the July 2026 FSiF also summarised future changes to overseas capital frameworks which would likely bring US requirements closer in line with those applied in the UK and the EU.

As set out in this FSiF, following a review of risk-weighted capital requirements relating to domestic exposures, the PRA will consult on changes that would lower minimum requirements related to domestic lending.

Domestic-related capital requirements include the UK CCyB, other systemically important institutions buffers (O-SII buffers) and Pillar 2A capital for credit concentration risk. The FPC and PRC reviewed the role and calibration of the individual measures and judge that each domestic-related capital requirement fulfils a distinct and important role.

The Committees noted, however, that the sum of capital requirements for cyclical risk, geographic concentration and systemic importance tended to be higher for more UK-focused banks, compared to firms that were more internationally active. At the same time, results from recent stress tests had not suggested that banks which undertake a greater portion of their lending domestically were more exposed to cyclical risks than those that undertake more of their activity overseas. While these outcomes did not necessarily indicate a change in capital requirements was warranted, the FPC and PRC nevertheless considered it important to revisit the calibration of each component to ensure it remained appropriate in aggregate.

Following its review, the FPC supports two changes to the calibration of the framework:

The changes in respect of domestic-related requirements would reduce system-wide risk-based Tier 1 capital requirements by around 30 basis points, taking the system-wide level of Tier 1 capital requirements that count towards the FPC’s benchmark to 12.8%. For domestically focused systemically important banks, system-wide risk-weighted requirements would fall by 60 basis points, from 13.6% of RWAs to 13.0%. The reduction in Tier 1 requirements for ring-fenced banks, including the ring-fenced entities of global systemically important banks (G-SIBs), resulting from these changes is also expected to be around 60 basis points of risk-weighted Tier 1 capital requirements.

The FPC judged that these changes would make the distribution of capital more proportionate across UK and international lending while maintaining a level of resilience consistent with its benchmark for system-wide capital requirements of around 13%. The framework would continue to ensure that systemically important banks held more capital than non-systemic banks, that geographic concentration risk was reflected in capital requirements, and that releasable buffers were available to support lending to UK households and businesses in stress.

Section 2 discusses this work on capital requirements related to domestic exposures in more detail.

In July 2026, the FPC and PRA agreed to consult on a package of measures to make the leverage ratio framework more proportionate and better targeted.

Leverage ratio capital requirements are an important part of the capital framework and an effective complement to risk-weighted capital requirements. They make the system more robust against the inherent errors and uncertainties in measuring risk when assigning risk weights and help to curtail balance sheet growth that is unsustainable from a systemic perspective.

Over the past decade, leverage ratio requirements have become more binding, partly due to the fall in banks’ average risk weights. There is some evidence that this has been driven by a reduction in the underlying riskiness of banks’ exposures. But there has also been growth in more complex and opaque forms of lending where the leverage ratio may be particularly effective in guarding against errors in risk measurement. Declining average risk weights are to some extent to be expected in a framework with both leverage and risk-based capital requirements, as banks are incentivised to allocate capital and structure exposures to minimise their binding constraint.

The FPC’s review found evidence that the UK’s implementation of some elements of the leverage ratio framework had resulted in unintended consequences, particularly associated with the countercyclical leverage ratio buffer (the CCLB) and its interaction with the increase in neutral rate for the UK CCyB from 1% to 2% in 2019. In July, the FPC set out a package of measures that would address these unintended consequences and make the framework more proportionate and more effective by being better targeted. These measures include three elements:

The general leverage ratio buffer would be releasable, if necessary to zero, to help ensure that banks can absorb losses in an economic or financial market stress while continuing to support the real economy and the functioning of financial markets. If, on the other hand, the FPC were to in future judge that risks were heightened and that additional resilience was warranted, it could consider increasing the general leverage ratio buffer above 25 basis points. Like all buffer requirements in the UK capital framework, the general leverage ratio buffer would be met with CET1 capital.

In Q3, the FPC assessed the implications of this package on banks’ provision of market-based leverage and the resilience of core sterling markets. The FPC agreed to proceed with the proposed leverage ratio reforms having judged that market-based reforms would be the most effective means of ensuring risks to core sterling markets which could arise from increased market leverage were well managed. The Bank expects to consult on the leverage ratio package in early 2027 and intends to publish a Roadmap in the first half of 2027 setting out how it would take forward gilt repo market reforms.

The Bank would expect to adjust the leverage ratio hurdle rate in the Bank Capital Stress Test to take account of these proposals. Taken together, this package would reduce the leverage ratio that large UK banks need to maintain by around 20 basis points in aggregate, with the impact varying by bank. This would leave leverage ratio requirements for UK large domestically focused banks and G-SIBs within the range of other jurisdictions globally.

Banks currently maintain capital in excess of UK regulatory requirements – sometimes worth several percentage points of risk weighted assets, driven by a range of factors including impediments to the use of regulatory capital buffers.

Regulatory capital buffers are intended to be used to absorb losses and to help maintain the provision of services to the real economy in a downturn. Evidence from the Covid-19 pandemic suggests that releasing capital buffers can support the real economy by reducing incentives for banks to take defensive actions to preserve capital, such as deleveraging during stress.

But a range of interrelated factors can impede their use in practice, including the role of MDA restrictions and uncertainty around the supervisory response when buffers are used. This could encourage banks to prioritise maintaining capital ratios by procyclically reducing the supply of lending to creditworthy households and businesses in a stress, thereby amplifying shocks. This can also contribute to how much capital banks hold above regulatory requirements in normal times. Other contributing factors include investor and rating agency expectations, banks’ business models and strategic plans (including planned share buybacks or mergers and acquisitions activity), regulatory requirements set by overseas regulators and capital volatility.

As part of the capital review, the FPC and PRA have taken steps to increase banks’ confidence in using capital that would otherwise be held in excess of requirements. As set out above, the reduction in the FPC’s benchmark for the appropriate level of capital requirements is intended to give banks greater certainty that reductions in capital requirements that were already in train – arising from a reduction in systemic importance of some banks and improvements in risk measurement – will endure. In turn that should enhance banks’ confidence in using their capital resources to support the economy.

In addition, to address factors impeding the usability of regulatory capital buffers in practice:

These proposed changes build on wider steps already being taken by the Bank and the PRA to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the framework.

Proportionality is an integral part of the UK prudential framework and the Bank and the PRA have taken significant steps to ensure that prudential outcomes are achieved efficiently, avoiding unnecessary regulatory burden. Progress has already been made on a number of issues outside the capital review.

The Bank has moved to a biennial frequency for its main Bank Capital Stress Test, representing a reduced frequency compared to the annual cyclical scenario tests under the previous approach. This updated approach reflects the build up of capital since the global financial crisis and the need to be proportionate, yielding material efficiency gains. The Bank has also made changes to the Bank Capital Stress Test to avoid earlier loss recognition under the IFRS 9 accounting standard resulting in an unwarranted increase in capital requirements through its impact on stress test results.

The implementation of Basel 3.1 at the beginning of 2027 will deliver a better balanced and more risk-sensitive approach to calculating regulatory capital – aiming to support the resilience of the banking system, the UK’s growth and competitiveness, and alignment with global standards. The policy has been adjusted following feedback, in areas where the evidence received suggested too much conservatism in the PRA’s original proposals, or where the proposals would have been too difficult or costly to implement in practice. This has included adjustments to the treatment of SME and infrastructure lending and the calibration of certain off-balance sheet conversion factors.

title: THINK Ahead: The ECB’s new boss has timing on his side - ing think
summary:
Like most things in life, being a successful central banker is as much about timing and luck as experience and skill.

New ECB president Pablo Hernández de Cos has plenty of the latter. And whisper it, but his timing looks rather good, too.

Sure, on the face of it, the inheritance looks grim: inflation at 4%, high energy prices, wobbly stock markets and bond market tensions that haven’t exactly gone away. A December ECB rate hike looks inevitable. But how much of that will still matter when De Cos takes office in February?

By then, inflation may well be past the peak. Maybe it already is. November's unexpectedly soft French and Spanish figures point to a drop in next week's eurozone headline rate. Cheaper petrol is clearly part of this, but French services and Spanish core inflation point to reduced pressure elsewhere, too.

Admittedly, that doesn’t mean inflation is set to drop back immediately. Higher natural gas prices are only now reaching utility bills, which is likely to keep energy's overall contribution to inflation elevated into spring or early summer – even as the impact of high petrol and diesel prices should fade rapidly from March.

In the end, though, this is a bit of a moot point. Four per cent inflation may be an uncomfortable place for central bankers, particularly those who worry about its impact on consumer and business expectations.

But unless you think energy prices will start climbing again in the winter and next spring, then it’s only a matter of time before their impact on inflation starts to wane. Our forecasts have headline inflation undershooting the ECB's target in the second half of 2027.

What really seems to matter now for officials is not so much the level of energy prices at any given time, but what they tell us about the uncertainty surrounding the Iran war. Andrew Bailey at the Bank of England has made it clear this latter point will have a strong bearing on its December decision.

The ECB and BoE rate hikes so far have been partly justified as an insurance against the tail risk that things get very ugly in the energy markets.

Those tail risks do tentatively seem to be fading, though. Sure, a lasting US-Iran agreement feels like a long shot right now. Yet Middle Eastern oil has continued flowing despite attacks on shipping and threats to infrastructure. The longer that continues, the less plausible the worst-case scenarios become, even without a peace deal. I’d argue central bankers should already be starting to think this way at their December meetings.

That thinking is already playing out in energy markets, too. Notwithstanding market moves over the past few days, November has seen a sharp drop in the risk premium baked into crude oil prices. Barring renewed escalation, our energy team expects European gas prices to almost halve by the second quarter, with Brent crude below $80/bbl.

Then there are second-round effects, which are still conspicuous by their absence. Barring the slight increase in core inflation so far, there’s still no strong sign that higher energy prices are bleeding out across the inflation basket. My measure of inflation in energy-intensive categories has still not risen this year:

The ECB seems to agree with this assessment, but officials understandably want more evidence. Firms may have been better placed to absorb the initial shock than in 2022, while gas prices have only recently risen more sharply. The hawks would argue that this resilience can only last so long without companies putting up prices.

But fast-forward another three months, when De Cos takes office, and those arguments will start to look a little thin if there’s still no sign of inflationary pressure outside of energy.

There are two things in particular I’d keep an eye on before then. One is food, where inflation has started to inch higher off a very low base. But neither producer nor import prices point to an imminent spike. Yes, some agricultural commodities are 10-15% above February levels, not helped by this summer's drought. But that's offset by fertiliser prices, which have reversed their initial war-driven surge.

And while we’re on the topic of commodities, industrial metal prices are down on pre-war levels, while shipping costs seem to have peaked too. That should keep a lid on core goods prices.

Then there are wages, which also offer little evidence of a broader inflation problem so far. Inflation categories (mostly services) that are sensitive to wage growth have not accelerated this year. The ECB's negotiated-wage tracker does not suggest a material pickup in 2027, either, although plenty of these deals are still yet to be agreed.

Needless to say, none of this guarantees an easy presidency. De Cos will have to decide early on whether another rate hike is needed in March (we currently think it won’t), while navigating an increasingly fraught European political backdrop. Still, he may find that the hardest part of the current inflation fight is already behind him. And for a new central banker, a little bit of good timing never hurts.

James Smith

title: Trump tariffs brought EU and Indonesia closer, minister tells Euronews - Euronews.com
summary: US tariffs pushed the EU and Indonesia closer as they negotiated a trade deal, Indonesia's economy minister told Euronews in an exclusive interview.Airlangga Hartarto expects the deal, signed in Brussels on Saturday after a decade of talks, to lift trade between the two sides by 50% within three years.Asked whether US President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs had helped bring the talks to a close, Hartarto said: "I think there is an impact of the parallel negotiation with the US". Jakarta has been negotiating tariffs with Washington alongside its talks with Brussels.The EU and Indonesia struck a political agreement in July 2025, two days before Trump announced a deal setting a 19% US tariff on Indonesian goods. On Wednesday, Washington proposed new tariffs on some goods from 14 trading partners, including the EU and Indonesia.EU-Indonesia goods trade was worth €28.9 billion last year, according to the European Council. The minister said the 50% goal had been discussed with EU partners and business groups from both sides.He called the two economies "not competing but compatible", since they make different products and can meet each other's needs.Investor confidenceHartarto also played down a downgrade warning from MSCI, whose stock indices are tracked by funds worldwide.In October, the index provider proposed downgrading Indonesia from "emerging" to "standalone" status, which would remove Indonesian shares from its emerging markets indices. It plans to decide by the end of June 2027.Jakarta's benchmark stock index, the IDX Composite, has fallen roughly 38% this year.The minister likened the warning to a broken window. "So basically this is an issue of a window that is broken by somebody, right?" he said.Asked whether he meant that everything looks broken to investors through that window, he agreed and said Indonesia's economy was in better shape than the MSCI warning suggested.He described Indonesia's growth as "one of the highest" in the G20. The economy grew 5.45% in the first nine months of 2026 from a year earlier, according to Statistics Indonesia, the national statistics agency.Jakarta is reforming its capital market to improve transparency, he added.Hartarto also said next week's New Asia Forum, an investment conference in Bali, could yield deals worth up to $30 billion (€27.4bn). "I think the potential of $30 billion is there," he told Euronews.That figure is the forum's target for the whole region. Danantara, the Indonesian sovereign wealth fund backing the forum, expects that about 40% to 50% will go to Indonesia.Indonesia plans more of these events to promote investment, including one with the EU that the minister has discussed with EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.Chip ambitionsMathias Cormann, Secretary-General of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), launched two reports in Jakarta this week as Indonesia aims to join the Paris-based group of mostly wealthy economies by 2028.According to the minister, one report looks at how Indonesia can benefit from the digital economy by developing semiconductors. The other, the OECD's latest economic survey, found Indonesia would need growth averaging 5.8% a year for 20 years to become a high-income country by 2045.On current productivity trends, though, growth would slow to about 3.5%, the OECD warned. The minister said the 5.8% figure was in line with the government's plans, in which chips play a big part."Indonesia has already made a contract with Arm," he told Euronews as an example of the moves the country is making to become a bigger player in the global AI economy.Danantara signed a framework agreement with the British chip designer in London back in February.Through the agreement, Indonesia is training up to 15,000 engineers in AI and semiconductors and will acquire six pieces of chip-design intellectual property, the minister said.Year-end deadlinesIndonesian exporters face two deadlines at the turn of the year.From 30 December, the EU's twice-delayed deforestation regulation (EUDR) will require large and medium-sized companies to prove that palm oil, coffee, cocoa, rubber and other goods they sell in the EU were not produced on land deforested after 2020.According to the minister, the rules were discussed separately from the trade deal.Indonesia is ready to comply, he said, but has asked for schemes such as its own national Indonesian Sustainable Palm Oil (ISPO) certification to count towards compliance. That request is still being discussed, he added.On 1 January, Indonesia also leaves the Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP), under which the EU cuts tariffs for developing countries. Exports that currently benefit from the scheme will then face standard EU duties until the trade deal applies.Hartarto is confident the agreement will be in place in time. He said it was being brought to the European Parliament "so that on the first of January next year it will be implemented".Indonesia's embassy in Brussels has been in contact with several MEPs, who have given strong support, according to the minister.The Parliament's legislative tracker lists 14 December, the first day of its last plenary session of the year, as a provisional date for its vote. The file is still at the preparatory stage, and the Parliament said on signing day that the exact timeline had not yet been agreed. MEPs cannot amend the deal, only approve or reject it.Once both sides have completed their internal procedures, the deal will apply provisionally, likely in early 2027, according to the European Commission.

title: Crude oil prices near $97 as West Asia tensions revive supply fears; OPEC+ meeting in focus - The Economic Times
summary: Crude oil prices climbed to their highest level in nearly three weeks on Friday, putting Brent crude on track to snap a three-week losing streak, as escalating geopolitical tensions in West Asia raised concerns over disruptions to global oil supplies. The rebound comes ahead of a crucial OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29, where producers are expected to discuss their 2027 output strategy.Brent crude futures rose 0.8% to $97.30 a barrel on Friday, their highest level since November 9, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures gained 2.6% to $85.85 a barrel compared with Wednesday’s close, according to Reuters. There was no settlement for WTI on Thursday because of the US Thanksgiving holiday.The rally follows a sharp recovery in prices over the past few sessions, driven by fresh attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Middle East. Brent had fallen below $88 a barrel earlier in the week as concerns over an emerging global supply surplus outweighed geopolitical risks.The latest escalation has brought the possibility of supply disruptions back into focus. Yemen’s Houthi militants claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery, one of the kingdom’s largest refining facilities and a major crude export hub. The group also claimed attacks on other Saudi targets.Separately, Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery temporarily suspended some operations after a projectile struck the facility on Thursday, killing a worker and injuring several others, according to the kingdom’s Energy Ministry.Shipping activity through the Strait of Hormuz has also come under pressure. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two tankers had exploded and caught fire after striking sea mines near Oman’s Khasab port while attempting to cross the strait. The waterway is a critical transit route for global energy supplies, carrying a substantial share of the world’s seaborne oil trade.The attacks have raised concerns that the recovery in crude exports from the Persian Gulf could be disrupted, adding a geopolitical risk premium to oil prices. Analysts at ANZ said Brent could move above $100 a barrel, although such a move would increasingly require evidence of an actual constraint on deliverable supplies.Also Read | MCX silver prices hit 6% upper circuit at Rs 1.54 lakh/kg. Why are people buying the white metal on Black Friday?However, expectations of ample global supplies continue to limit the upside in crude prices. Brent remains significantly below its levels earlier in the month, despite the recent rebound. The International Energy Agency has flagged the possibility of a supply surplus in the fourth quarter, while expectations of rising production have weighed on market sentiment.US crude inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, according to the Energy Information Administration. The increase was smaller than analysts’ expectations of a 1.5-million-barrel build, offering some support to prices.OPEC+ meeting in focusInvestors will now turn their attention to Sunday’s OPEC+ meeting, where member countries are expected to review production policy for 2027. The group is likely to maintain its existing output targets through at least the first quarter of next year, according to sources cited by Reuters.The meeting comes amid competing pressures for the producer alliance. While geopolitical disruptions have increased near-term supply risks, concerns about a potential global surplus could make producers cautious about raising output.Oil prices will depend on whether the latest geopolitical developments translate into sustained supply disruptions or remain largely a risk premium in futures markets.

title: China Has More Than Enough Energy to Weather the Winter - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: China has enough thermal coal, natural gas, and enough reliable power backup to meet peaks in winter demand, Chinese state-owned news agency Xinhua reports. The State Grid Corporation of China anticipates a peak load of 1.24 billion kilowatts kW this winter, up by 72 million kW from a year earlier, while its peak reliable supply capacity is estimated at about 1.3 billion kW, a 90 million kW increase year-over-year. The rise in supply capacity has exceeded the increase in peak load, which should be enough to meet peak demand, Xinhua says. China’s coal supply is also sufficient to meet peak thermal power demand as domestic production has rebounded from the lows in the spring and summer following the deadliest mining disaster in years in May 2026. Natural gas supply will also meet demand, despite the falling LNG imports, due to rising cheaper domestic supplies and sluggish industrial growth. Japan is expected to overtake China as the world’s largest LNG importer this year, for the first time since 2022, as high spot LNG prices and comfortable storage levels in China limit purchases, analysts say.    Current weather models predict a milder winter for China, but with more frequent short-lived cold snaps. Unlike China, Europe faces the winter months with decade-low gas inventories and will have to pay up for spot LNG supply to meet winter demand.   The Chinese pullback from LNG imports could be welcome news for Europe, which needs to compete with Asia for spot supply in the absence of most of Qatar’s LNG cargoes and the ban on imports of Russian LNG taking effect on January 1. Europe’s benchmark gas prices have eased from the four-year high of over 100 euros per MWh in late October, but they are still nearly triple compared to $33 30 euros per MWh at this time last year. By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

title: Japanese Yen slips as calmer equity markets lifts US Treasury yields - www.tmgm.com
summary:
USD/JPY edges higher on Friday as a calmer mood in stock markets lifts risk appetite, helping US Treasury yields and the US Dollar (USD) regain ground after the recent tech sell-off. At the time of writing, the pair trades around 159.50 and is on track to end the week higher.

As equities stabilise, demand for government bonds fades. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield climbs to around 4.91% after touching a more than two-month low of 4.80% on Wednesday. Its Japanese counterpart trades near 2.63%, keeping the yield gap in the US Dollar’s favour.

The US Dollar Index (DXY), which tracks the Greenback’s value against a basket of six major currencies, trades around 103.93, up 0.13% on the day and still close to Monday’s 20-month high of 104.53.

Expectations of further Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hikes also support the Greenback. Traders have fully priced in a rate hike in December and expect more increases in early 2027 after several Fed officials warned that inflation remains too high and signalled that tighter policy may be needed to bring it back to 2%. Attention now turns to next week’s US Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) report for clues on the timing and pace of further hikes.

Meanwhile, the Bank of Japan (BoJ) remains on a tightening path, but expectations of further rate hikes have offered little support to the Yen as interest rates abroad remain well above Japan’s.

Analysts at Danske Bank highlight that “in Japan, Tokyo core inflation excluding fresh food rose to 2.9% y/y in November (cons: 3.0%, prior: 2.6%), its fastest pace since July 2025.” They note that “the increase was partly driven by the end of government utility subsidies, but prices also rose across a broad range of goods and services,” pointing to a more broadly based rise in inflation rather than a purely policy-driven effect.

Danske Bank adds that “JPY weakened modestly after the release, but overall, the print still supports the case for a rate hike at the BoJ's meeting on 17-18 December, with focus now turning to Governor Ueda's speech on Monday for hints on December and the future rate path.”

While the wide interest rate gap between the US and Japan continues to favour the Greenback, traders may be reluctant to take aggressive bullish positions in USD/JPY near the 160.00 mark, given the risk of another intervention by Japanese authorities.

The table below shows the percentage change of Japanese Yen (JPY) against listed major currencies today. Japanese Yen was the strongest against the Swiss Franc.

The heat map shows percentage changes of major currencies against each other. The base currency is picked from the left column, while the quote currency is picked from the top row. For example, if you pick the Japanese Yen from the left column and move along the horizontal line to the US Dollar, the percentage change displayed in the box will represent JPY (base)/USD (quote).

title: Oil Surge Pushes Indonesia to Mull First Subsidized Fuel Price Hike in Years - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: Indonesia, the largest economy in Southeast Asia, has discussed hiking the price of subsidized fuel for the first time since 2022, as the weakening local currency and persistently high oil prices weigh on government outlays for funding the subsidies. Indonesia, the world’s fourth-most populous country, hasn’t removed or reduced subsidies for gasoline and fuel amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis. The country, a net oil importer despite having domestic oil production, has subsidized fuel in one form or another since it gained independence in the 1940s. This year, the spike in oil prices has significantly raised the government’s spending on subsidizing fuels and keeping them well below market rates. Currently, gasoline and diesel are being sold in Indonesia at about half and less than a third, respectively, of their fair-value price. As a result, Indonesia’s budget has been strained, its currency, the Indonesian rupiah, has crashed to an all-time low against the U.S. dollar, and the stock market tumbled amid loss of investor confidence. Indonesia is now reportedly considering hiking the price of subsidized fuel in early 2027, in what would be the first such move since 2022, state officials and industry sources told Reuters on Friday. Indonesia last week held a meeting to discuss a potential price hike for subsidized fuels. The meeting included representatives of the economy ministry, state energy giant Pertamina, and Bank of Indonesia, the central bank, according to Reuters’ sources. However, no decision on whether to hike fuel prices has been reached at the meeting. The size of a potential increase hasn’t been discussed, either, the sources told the publication. Due to the spike in international crude oil prices, Indonesia’s government will have to spend as much as $27.2 billion 500 trillion Indonesian rupiah on fuel subsidies this year alone. The sum would be 30% higher than the original estimate for subsidies before the Iran war hit oil supplies and hiked international oil and fuel prices. By Charles Kennedy for Oilprice.com

title: Gold price today jumps 4% as metals rebound from 52-week lows - TradingView
summary:
The gold price today jumped 4% on Friday, November 27, 2026, extending a sharp rebound from this week's 52-week low as buyers returned to precious metals in thin post-Thanksgiving trade.

COMEX gold February futures (GCG2027) traded at $3,708.40 an ounce at 09:29 UK time, up $143.80 from Wednesday's settlement of $3,564.60.

What happened to the gold price today?

The rally came in two bursts during Asian hours. February gold climbed from about $3,600 at 01:45 UK time to $3,664.20 by 02:35 UK time, then spiked to $3,693.90 at 05:30 UK time.

It went on to touch $3,712.80, the session high, around 09:00 UK time. At $3,708.40, the contract is 7.4% above Wednesday's low of $3,453.80, reached at 15:15 UK time.

The expiring December contract (GCZ2026) was at $3,680.40, up 4.1%. It set a 52-week low of $3,425.20 on Wednesday.

Why is the gold price rising today?

There was no single trigger. The move was part of a broad rebound across metals and risk assets.

COMEX silver jumped more than 10%, and March copper rose 5.1%.

S&P 500 E-mini futures were up 1.9% from Wednesday's settlement.

China added a tailwind. At 12:25 Beijing time (04:25 UK), the government published a State Council statement pledging new measures to steady the stock market and "ample liquidity" via state fund Central Huijin.

Gold's second leg higher came about an hour later, during the afternoon session in China. The Shanghai Composite closed 3.7% higher at 3,606.49, while the tech-heavy ChiNext jumped 11.6%.

The usual drivers do not explain the move. The US dollar index was little changed at 103.83, and the 10-year Treasury yield was 4.92%, up from 4.86% on Wednesday.

What happens next for gold?

Rate expectations have not shifted. A 25 basis point Federal Reserve hike at the December 8-9 meeting traded at 93 cents (93%) on Kalshi at 09:30 UK time.

That matters because gold pays no interest. Higher rates raise the cost of holding it, which helped drive last week's sell-off.

US markets close early today, with the NYSE shutting at 13:00 ET (18:00 UK time), so liquidity may stay thin. The next big test is the November jobs report on December 4 at 13:30 UK time.

Traders will watch whether February gold can hold above $3,600, the level it traded around for most of Thursday.

title: Kyiv offers Black Sea ceasefire, as Putin expands Russia’s navy - Al Jazeera
summary:
Ukraine has presented a proposal for a possible ceasefire in the Black Sea, as Kyiv seeks to protect its grain exports amid escalating attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the proposal on Friday during the “Food from Ukraine” conference, saying Kyiv was ready to restore freedom of navigation and ensure the uninterrupted export of agricultural products.

“We are now awaiting a response from Russia. All of our proposals have been conveyed,” Sybiha said.

Moscow has sought to include oil transportation in the proposed ceasefire deal, but the Ukrainians say that issue belongs in a broader energy ceasefire.

He accused Russia of repeatedly putting forward “unrealistic demands” in response to Kyiv’s proposals, according to Suspilne, Ukraine’s national broadcaster.

The Ukrainian proposal was being considered, as Russian President Vladimir Putin attended a flag-raising ceremony for a new nuclear-powered submarine, which Moscow claims is the first to be equipped with Russia’s Zircon hypersonic missile. Putin said he was confident that plans to build a powerful naval force would be implemented on time and in full, Russian news agencies reported.

Previous attempts at a ceasefire

The latest ceasefire initiative comes amid growing international concern over the security of commercial shipping and global food supplies. Ukraine and Russia are both major agricultural exporters , and attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have disrupted shipments transiting through the Black Sea.

A previous UN- and Turkiye-brokered agreement allowed Ukrainian grain exports to resume following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

However, Moscow withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, prompting Kyiv to establish an alternative maritime export corridor.

In August, Reuters reported that Ukraine had conveyed an earlier proposal through a third party for both sides to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. At the time, Ukrainian grain exports had fallen 76 percent year-on-year, as shipowners avoided ports in the Odesa region following repeated Russian strikes.

International efforts to secure a limited ceasefire have since gained traction.

On October 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was reviewing proposals from Turkiye and India to facilitate uninterrupted grain and energy shipments.

The diplomatic impasse also comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his frustrations with US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.

In an interview with the BBC on Friday, Zelenskyy criticised Trump for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” following their meeting in China last week.

“It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” Zelenskyy said.

He also criticised Washington for what he described as excessive neutrality in its dealings with Moscow, arguing that the US should use its influence to pressure Russia into meaningful negotiations.

“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor … it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.

After talks in Florida on Wednesday, the NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called on Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and urged a peaceful resolution as soon as possible.

Rutte has also stressed that any eventual peace agreement or long-term ceasefire must include security guarantees for Ukraine.
