title: US to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized factories - The Miami Times
summary:
President Donald Trump speaks during an event to announce new tariffs in the Rose Garden at the White House, April 2, 2025, in Washington.

The Trump administration announced a set of broad new tariffs Wednesday on imports from China, the European Union, Taiwan and 11 other countries in response to their alleged overproduction of factory goods that have disadvantaged American firms.

The new tariffs are also intended to help replace the revenue lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that President Donald Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, told CNBC that many U.S. trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”

The proposed duties range from 15% to 35% and could cover roughly three-fifths of U.S. imports, though the administration also proposed exemptions for products such as semiconductors and other high-tech goods from Taiwan and South Korea, which are crucial to the artificial intelligence buildout.

While sweeping, the tariffs largely replace those first imposed last April and should have a modest impact on inflation and growth, economists said.

The duties “were widely expected, are relatively small, and would return us roughly to where we were earlier in the year,” Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics, said.

Yet the announcement demonstrates the Trump administration’s willingness to continue imposing tariffs even after voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. About two-thirds of voters said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll , a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.

Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy.

“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this — they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

The administration will next seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing January 25, suggesting the duties won’t take effect until February or March.

Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the Finance Committee next year, said he will “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”

“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”

Still, any effort to overturn them faces steep odds , even after Democrats take control of both chambers in January. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

The small business advocacy group We Pay the Tariffs, which urged Congress to roll back all tariffs after the election, slammed Wednesday’s maneuver.

“Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses,” Dan Anthony, executive director of the group, said in a prepared statement. “Customers can’t afford more price increases, but small businesses can’t afford to absorb tariffs on top of tariffs either.”

The levies will be imposed pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 , which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.

The administration said the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes .

Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after trade talks stalled. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

Brazil’s government expressed indignation over the proposed tariffs and threatened retaliatory measures.

“The USTR’s unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process,” it said in a statement. “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat.”

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”

For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

The U.S. and China last year reached a trade truce that is set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30 billion worth of Chinese goods in line with the truce.

Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could come up again.

On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs again stated its opposition while calling for the U.S. to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Some analysts criticized the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behavior.”

Goldman Sachs calculates that the proposal would return most tariffs on the affected countries to where they were before the Supreme Court ruling in February. Goldman also estimates that if implemented, the import taxes would increase the overall U.S. tariff rate from 7.8% to 9.2% and have “a very small incremental impact” on inflation.

The new import taxes are targeted to specific products and would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

Nor would they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.

Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. Two other countries face pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.

The USTR posted extensive reports on each country’s alleged unfair trade practices, with the report on China reaching 456 pages. The Section 301 law requires specific analysis of each country’s trade practices to pass legal muster.

Wednesday’s duties will likely face legal challenges, as Trump’s forced labor tariffs already have. At least some of the forced labor duties could be overturned, said Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and former official in Trump’s first term who also served in the Biden administration, because the USTR didn’t provide extensive evidence for each of the 60 countries affected by those duties.

title: Iran says oil tanker explodes after hitting naval mine in Strait of Hormuz; oil price continues to rise - The Star
summary:
THE MIDDLE EAST (Bernama-Anadolu): Iran said on Friday that an oil tanker exploded after striking a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, while another tanker was forced to turn back, Anadolu Ajansi (AA) reported, citing Iran's Fars news agency.

It also meant oil prices were set to snap a three-week losing streak on Friday, riding four sessions of gains, as attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure fanned concerns over Middle East supplies.

Brent crude futures edged up 3 cents to US $96.60 a barrel by 1239 GMT. Brent hit its highest since November 9 earlier in the session, but stayed shy of the $100 mark.

US West Texas Intermediate crude futures at US$85.14 a barrel were up $1.46, or 1.7%, from Wednesday's close. There was no Thursday settlement for WTI because of the US Thanksgiving holiday.

In a statement carried by the news agency, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said two oil tankers attempted to "secretly pass through an unauthorised route north of Ghavam Island on Friday morning."

One of the tankers exploded after colliding with a naval mine, while the other was forced to turn back, the statement said.

The IRGC Navy did not identify the tankers or provide details about their crews, possible casualties or the extent of the damage.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate with attacks on Israeli and US military facilities in Arab countries.

Tehran and Washington signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but its implementation stalled over disagreements about freedom of navigation through the strait.

Tehran has repeatedly linked reopening the waterway to its demands for an end to US and Israeli hostilities, security guarantees against renewed attacks, and the lifting of US sanctions and restrictions on Iranian ports.

Reuters reported that prices have retreated in recent weeks as investors were relieved that US President Donald Trump did not step up military action on Iran after the midterm elections.

However, Iran has continued to attack ships transiting the key waterway of the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting oil exports, while Yemen's Houthis have struck Saudi Arabian infrastructure.

"(The) price in the Bay of Oman currently seems to signal that there is ample supply of crude oil available. But assuming that this is a stable status quo is probably a faulty assumption," said SEB analyst Bjarne Schieldrop.

"Add in the Houthis and what they do to Saudi Arabia and their semi-control of the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, and you may not want to sit short oil, to put it mildly."

Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery temporarily halted some operations after a projectile struck it on Thursday, killing a Nepali worker, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said.

The strike was the latest blow to key Saudi facilities, a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom's largest refinery and a major crude export hub.

OPEC+, which includes Saudi Arabia and Russia, has an agreement in principle to maintain oil output targets for at least the first quarter of 2027 at a meeting on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the talks said.

Separately, 10 people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the US administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year and blocked Venezuela from paying its membership dues.

Ukraine has intensified drone attacks on Russian oil refineries since the end of October, with the latest incident causing a fire at the Slavyansk ECO refinery in Russia's southern region of Krasnodar.

Separately, fires disrupted activity at Thailand's Bangchak refinery and Venezuela's Amuay refinery on Thursday.

title: NASA Wanted a 100-Kilowatt Reactor on the Moon but Is Settling for 20 - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
summary: In August 2025, Washington promised a 100-kilowatt nuclear reactor on the Moon by 2030, ahead of China and Russia. "We're in a race to the moon, in a race with China to the moon," NASA's then-interim chief Sean Duffy said, warning that whoever landed a reactor first could declare a "keep-out zone" around it. But the reactor NASA put out to bid on November 23 is one-fifth that size. Lunar Reactor-1 LR-1 will generate 20 kilowatts, enough for about 16 American homes, and it will run on high-assay low-enriched uranium HALEU, a fuel the Energy Department says US suppliers can't yet provide. Duffy's target was more than double the 40-kilowatt designs NASA had been funding, and experts doubted it. Katy Huff, the Energy Department's former top nuclear official, said she found "no evidence" that anyone had thought about the 100-kilowatt figure "beyond it being bigger." In an earlier interview, she said going from 40 to 100 kilowatts "is not a matter of simply turning up the knob." Randy Bell of the Aerospace Corporation said a 100-kilowatt reactor would be very large and difficult to land, TechTimes reported. In April, the White House lowered the target. A memo on space nuclear power set the 2030 lunar reactor at a minimum of 20 kilowatts and pushed the 100-kilowatt version into the 2030s, without saying why. NASA wants bids by December 21 for a reactor that is ready to launch by 2030 and can run for five years without maintenance. Related Goldman Sachs Sees U.S. Natural Gas Demand Surging on Data Center Boom The reactor has to survive more than two weeks of total darkness at the lunar south pole, keep running after any single failure, and operate with little contact from Earth. It also has to be shielded so astronauts a kilometer away get no more than 5 rem a year of extra radiation, according to Nuclear Newswire. Companies that win the contract get 18 months to build and test a non-nuclear version. The real reactor won't run at power until it reaches the Moon. Russia and China are aiming later. Roscosmos chief Yury Borisov said in 2024 that the two countries plan to install a power plant on the Moon around 20332035. In December 2025, Roscosmos hired the Russian space contractor Lavochkin to build one by 2036, with Russia's state nuclear company Rosatom involved, to power the China-led lunar base Russia has joined. Neither country has said how big it will be. NASA plans to spend $20 billion over seven years on a base near the lunar south pole with habitats, pressurized rovers and nuclear power, and it plans to launch the base's first element in December. SR-1 Freedom, a 20-kilowatt nuclear-electric spacecraft bound for Mars, is due to fly in 2028 and will supply data for LR-1's design. "SR-1 Freedom is our Nautilus, and she will launch in 2028," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in October. Fueling the reactor may be harder than building it. HALEU is uranium enriched to between 5% and 20%, richer than ordinary reactor fuel. Russia's state nuclear company Rosatom has been the only commercial seller, and China can also make it at scale, according to POWER magazine. The United States has no commercial supply. The Energy Department says HALEU is "not currently available" from US suppliers, so it is drawing the fuel for NASA's 2028 Mars spacecraft from government stocks, including material held by the nuclear weapons agency. It has not said where LR-1's fuel will come from. In January, Washington committed $2.7 billion to domestic uranium enrichment, including $900 million to Centrus Energy, which expects to produce new HALEU in Ohio by 2029. The Government Accountability Office warned in August that production "is unlikely to scale quickly enough" to meet demand. That leaves NASA's reactor depending on a fuel plant not expected to be online until 2029, a year before the reactor is due on the launch pad. By Charles Kennedy for Oilprice.com

title: Russia Extends Jet Fuel Export Ban Until March 2027 - The Moscow Times
summary:
An airport fuel truck fills up a passenger plane.

Gazprom Neft

The Russian government announced Friday that it will extend its ban on jet fuel exports until the end of March 2027 as the domestic energy market continues to feel the strain from Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries.

Russia first banned jet fuel exports in June following Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries that led to slumps in domestic production and localized shortages. That embargo was set to expire on Monday, Nov. 30.

The extension of the ban runs from Tuesday, Dec. 1 until March 31, 2027.

Exceptions are made for international intergovernmental agreements, as well as humanitarian aid shipments and supplies to the Russian military, Baikonur spaceport in Kazakhstan and Russian operations in the Svalbard archipelago off Norway.

Three additional exemptions are marked “for official use” in the published decree signed by Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.

Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak acknowledged earlier this week that the situation in Russia’s domestic fuel market remains “quite tense” due to ongoing repairs of several major oil refineries.

“There’s definitely a deficit, which is being covered by external supplies,” Novak told reporters on Wednesday, adding that fuel is being imported from both neighboring and distant countries.

He said authorities will decide next month whether to continue importing gasoline in 2027 and extend current gasoline export restrictions, which expire in January.

“It will depend on the ability to process [fuel] and supply the domestic market,” Novak said.

title: China Challenges Mexico’s Tariffs as Trade Talks Continue - Mexico Business News
summary:
Join our expert contributor program

China has called on Mexico to reconsider its tariff policy and avoid external interference in bilateral trade, following talks between officials from both countries in Beijing. At the same time, Mexico is seeking to reduce its trade deficits with China and Asia-Pacific economies by expanding export access, strengthening rules of origin and promoting joint manufacturing projects.

“The proposal is to reduce this disparity between imports and exports decisively and quickly,” Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said during the 11th meeting of the Mexico-China High-Level Working Group, according to El CEO .

China’s Ministry of Commerce spokesperson He Yadong responded that Beijing opposes unilateral tariff increases and wants commercial differences addressed through dialogue. He also urged Mexico to avoid what he described as interference from third parties, a reference to the United States and its efforts to restrict Chinese goods entering North American supply chains.

The discussions take place as Mexico maintains tariffs of up to 50% on selected imports from countries without a free trade agreement with the country. The measures, which took effect in January 2026, cover 1,463 tariff lines across 17 sectors, including automotive, steel, aluminum, plastics, textiles, footwear, appliances and consumer goods.

The policy forms part of the federal government’s efforts to strengthen domestic production and reduce reliance on imports. It also comes amid US pressure for Mexico to tighten controls against the transshipment of Chinese goods through its territory ahead of the review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

However, the tariffs have not eliminated Mexico’s dependence on Chinese suppliers. A Mexico Business News report published in July found that China remained Mexico’s second-largest trading partner, with a 12-month trade deficit of US$123.3 billion in April 2026, based on Banorte estimates. Electronics, telecommunications equipment and machinery represented a significant share of imports.

A separate Mexico Business News analysis published in August examined conflicting trade figures. While China’s Ministry of Commerce reported a 28.4% annual decline in imports from China between January and May, separate Mexican trade data showed imports from the country increasing by 5.23% between January and April, reaching US$42.85 billion. The difference highlights the need to distinguish between data sources, periods and product categories when assessing the effects of the tariff policy.

Mexico’s discussions with China also focus on expanding access for Mexican agricultural and food products. During the Beijing meeting, Ebrard asked Chinese authorities to accelerate pending export protocols for products including avocados, lemons, beef, pork, sorghum and processed aquatic products. According to El CEO, Mexican exports to China reached US$11.1 billion between January and September 2026, while imports from China totaled approximately US$106 billion over the same period.

The government is also seeking to diversify trade relationships through the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), known in Spanish as TIPAT. At the agreement’s ministerial meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, Ebrard reported that Mexico exported US$31 billion to member economies between January and September 2026, compared with imports exceeding US$88 billion. The resulting deficit surpassed US$57 billion, according to Milenio .

Mexico proposed strengthening rules of origin and product traceability to prevent illegal transshipment, while encouraging joint investment and production arrangements in electronics and digital industries. These proposals aim to increase the participation of Mexican companies in regional supply chains rather than relying exclusively on tariff measures to address trade imbalances.

China and Mexico have also agreed to establish a working group to discuss tariff reduction, according to China’s Ministry of Commerce . The discussions will test whether both governments can address market-access concerns while maintaining their respective trade policies.

title: International Oil Prices Drop Despite Middle East Supply Concerns... Brent Falls 1.2% : Finance : JKN - 재경일보
summary:
Oil prices fall despite Middle East supply concerns; Brent drops 1.2% (Photo: Yonhap News)

International oil prices fell on the 27th despite ongoing concerns over crude oil supply disruptions in the Middle East. Brent crude closed at $95.44 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) closed at $83.08.

Brent crude rose 3.1% for the week, marking its first weekly gain in four weeks, while WTI fell 0.4% over the same period.

International oil prices moved as the market weighed supply forecasts and the policies of oil-producing countries, even amid rising tensions in the Middle East. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has previously raised the possibility that the global oil market could return to a supply surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Incidents threatening the supply of crude oil and petroleum products continue to occur across the Middle East. Attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz by Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabian energy facilities by Yemen's Houthi rebels have increased anxiety regarding maritime transportation and production and refining facilities.

The Saudi Arabian Ministry of Energy announced on the 26th that the Jazan refinery facility suffered a fire following an attack by a hostile aerial projectile. The fire was extinguished, but one Nepalese worker was killed, several others were injured, and operations at some facilities were temporarily suspended. The Saudi side identified the Houthis as the perpetrators of the attack.

The IEA assessed that energy transport disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz have continued through November, and that supply risks occurring in the Middle East, the Red Sea, and Russia are simultaneously impacting the international energy market. Global oil supply in October increased by 2.3 million barrels per day from the previous month to 105.4 million barrels, and crude oil exports from the Gulf region also partially recovered.

Market attention is focused on the 42nd OPEC and non-OPEC ministerial meeting to be held on the 29th. OPEC previously decided to maintain December oil production at the levels required for September 2026, and there are expectations that this meeting will result in maintaining production targets for the first quarter of next year at current levels.

OPEC has pointed out that attacks on energy infrastructure and disruptions to international maritime transport routes could increase supply security concerns and market volatility. While the IEA analyzed that Gulf region exports have not yet fully recovered to pre-war levels, it forecasted that market supply and demand conditions could change if the increase in supply continues.

summary: Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, vowed on Friday to break the US blockade, according to Iranian state media."Neither will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened, nor will we allow the blockade to remain in place," state media reported Mokhber as saying. title: Russia Extends Jet Fuel Export Ban by 4 Months Until March Next Year - news.sbs.co.kr
summary: ▲ A Russian oil refinery burning from a Ukrainian airstrike (File Photo) The Russian government announced that it has extended the jet fuel export ban, originally set to expire on November 30, by four months until March 31, 2027. The export restriction also applies to fuel purchased through exchanges, but does not apply to supplies under international intergovernmental agreements. This measure was taken to stabilize the domestic fuel market, which has been destabilized by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refining facilities. "This decision was made to maintain a stable situation in the domestic fuel market," the Russian government stated. Previously, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak acknowledged the tight fuel market situation on November 25, saying that "the situation in the fuel market is urgent with a number of refineries undergoing repairs." At the time, Deputy Prime Minister Novak said that in addition to extending the jet fuel export ban, the government would review next month the extension of the gasoline export ban, which is currently set to run until January 31 of next year. Although Russia is the world's second-largest crude oil exporter, it has already been importing gasoline from countries such as India, Kazakhstan, and Turkey due to unstable energy supply and demand. Deputy Prime Minister Novak stated that fuel imports will continue at least until the end of the year, depending on crude processing capacity and domestic market supply conditions. title: OPEC+ set to keep oil output targets steady amid Iran war uncertainty - Iran International
summary:
OPEC+ has reached a preliminary agreement to keep oil production targets unchanged in the first quarter of 2027 amid uncertainty over the Iran war and disagreements over members’ production capacity, Reuters reported Friday.

In a televised interview earlier this week, Pezeshkian said he wore a jacket because his office was cold, slept wearing one at home and would move to a smaller room if temperatures fell further to save energy.

What supporters portray as personal austerity and solidarity with the public has become a political controversy, with some critics comparing the president's gestures to the populist style of former president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.

Tabnak, a news website close to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, published an article titled "Mr. Pezeshkian, Your Dark Room Is a Display of Weakness."

The article acknowledged that the president presumably intended to demonstrate solidarity with Iranians facing difficult conditions and encourage energy conservation.

"But does staging a blackout in the president's workplace, especially when the country remains engaged in a difficult and costly war, really send the right message to society and beyond its borders?" it asked.

The website argued that a country at war and resisting foreign pressure should project effective management and strength.

‘Have a wonderful winter’

The conservative newspaper Farhikhtegan also criticized Pezeshkian in an article titled "The Wrong Signal from the Dark Room," describing the gesture as a staged performance. Instead of communicating "resistance," it argued, the president had conveyed "shortage" and "passivity."

Farhikhtegan also cited Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's readiness to reopen the Strait of Hormuz for two days as another example of what it called the government's "message of weakness."

Hardline analyst Ali Abdi questioned the president's public presentation during a roundtable discussion in a video published Friday by Hokmranan Online.

"Have people ever seen pictures of Putin or Zelensky sitting in a dark room after five years of war?" he asked.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appeared to seize on the images, sharing a Washington Post report about Pezeshkian's dimly lit, unheated office with a mocking message on X.

"Good job, guys. Have a wonderful winter," Bessent wrote.

‘Populist behaviour’

The controversy has revived comparisons with former president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, who cultivated an image of modest living and informality as part of his populist appeal.

Similar comparisons emerged in November last year after photographs showed Pezeshkian playing soccer alongside members of Iran's national team at the country's National Football Center.

The news website Rouydad24 argued at the time that the episode might appear to be a friendly encounter with players but, viewed alongside the president's other public appearances, revealed a pattern.

"The more critical the country's situation becomes, the more populist President Pezeshkian's behavior becomes," the website wrote.

‘Being honest’

Government officials defended the president's gestures as an appeal for energy conservation during wartime.

Spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani described his conduct as courageous and honest, saying it demonstrated the need to conserve energy under difficult conditions.

Elias Hazrati, head of the government's Information Council, said Pezeshkian had turned off the lights to encourage conservation, strengthen economic resilience and help the country withstand pressure from Trump and the United States.

The president did not need to sit behind a desk in a hall filled with chandeliers to demonstrate Iran's greatness, Hazrati argued.

The reformist newspaper Sazandegi offered a broader defense in a Wednesday editorial titled "The Neorealist President."

It argued that Pezeshkian's behavior reflected honesty and a refusal to mislead the public. His jacket, remarks about energy conservation and dimly lit office challenged a longstanding tradition in Iranian politics of concealing uncomfortable realities while projecting an image of perfection.

"His primary responsibility is to see reality, not conceal it, be honest with the people, and have solutions for overcoming the situation—and to implement those solutions with all his strength and capacity," the editorial said.

“We know how heavily high prices and instability weigh on your lives,” Abdolnaser Hemmati wrote in an open letter to Iranians. “People have the right to be worried, to ask questions and to demand results from officials.”

Hemmati said sanctions and the US naval blockade had made trade more expensive and restricted Iran’s access to its financial resources. Those pressures, together with the strain on state revenues, were affecting both the exchange rate and the prices Iranians pay, he said.

Two days earlier, Hemmati had credited central bank intervention with keeping the currency market relatively stable over the previous two months. The dollar crossed 2.9 million rials that day, up from about 1.6 million in early April. By Friday, the rial had lost about 45% of its value against the dollar over that period.

“The foreign currency constraints are real,” Hemmati wrote, though he rejected the suggestion that Iran had reached a deadlock. He also dismissed talk of an imminent economic collapse, saying the central bank had supplied more than $32 billion in foreign currency for imports through official channels. He gave no timeframe for the figure.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in an interview with Iran International last month, warned Iranians to stock up on gasoline and heating fuel ahead of expected shortages, predicting the economy would shrink by more than a quarter in the year ending March 2027.

“I would predict that from March of '26 until March of '27, the economy would contract more than 25 percent, which is more than the Soviet Union contracted after its collapse,” Bessent said, adding that the campaign was intended to pressure Iran's leadership rather than its population.

On Thursday, Iraqi forces closed Sheikh Saleh, a crossing in Iran's western Kermanshah province, the Mehr news agency reported, citing the governor of Salas-e Babajani county. He said Baghdad had acted on a central government order to shut "unofficial" crossings with neighboring countries.

About 300 trucks loaded with goods and building materials were stranded, Kermanshah's customs chief said, and would be rerouted through other crossings.

The same day, Iraq's border forces closed the Bashta crossing with Iran and the al-Waleed crossing with Syria, both run until now by the Kurdistan Regional Government, Reuters reported, citing Iraqi state media.

There were unconfirmed reports that a third crossing, Shoushmi, in Kermanshah's Paveh county, had also been shut. Kermanshah's customs chief said he had received no official notice of it.

Washington asked for this. On November 8, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said the US Treasury had formally asked Baghdad to close all its crossings with Iran except two, one in the Kurdistan region and one elsewhere in Iraq.

"There are many official and unofficial crossings with Iran, and closing them all is difficult and affects our economy," he told Al Jazeera.

Trade between the two countries is worth $15 billion to $18 billion a year, he said, including about $4 billion in Iranian gas.

The day before, US Central Command had set up Task Force Iron Gate, a unit of about 20 military and civilian staff in Florida, to disrupt the movement of weapons, dual-use technology, sanctioned goods and illicit revenue across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Without US personnel at the crossings, it relies on neighboring governments, chiefly Iraq, Turkey and Pakistan, to do the closing.

Iraq and Iran share a border of about 1,600 kilometers, with nine official crossings and many unofficial ones. Over the past six weeks, Baghdad has closed and reopened them one by one, usually citing technical reasons.

On October 21, Iraq closed Chazabeh, known in Iraq as Sheeb, between Iran's Khuzestan province and Iraq's Maysan, citing inadequate preparations.

An adviser to Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said Iran had "deliberately undermined Iraq's security," with people linked to it crossing without permits.

Truckers and traders in Maysan protested over rising prices, and the provincial council chairman, who threatened civil disobedience, was briefly detained. Chazabeh reopened on November 10.

On November 13, Iraq closed Somar, known in Iraq as Mandali, between Kermanshah and Iraq's Diyala province, for what it called maintenance before the rainy season. It is still closed.

On November 26, Sheikh Saleh and Bashta followed.

Major crossings such as Mehran, which carries millions of Iranian pilgrims to Karbala each year, remain open.

With its ports under US naval blockade since July and seaborne oil exports all but stopped, Iran depends more than ever on land routes for imports, exports and cash.

Iraq is one of Iran's largest export markets, its biggest buyer of gas and electricity, and a long-standing route around sanctions, through fuel smuggling, currency trading and companies fronting for Iranian interests.

Pro-Iran factions in Baghdad have pushed back. The Badr Organization's bloc in parliament condemned what it called American interference in Iraq's border policy and demanded the crossings reopen, and the Asaib Ahl al-Haq bloc asked why the government's technical explanations differed from the foreign minister's account.

The Revolutionary Guards dismissed Iron Gate, saying Tehran had made arrangements to keep trading with its neighbors.

The pressure comes from more than one direction. Iraq's oil revenues still pass through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, an arrangement dating from the 2003 US-led invasion, and Washington warned Baghdad this year that it could cut off access to them if Iraq did not reduce Tehran's influence in its government, Reuters reported.

US officials also discussed with Zaidi the idea of Iraq leaving OPEC, Reuters reported. The prime minister raised it with his cabinet, but the oil ministry opposed it and proposed seeking a higher production quota instead. The US government said the issue had not been raised in high-level talks.

The closures in the Kurdistan region are also part of a separate fight. On Tuesday, Zaidi ordered federal authorities to take over all crossings run by the Kurdistan Regional Government, and the federal oil ministry to take over oil fields held by Kurdish security forces in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces.

After the Kurdistan Regional Government objected, Iraq's Federal Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that Baghdad could deploy federal forces along all international borders, including in the region.

Thousands of people protested in the Kurdistan region on Thursday, while supporters of the prime minister rallied in Mosul.

The moves came a week after Zaidi sent troops into Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah, over an oil smuggling network.

Not all of Baghdad's moves answer to Washington. The operations against smuggling, the push into Jurf al-Sakhar and the takeover of the Kurdistan region's crossings and oil fields also concentrate power in the central government, a goal that overlaps with US demands but is not the same thing.

Both standoffs turn on control of oil, borders and the money that flows across them, and both put Zaidi, who came to power after Washington opposed the return of Nouri al-Maliki, a longtime ally of Tehran, at odds with powerful forces at home.

Iraq cannot easily cut its ties with Iran. It depends on Iranian gas and electricity, particularly in summer, and Iran-aligned factions sit in parliament, in the governing coalition and in the Popular Mobilization Forces, the state-funded umbrella of armed groups. Moving against them too fast risks unrest at home.

Even Iranian media now describe a shift. Baghdad "appears to be redefining its relations with Tehran," the Iranian news site Rouydad24 wrote on Thursday, in a course that is "less a separation than an effort to increase Iraq's bargaining power with both sides."

Tehran says it can ride out the squeeze. Iran's diplomats, especially in neighboring countries, were working "around the clock" to meet the country's needs and keep trade routes open, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in the northeastern city of Mashhad.

"The goal is for the enemies to know that besieging Iran is not possible, and that they cannot besiege our country," he said.

They describe a range of domestic measures as “self-sanctions,” pointing to restrictions on foreign currency transactions, banking and customs procedures, and price controls that make it more difficult for businesses to operate.

The criticism has taken on renewed significance as Iran faces restrictions on maritime trade and oil exports. Critics say the government has focused on the consequences of external pressure while doing too little to strengthen domestic production or expand trade through land borders and barter arrangements.

On Wednesday, Hassan Ghashghavi, the spokesman for parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, urged the government to support producers during what he described as an “existential war.”

Manufacturers, he said, need access to foreign currency and raw materials to stay in business and avoid bankruptcy.

“Given the existing capacities, the country’s main problem is not a lack of resources but weak management,” Ghashghavi said.

‘Domestic sanctions’ on producers and exporters

Amir Sayyah, an economic advisor to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf during 2024 presidential debates, told the state TV that the government is making it harder for Iranian entrepreneurs and exporters to operate under already difficult conditions.

“The biggest problem with our economy, apart from foreign sanctions – and I’m not denying foreign sanctions – is domestic sanctions,” Sayyah said on the Be Vaghte Iran (Iran Time) TV debate.

“Whoever can negotiate should go and resolve [the foreign sanctions]. Whoever can find a way around them should do so. But as for domestic sanctions ... if [the enemy] is stabbing us from the front, the government and all these executive agencies should not stab [producers and exporters] in the back.”

Sayyah argued that Iranian businesses could maintain production, trade and financial transactions despite international sanctions if domestic authorities gave them room to operate.

He said currency exchange companies were capable of transferring money from countries such as the United States to destinations in Europe, the Middle East and East Asia, but that the government had failed to make use of their services.

Easing administrative and regulatory restrictions, he argued, would allow businesses to operate more freely without waiting for foreign sanctions to be lifted. He said it would also strengthen Iran’s economic position in any negotiations with Washington.

One of the main obstacles facing exporters, according to Sayyah, is the requirement to bring their foreign currency earnings home at exchange rates set by the central bank. Those rates can put exporters at a financial disadvantage, he said, discouraging them from bringing their earnings back and reducing the supply of foreign currency at home.

“An exporter who earns foreign currency for the country despite sanctions should be regarded as part of the national effort to counter the blockade, rather than being treated as a violator by government agencies,” he said.

Sayyah said the administration of former President Ebrahim Raisi and the parliament at the time had removed some regulations that hampered producers and exporters, but that the work had stalled under Pezeshkian.

Government faces criticism over its economic response

Pezeshkian has repeatedly spoken about the difficulties posed by what he calls economic warfare, arguing that they are more complicated than those of military confrontation.

He has pointed to a shortage of funds and to shortfalls in electricity and natural gas supplies that are expected to lead to scheduled power cuts this winter.

The president has backed diplomacy, arguing that ending the current state of “neither war nor peace” is necessary to ease economic pressure and uncertainty.

His government has drafted next year’s budget around two scenarios, reflecting uncertainty over how long the maritime blockade will last.

The first assumes that current conditions will persist, requiring sharp spending cuts and a halt to new infrastructure projects. Under that scenario, the government would reserve all available foreign currency for essential goods and medicine.

The second envisages the lifting of restrictions and a gradual recovery in the supply of foreign currency, allowing the government to resume reconstruction and infrastructure projects.

Conservative and hardline critics have taken issue with how often the president and his ministers discuss the country’s economic difficulties. They argue that repeated warnings about electricity and gas shortages, scheduled power cuts and limited funds frighten the public and reinforce what they describe as Washington’s psychological warfare.

Hardliners have urged the government to do more to counter the blockade by expanding barter trade and helping domestic producers make fuller use of their capacity.

Imports and non-oil exports fall

The value of Iran’s non-oil exports fell 28.2% between the beginning of April and the end of August compared with the same period a year earlier, according to Foroud Asgari, head of Iran’s Customs Administration. Non-oil exports were down 32.5% from the corresponding period in 2024, before the war.

Imports fell from $23.02 billion to $17 billion, a 26.1% decrease from a year earlier. Compared with the same period in 2024, imports were down 38%, a steeper decline than for non-oil exports.

A substantial share of Iran’s imports consists of raw materials, intermediate goods and machinery used by domestic manufacturers. Economists warn that reduced access to those goods could further undermine production in an economy already under pressure from sanctions and the blockade.

Limits of land routes

Economist Mohammad-Mehdi Behkish has argued that the blockade presents a problem beyond the financial obstacles Iranian businesses faced under previous sanctions.

Even when importers find a way to transfer payments to foreign suppliers, they still face the challenge of getting the goods into the country, he said.

Iran has traditionally conducted a substantial share of its foreign trade by sea. Its land routes have limited capacity and cannot handle the volume of goods previously carried by ship, Behkish argued.

IRNA called the practice, known in Iran as zirmizi, or "under the table," a possible form of "modern-day extortion" that exploits patients' dependence on their doctors and their fear of losing treatment.

Patients have reported demands for hundreds of millions of rials for routine operations such as removing an appendix or tonsils, and several billion rials for specialized treatment such as bone marrow procedures, IRNA said. One hundred million rials is about $36, and 3 billion rials about $1,070, at a time when the monthly minimum wage is about 166 million rials, or $59.

The payments fall outside insurance and can bypass hospital accounts through cash, personal bank accounts, intermediaries and installments. Patients have told Iran International that some doctors demanded cash or gold coins before performing surgery.

Fear of delayed surgery, retaliation or losing follow-up care keeps many patients from reporting unauthorized charges, which weakens a system of oversight that depends on formal complaints.

Many cases referred to the Government Discretionary Penalties Organization end in acquittal for lack of evidence, such as missing receipts, Deputy Health Minister Sajjad Razavi told local media last month.

There are no reliable figures, said lawmaker Mohammad Jamalian, who heads a parliamentary committee investigating the payments, because so few violations lead to complaints.

In August, the head of the Medical Council, Mohammad Raeeszadeh, cited a survey of more than 60,000 people in which only 5.6 percent said they had paid above approved rates. IRNA questioned the survey's method and whether it counted payments that went unreported.

Iranian patients are paying 55 to 75 percent of their healthcare costs out of pocket this year, and some medicine prices have risen 400 to 500 percent, Hosseinali Shahriari, chairman of parliament's Health Committee, said in September.

Nearly half of those who answered a voluntary Iran International audience survey from October 30 to November 3 said they had postponed treatment or medication because of rising prices. Rising costs have also pushed patients from private hospitals into overstretched public ones.

Much of the strain comes from the state itself. Hospitals and doctors say official tariffs are too low to cover costs, and some state-run basic and supplementary insurers are seven to eight months behind on their payments, Raeeszadeh has said.

None of that justifies unlawful charges, IRNA said, adding that fixing medical pricing and health financing was the job of policymakers, not patients. It called for insurers to pay on time, for transparent hospital billing, for protection for patients who report violations, and for disciplinary cases to be made public.

title: [MARKET UPDATE]: Dollar climbs, weighing on precious metals; Crude also pressured amid lack of clear catalysts - Newsquawk
summary:
: Dollar climbs, weighing on precious metals; Crude also pressured amid lack of clear catalysts.

Episodes in which a firmer dollar leans on the precious complex and crude sells off without a discrete driver have tended to resolve as positioning and funding events rather than a change in underlying fundamentals, and they have a history of reversing once the currency impulse fades. The transmission for metals runs through the real rate and FX channel, since non-yielding assets are marked against the dollar; for crude the linkage is looser, more a function of broad risk tone and the absence of a supply catalyst than of the exchange rate itself, which is the distinction that matters when judging persistence. The worth watching element is whether the dollar bid reflects rate repricing at the front end or a defensive flow, as the former tends to leave a longer tail on metals than the latter. On previous occasions of this kind, confirmation has come from the term structure and inventories rather than the headline move. In the absence of a named catalyst the signal is directional and low conviction by construction.

title: Chinese biz community urges US to withdraw proposed tariffs - chinadailyhk
summary:
BEIJING – The Chinese business community has urged the United States to withdraw its proposed additional tariffs on China and 13 other economies following a Section 301 investigation into alleged "structural excess capacity" in manufacturing sectors, the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT) said on Friday.

The Office of the United States Trade Representative recently announced findings of its Section 301 investigation and proposed imposing additional tariffs on 14 economies, including China.

"The Chinese business community firmly opposes this," a CCPIT spokesperson said, adding that the community rejects the claim of "structural excess capacity" as a false narrative and opposes the US side using the allegation as a pretext to interfere in normal China-US economic and trade exchanges.

Assessments of industrial supply and demand conditions should take into account factors including global market demand, technological progress and investment cycles, the spokesperson said.

Trade surpluses are shaped by multiple factors such as the international division of labor, market demand and macroeconomic conditions, and trade surpluses alone are insufficient to determine structural excess capacity.

Tariff wars and trade wars benefit no one, the spokesperson said, adding that broad-based tariff hikes will push up procurement costs for US downstream enterprises, place additional burdens on consumers and disrupt global industrial and supply chains.

The Chinese business community calls on the US to withdraw the proposed tariff measures and resolve relevant issues through consultations with China on the basis of equality, respect and mutual benefit, to maintain stable and sound China-US economic and trade relations, the spokesperson said.

The CCPIT will continue to follow the concerns of Chinese and US enterprises and foster practical cooperation and communication among the business communities of China, the US and other countries, added the spokesperson.

title: Why is the Japanese Yen weakening as calmer equity markets push US Treasury yields higher? - www.tmgm.com
summary:
Improving risk appetite supports a modest rise in USD/JPY on Friday, with calmer stock markets allowing US Treasury yields and the US Dollar (USD) to recover following the recent technology-led sell-off. Trading near 159.50 at the time of writing, the pair remains on course for a weekly gain.

Demand for government bonds is easing as equity markets find their footing. Having hit 4.80% on Wednesday, its lowest level in more than two months, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen to around 4.91%. The corresponding Japanese yield stands near 2.63%, leaving the yield differential supportive of the US Dollar.

At around 103.93, the US Dollar Index (DXY) is 0.13% higher on the day and remains within reach of Monday’s 20-month peak of 104.53. The index measures the Greenback against a basket of six major currencies.

Further support for the Greenback comes from expectations that the Federal Reserve (Fed) will raise rates again. Following warnings from several Fed officials that inflation is still too high and that tighter policy may be required to return it to 2%, traders have fully priced in a December rate hike and anticipate additional increases in early 2027. Next week’s US Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) report is now in focus for indications of when, and how quickly, further hikes may follow.

Although the Bank of Japan (BoJ) continues to tighten policy, expectations of additional rate increases have done little to underpin the Yen. Interest rates outside Japan remain substantially higher.

A broader rise in inflation, rather than an effect driven solely by policy, is highlighted by analysts at Danske Bank. They observe that “in Japan, Tokyo core inflation excluding fresh food rose to 2.9% y/y in November (cons: 3.0%, prior: 2.6%), its fastest pace since July 2025.” Explaining the underlying drivers, they note that “the increase was partly driven by the end of government utility subsidies, but prices also rose across a broad range of goods and services,” indicating that price pressures have become more widespread.

On the market reaction and policy outlook, Danske Bank says that “JPY weakened modestly after the release, but overall, the print still supports the case for a rate hike at the BoJ's meeting on 17-18 December, with focus now turning to Governor Ueda's speech on Monday for hints on December and the future rate path.”

The risk of renewed intervention by Japanese authorities may discourage traders from building aggressive bullish USD/JPY positions close to 160.00. This caution persists even as the sizeable US-Japan interest rate differential continues to support the Greenback.

title: Oil prices reverse course and fall ahead of deadline: OPEC+ grapples with the quota allocation problem. - Vietnam.vn
summary:
(Dan Tri Newspaper) - Ahead of the crucial OPEC+ meeting on November 29th, crude oil prices unexpectedly fell despite fluctuating supply from the Middle East. Internal quota disputes are casting a dark shadow over the market.

At the close of trading on November 27th (early morning of November 28th in Vietnam time), world oil prices continued to cool down. Despite the persistent warning signs of supply disruptions in the Middle East, international investors are now focusing all their attention on the OPEC+ alliance's production policy negotiations.

According to Morningstar, on the ICE Futures exchange, Brent crude oil futures for January 2027 fell 1.2% (equivalent to $1.13), to $95.44 per barrel. However, overall for the week, Brent crude oil prices still maintained a 3.1% increase, breaking the previous three-week slump.

Meanwhile, on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), WTI crude oil prices fell 0.7% to $83.08 per barrel, completing a fourth consecutive week of declines with a 0.4% drop.

World crude oil prices are under pressure to adjust ahead of the key OPEC+ policy meeting (Photo: ScanX).

The decline in crude oil prices is occurring amid renewed risks of infrastructure disruption in the Middle East. The Saudi Arabian Ministry of Energy confirmed that the Jazan refinery, owned by Aramco, was attacked on November 26th, causing a fire that killed one worker and forced several units to temporarily shut down for safety inspections. Simultaneously, incidents targeting oil tankers continue to occur in the waters around the Strait of Hormuz.

According to preliminary data from commodity analytics firm Kpler, crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have now plummeted to only 31% of their previous normal levels. Alex Booth, research director at Kpler, points out that while Iraq's exports remain generally stable, delays in many shipments scheduled for November and December are raising concerns about the reliability of the short-term supply chain.

Despite the ever-present risk of localized shortages driving up risk costs, the oil market has been dominated by concerns about oversupply for almost a month. Phil Flynn, senior market analyst at Price Futures Group, noted that oversupply pressure has weighed on oil prices for the past four weeks. However, incidents targeting Saudi Arabian infrastructure and the Strait of Hormuz are bringing risk-off factors back into the market.

Investors are awaiting production decisions at the OPEC+ meeting on November 29th. At the event, the alliance will discuss its production policy for 2027, as the current agreement is set to expire at the end of this year. Three sources close to the matter told Reuters that OPEC+ is likely to opt for the safe option of maintaining production quotas for the first quarter of 2027 rather than making significant adjustments to current levels.

The biggest sticking point right now lies in the issue of allocating sustainable quotas to each member. Notably, according to Oilprice, Iraq is actively negotiating to raise its production ceiling. Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said the country needs a higher quota to find more funding for energy infrastructure development. Baghdad wants future quotas to be calculated based on a capacity of 6 million barrels per day, instead of the current 4.431 million barrels per day.

Nevertheless, Iraq's aspirations faced a major obstacle when an independent assessment unit appointed by OPEC+ estimated its actual production capacity at only about 4.9 million barrels per day. This result significantly narrowed Baghdad's negotiating advantage.

Observers have also noted speculation that the US had encouraged Iraq and Venezuela to leave OPEC after the UAE withdrew from the organization in May due to disagreements over quotas. However, the Iraqi Ministry of Oil chose to remain and negotiate its interests instead of leaving.

Barbara Lambrecht, an analyst at Commerzbank, predicts that the weekend meeting may end without a definitive decision, forcing the group to maintain its current quotas. With the exception of Iraq, most OPEC+ members are producing significantly less than their assigned targets, while Russia has virtually no room to increase production further.

Concurring with this view, Hamad Hussain, a senior economist at Capital Economics, warned that cracks in quota negotiations could weaken the bloc's position. He argued that a more divided and less cohesive OPEC+ would lead to greater oil price volatility and, over time, increase the risks of lower oil prices.

Ukraine’s General Staff said it targeted the Yefremov Industrial Rubber Plant in Russia’s Tula region and said the strike was carried out in collaboration with the “Black Spark” movement inside Russia.

Ukraine’s state-owned “Private One” defense technologies foundation said “Images circulating online recently show a Ukrainian laser system intercepting an enemy jet-powered drone,” and the foundation said laser-based air-defense systems remain experimental. In the early hours of Saturday, Moscow’s mayor said air defences had shot down 10 drones heading toward the capital.

Sybiha told the “Food from Ukraine” conference that “We are ready for a cease-fire,” and he said Kyiv was grateful to India, Turkey, and Egypt for their roles in de-escalating tensions in the Black Sea and for mediation efforts.

Sybiha said Russia had proposed Ukraine suspend attacks on the Russian oil sector under the truce, but Kyiv would only consider that as part of a bigger energy ceasefire deal.

The BBC reported that Zelensky criticized Trump for describing Vladimir Putin as “my friend,” and Zelensky said, “It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” in an interview broadcast on November 27.

The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Zelensky was “insulting his counterpart,” and the Kremlin said Zelensky “is not willing to follow the path of (a) peace settlement”.

Ukraine’s offer came as France 24 said Russia attacked two foreign grain carriers near Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Odesa, and Ukraine said grain shipments from its key Black Sea ports around Odesa have all but stopped since late July.

President Vladimir Putin attended a ceremony marking the entry into service of a new nuclear submarine at Sevmash’s shipyard in Severodvinsk, northwestern Russia, with a flag-raising ceremony on the submarine Perm. Putin said, “Russia is one of the few countries in the world capable of building such powerful nuclear submarines - weapons of global reach and impact,” and he said that by 2030 the Russian fleet is set to receive five more ballistic-missile submarines. The Al-Jazeera Net account said the Perm submarine was launched on Friday and that Putin recalled the Russian navy had taken delivery of four other Yasen-M-class submarines in the past six years.

Ukraine’s ceasefire proposal remained conditional on scope, with Sybiha saying Kyiv would consider oil-sector suspension only within a broader energy ceasefire agreement. The sources framed the ceasefire offer as a step toward protecting Black Sea food exports while Russia sought to include oil transportation, and the next state of negotiations depended on whether Moscow responded to Kyiv’s proposals.

title: Energy Market Wrap: Crude Oil Prices Surge, Brent Tops $96 - MarketForces Africa
summary:
With elevated global energy costs, oil prices rose this week as geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and attacks on energy infrastructure heightened supply security concerns.

These key developments in the energy space outweighed the downward pressure from recovering oil shipments and expectations of a global supply surplus.

International benchmark Brent crude futures for January delivery traded at $96.70 per barrel on Friday, up 4.5% from last Friday’s close of $92.57.

US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures for January delivery stood at $85.28 per barrel, up around 1.5% from $83.98 a week earlier.

Oil prices were influenced this week by opposing supply and geopolitical factors, as the recovery in crude shipments from the Persian Gulf and the resumption of Libyan exports eased concerns over supply disruptions, while attacks on energy infrastructure and renewed tensions in Middle East kept supply security risks in focus.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global oil supply is expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter of the year, citing a rapid recovery in regional production and stabilizing supplies.

The recovery in shipments from the Persian Gulf and a rebound in regional exports also eased concerns over potential supply disruptions, putting downward pressure on prices.

However, US President Donald Trump’s remarks that he could resume attacks on Iran, alongside attacks targeting maritime transport and energy infrastructure in the region, continued to fuel concerns over supply security around the Strait of Hormuz.

Attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure further heightened these concerns. Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi group said it had targeted the Rabigh oil refinery, while the Saudi-led Arab Coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government reported an attack on the Jazan oil refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia.

Russia’s attacks on energy and port infrastructure in Ukraine, as well as an attack targeting a refinery belonging to Russian oil company Lukoil in the Perm region, more than 1,500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, also added to supply concerns.

On the supply side, Libya’s National Oil Corporation (NOC) resumed crude oil flows from the Sharara oil field following the reopening of its pipeline, according to international media reports, adding to expectations of improved supply.

Meanwhile, US inventory data provided some support to prices, limiting the downward pressure from improving supply prospects.

According to data released by the Energy Information Administration (EIA), US commercial crude oil inventories rose by approximately 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels, below market expectations of an increase of around 2 million barrels. title: The ECB set to raise interest rates in December - Eunews
summary:
[foto: imagoeconomica]

Brussels – The European Central Bank is set to raise interest rates at its meeting on 17 December . A concrete intention, but one that has merely been postponed. Because in the minutes of the October meeting , during which it was decided to keep the three key interest rates unchanged , it was made clear that the intention to tighten monetary policy was already in place. Still, the decision was taken to postpone what appears to be an inevitable course of action.

“ Several members noted that, given that the data received since the Governing Council’s September meeting had confirmed the case for a further tightening of monetary policy, they might have supported an increase in interest rates as early as this meeting, ” that is, the October meeting, according to the minutes. In the end, however, despite general concerns, “all members, including those seeing a case for acting at the current meeting, supported the decision to keep policy rates unchanged.”

The conditions for raising the cost of borrowing had therefore already materialised. Still, the ECB’s Governing Council opted for a cautious approach because, as the minutes emphasise, “ given that a further rates hike is necessary , unless the inflation outlook improved significantly, the only issue is timing. “

Ultimately, it appears that the ECB, judging by the reports, has chosen to meet market expectations in order to avoid creating tensions: “Financial markets and analysts expected no rate change at the current meeting and attached a high probability to a hike at the next monetary policy meeting in December.​” This, then, explains the reason for the pause.

Barring any major changes, therefore, the ECB could be set to deliver a Christmas present that would certainly not be welcomed by households and businesses, who would see the cost of mortgages and loans rise. But the situation seems inevitable, not least because it was already averted by the postponement in October.

Behind the ECB’s intentions is the observation that “ the spread between the price of refined diesel and that of crude oil has widened , owing in large part to supply disruptions in the Middle East and Russia, as well as a reduction in supply from China,” with knock-on effects for inflation. “Current high levels of prices for refined products are seen as worrying, as they could feed into transport, shipping, agricultural and production costs, spreading the impact beyond that of the direct energy component of inflation.” Furthermore, food commodity prices, particularly in Asia, “are also coming “ under pressure owing to adverse weather conditions linked to the “El Niño” phenomenon .” These are all reasons for tightening monetary policy.

title: US targets China, EU with new tariffs, citing overcapacity - Fulton Sun
summary:
WASHINGTON -- The United States announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump's push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional.

The rate for imports from China would rise to 20 percent, in line with the country's prior agreement with the Trump administration -- though that rate could double to 40 percent if talks between the two countries fall apart, according to a senior U.S. official. The official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday's announcement.

Products from the E.U. will be taxed at 15 percent in compliance with the United States' deal with the bloc, though that could also rise to as much as 20 percent, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative.

Tariffs will apply to items from economies the Trump administration accuses of overproduction in some domestic industries and hurting American companies. They are still subject to a public comment process and could change. A final action could come as early as January, the official said.

The new levies mark the latest effort by the administration to reinstate an expansive tariff agenda that included country-by-country levies implemented using emergency powers. Those were struck down by high-court justices in February, forcing Trump to invoke other legal authorities to advance his agenda.

It's a politically risky move. Democrats swept to a landslide victory in the midterm elections earlier this month thanks in part to voter anger over the cost of living and disapproval of the president's handling of the economy.

China and the E.U. could also retaliate, though initial signals from them were muted.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a briefing earlier Wednesday that the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on its exports was "political maneuvering" and said the two nations should work together to maintain their trade truce.

The announcement appears to comply with the 2025 trade agreement between the U.S. and the E.U., which capped tariffs at 15 percent on most of the bloc's exports. As a result, the move likely won't antagonize trans-Atlantic relations for now. European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said "we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity" and added the bloc expects new levies to abide by the tariff agreement.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new duties were designed to preserve existing deals while addressing overcapacity concerns.

"A lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it," Greer said Wednesday on CNBC. "We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in."

Imports from Japan, South Korea, Switzerland -- all prominent U.S. trading partners -- would be hit with a 15 percent rate. The number could go up to 25 percent for Korea and 20 percent for the other two, USTR said. Indian products would face a 17 percent charge if a trade pact with Washington is finalized, though that could increase to 25 percent.

India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said in a statement that it had "engaged constructively" during the investigation, and that any trade-related concerns should be addressed through U.S.-India talks for a bilateral deal. Vietnam's Ministry of Industry and Trade said it's prepared to participate in the next steps of the investigation, including public hearings to present its views.

Several smaller nations in Asia were also hit. Similar expected measures aimed at Mexico and Norway were not included but remain under consideration, the official said. Greer said on CNBC the U.S. has "had some very good conversations with Mexico" on the issue.

The tariffs follow a probe that began in March into alleged excess manufacturing capacity, utilizing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a process seen as more resistant to legal challenges than Trump's prior tariff wall. The tariff rates aren't expected to surpass already agreed-upon levels in trade agreements with each economy.

The move will test the tolerance of economic partners, who have largely held back from retaliating, opting instead to negotiate deals with the U.S. to minimize their tariffs. That dynamic could be on display next month, when Trump meets again with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of the Group of 20 summit. Their trade truce is set to expire in January unless the two powers agree to extend it.

"If we were to go beyond the 20 percent or something like that, they would view that as breaking our deal," Greer said,

The trade ambassador said Washington and Beijing are also "proposing to implement" tariff reductions under its new board of trade on around $30 billion of nonsensitive exports.

Greer signaled that the new levy will not stack on top of existing duties of 10 percent or 12.5 percent under a separate investigation into negligent enforcement of forced-labor laws. "Those are not really additive," he said on CNBC.

For products eligible to be hit by both sets of duties, only the higher rate would apply, the official said earlier.

The official added that there would be goods exempted from the tariffs, including oil and gas and food products that cannot be grown in the U.S. Other products that are already subject to sectoral duties, including tariffs on pharmaceuticals and critical minerals, are also exempted.

After the Supreme Court loss, Trump immediately announced plans to rebuild his tariff wall under a different legal authority. Under the Section 301 framework, the president can implement tariffs following an investigation into allegedly unfair foreign trading practices.

While Section 301 tariffs are seen as more legally sound and flexible than other powers Trump has eyed, they're also more time-consuming. An earlier investigation under the same legal authority into policies around forced labor from U.S. trading partners resulted in tariffs on some 60 economies. Those duties are currently facing legal challenges.

The new tariffs apply to Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam.

USTR also announced it is raising tariffs on imports from Brazil, altering a previously-conducted trade investigation into the country's digital policies and trade practices. The U.S. is considering increasing the out-of-quota tariff rate on raw and refined sugar and proposing a 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft.

The increased levy on imports from Brazil comes weeks after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro lost his presidential election bid to progressive incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
