title: Vietnam and India face the highest proposed tariffs in Trump administration's new trade package - Latin Times
summary: The Briefing: The Trump administration proposed new Section 301 tariffs on 14 major trading partners on November 25, targeting what it calls structural industrial overcapacity that disadvantages U.S. manufacturers. Vietnam (35%) and India (25%) face the steepest proposed rates among the 14 economies. China faces a proposed rate of up to 20%, with an alternative rate of up to 40% if consultations fail to produce a satisfactory resolution. The tariffs will not take effect immediately; a mandatory public comment period must conclude first, with implementation unlikely before early 2027. Months after the Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorise President Donald Trump to impose tariffs, the administration proposed a new round of duties under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the administration proposed fresh import duties on 14 major trading partners, citing industrial overcapacity practices that Washington says burden American commerce.The proposal, unveiled by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on November 25, 2026, concluded an eight-month investigation launched in March following the Supreme Court ruling. The 14 targeted economies are China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam.Vietnam and India Face the Highest Proposed RatesContrary to what early reports suggested, Vietnam and India are not simply at the high end of a moderate tariff range — they face the steepest proposed rates in the entire package. Vietnam would face a 35% overcapacity tariff, while India confronts a proposed 25% levy. Singapore is targeted at 20%, and Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand face 18%. The European Union, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan would be subject to a 15% rate.Administration officials confirmed that both Vietnam and India have absorbed significant manufacturing capacity that shifted out of China in recent years, making them strategic targets in this round. The proposed rates account for existing trade arrangements and other applicable duties, with certain exemptions and potential reductions for countries that reach agreements with Washington.China Remains the Focal PointEven so, China faces the most complex tariff structure. The new proposal would add a separate Section 301 measure addressing structural excess capacity. For China, the proposed rate is up to 20% on specified goods, calculated net of the applicable Section 301 rate under the investigation concerning imports produced with forced labor. The USTR's proposal includes an alternative rate of up to 40% if consultations with Beijing do not produce a satisfactory outcome. The existing 20% tariff arrangement was announced under the Kuala Lumpur Joint Arrangement reached by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on October 30, 2025.China's Foreign Ministry pushed back without hesitation. Spokesperson Guo Jiakun stated that "tariff wars serve nobody's interests" — a response that underscored Beijing's intent to maintain a posture of stability even as Washington signals willingness to escalate.The Legal Strategy: A More Durable FrameworkThe administration was deliberate in its choice of legal authority. Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 authorizes the USTR to investigate and respond to foreign trade practices deemed "unreasonable" or "discriminatory" — and historically, it has withstood judicial challenges far more reliably than the emergency powers the courts struck down earlier this year.U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the new tariffs are "targeted, not universal" and stressed that in most cases they would not accumulate on top of rates already set by prior bilateral agreements. He also indicated that Washington is in parallel talks with several of the 14 countries to reach a multilateral accord on excess capacity — positioning the tariff proposal simultaneously as enforcement and as leverage.A Narrower Political MarginThe announcement landed in a changed political environment. Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the November 2026 midterm elections, partly on a message of economic relief from tariff-driven price increases. The new Democratic majority, set to be seated in January, is expected to pursue investigations into the administration's trade policies and push legislation to curb executive tariff authority — an effort already underway through Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden's Congressional Trade Powers Reform Act.A senior White House official told reporters the administration does not anticipate immediate retaliation from the targeted countries, citing the ongoing nature of negotiations and the structure of the public comment process.Timeline: What Comes NextThe tariffs are proposals and are not yet in effect. Written comments are due by January 5, 2027, and USTR hearings are scheduled to begin on January 25. The agency has not announced a final implementation date. Mexico and Norway were among the 16 economies included in the investigations launched in March, but the USTR did not issue determinations for either country on November 25.The pattern mirrors the administration's earlier trade offensives: announce broadly, then negotiate bilaterally. Countries that reach trade agreements with Washington before the tariffs are finalized would be eligible for reduced rates — a mechanism that transforms the proposal into a pressure campaign as much as a policy outcome.

title: Crude Oil Near $100: Will Petrol and Diesel Prices Rise in India? OPEC+ Meeting Could Change the Game - theopenpress.in
summary:
Global crude oil prices are once again approaching the $100-per-barrel mark, raising fresh concerns for oil-importing countries such as India. After three consecutive weeks of decline, Brent crude ha…

Published By : Neeraj Singh , New Delhi

Last Updated: November 28, 2026, 19:07 IST

Global crude oil prices are once again approaching the $100-per-barrel mark, raising fresh concerns for oil-importing countries such as India. After three consecutive weeks of decline, Brent crude has recorded its first weekly gain in November as renewed tensions in West Asia threaten energy supplies and shipping routes.

On November 27, Brent crude futures settled at $95.44 per barrel, declining 1.2% during the session but gaining approximately 3% over the week. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude settled at $83.08 per barrel.

The latest movement has brought an important question back into focus: Could another rise in international crude prices make petrol and diesel more expensive in India?

The latest recovery in oil prices is largely linked to concerns about supply disruptions in the Middle East.

Attacks on energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and incidents involving commercial shipping have increased uncertainty across the global oil market. The Strait of Hormuz has become particularly important because it is a critical route for international oil shipments.

Preliminary data from commodity analytics firm Kpler indicated that oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz were only around 55% of pre-war levels in the week ending November 25.

When traders fear that fewer barrels could reach international markets, crude prices can rise even before a major shortage actually occurs.

India is among the world's largest oil-consuming economies, but it depends heavily on imported crude to meet domestic demand.

According to provisional government data, crude oil imports met approximately 88.7% of India's requirements in October.

The country's crude oil import bill reached $111 billion during April–October FY27, increasing 53.5% compared with the corresponding period a year earlier. Import volumes, meanwhile, rose by only 2.7%.

This difference highlights the problem: India is paying substantially more for crude even though the quantity imported has not increased at the same pace.

Every sustained increase in international oil prices can add pressure to India's foreign exchange requirements, trade balance and inflation outlook.

A rise in international crude oil prices does not automatically mean that petrol and diesel prices will increase immediately.

Retail fuel prices depend on several factors, including the rupee-dollar exchange rate, refining costs, transportation expenses, taxes and the pricing decisions of oil marketing companies.

If crude remains expensive for an extended period, fuel retailers may face greater pressure on their marketing margins. However, the timing and extent of any change in retail prices cannot be predicted from one day's international movement.

For consumers, the bigger concern is a prolonged period of expensive crude rather than a temporary market spike.

The next major development for the oil market will be the November 29 meeting of OPEC+, the group of oil-producing countries and their allies.

Producers are expected to discuss their output strategy for 2027. The market will closely watch whether the group maintains existing production targets or considers changes in supply.

A decision to restrict production could support international oil prices, particularly if geopolitical disruptions continue.

On the other hand, additional supply and a recovery in Gulf exports could help ease prices.

Some market forecasts also point towards a possible global oil surplus in 2027. That could provide relief to importing countries, although the actual outcome will depend on production decisions, demand and shipping conditions.

The impact of expensive crude is not limited to petrol pumps. It can spread across several parts of the economy.

The effects are not necessarily immediate, but sustained increases in energy costs can gradually reach households and businesses.

A fall below $90 remains possible if global supply improves, shipping conditions stabilise and geopolitical tensions ease.

However, further attacks on energy infrastructure, restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz or tighter OPEC+ production could keep prices elevated.

The coming days will therefore be important for traders, policymakers, oil companies and consumers.

Crude oil is once again approaching a level that could create economic challenges for India. With nearly 89% of domestic crude requirements met through imports, the country remains exposed to international price fluctuations.

The November 29 OPEC+ meeting could provide an important signal about the direction of oil prices in 2027.

For Indian consumers, the key question is not simply whether Brent crosses $100, but how long prices remain elevated and whether the pressure eventually reaches domestic fuel costs.

The next major oil market signal could come from the OPEC+ meeting—and its consequences may extend far beyond the global energy market.

title: The Iran war could shatter rising expectations of surplus oil supply in coming months - CNBC
summary:
In this article

Crude oil prices have sold off sharply in November as investors see a recovery in Middle East exports tipping the market into a surplus for the first time since the Iran war began.

Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, are down about 20% after approaching wartime highs in late October when the contract hit $118 a barrel.

U.S. West Texas Intermediate has also fallen about 21% after topping $104 a barrel in the same period. Brent closed at $95.44 a barrel Friday while WTI settled at $83.08.

U.S. retail gasoline prices have fallen well below $4 a gallon and diesel has eased below $6 a gallon.

In October, investors were pricing in the risk of a major military escalation in the Persian Gulf after the U.S. midterm elections. But President Donald Trump has held back so far from launching renewed military strikes against Iran after the Democrats wiped out Republican congressional majorities.

The selloff this month has likely gone too far, Giovanni Staunovo, a strategist at UBS, wrote in a note clients. The market has become "too comfortable with the supply outlook," Staunovo said. "The rebound in Gulf exports should not be mistaken for a normalization of the oil market," the analyst said.

The International Energy Agency has forecast an oil surplus beginning in the fourth quarter. This would represent a major turning point nine months after the Iran war triggered the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market.

Goldman Sachs sees a crude surplus of 2 million barrels per day in 2027 as Gulf producers continue to adapt their supply chains to war in the Middle East . Commodity and ship tracking firm Kpler sees oversupply of 3 million bpd next year.

"If the recovery in the Arabian Gulf region continues, we're going to have oversupply," said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush.

But predictions of a surplus assume a sustained recovery in flows from the Middle East. The IEA also cautioned that downside risks "persist as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security."

"If pigs had wings, they'd fly," said David Goldwyn, who served as the State Department's special envoy for international energy under President Barack Obama, in reference to the surplus forecast.

The more likely scenario is that oil prices trade in a wide range through the end of Trump's term as the security situation in the Gulf remains volatile, McNally at Rapidan said. During periods of relative calm, crude will trade between $70 to $80, he said. Prices could spike well above $100 when the conflict escalates, he said.

"We think there will be more disruptions, more risk and that those surpluses won't materialize next year," McNally said.

Trump recently told Fox News that he might launch renewed strikes on Iran after the new year. A major military escalation in the region would lead to structurally higher prices, said Goldwyn, the Obama administration official. Iran would likely retaliate against U.S. strikes with attacks on ports, refineries or processing facilities, he said.

Crude exports from the Middle East have rebounded since the summer, though they have trended lower in recent weeks and remain well below pre-war levels as tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz are attacked on a near daily basis.

At least 20 attacks on commercial ships have been reported this month, according to maritime security agencies. There were 35 such incidents in October, the highest level since the war began.

Middle east crude exports averaged 12.8 million barrels per day in the week ended Wednesday, about 24% below pre-war levels of 17 million bpd, according to Kpler data. Fuel shipments stood at 3.2 million bpd in the same period, down about 49% from 6.3 million bpd before the war.

Production has also increased in the Americas and demand has pulled back due to seasonal factors associated with the end of the summer driving season and refinery turnarounds, Goldwyn said.

Assuming a persistent surplus, JPMorgan forecasts Brent prices in the high $70s in the first half of 2027 before falling into the $60s in the second half of next year. Goldman Sachs sees Brent trading around $88 a barrel next year and WTI averaging about $78 barrel next year.

But Kpler warned the predicted surplus could easily tip into a deficit again if Iran or its Houthi allies bomb the United Arab Emirates export terminal at Fujairah or key Saudi infrastructure such as the kingdom's facilities at Ras Tanura, Yanbu or its East-West Pipeline.

Any further disruption to Mideast supplies would strike when the world's inventory buffers have already been drawn down to historic lows without time to restock them, Goldwyn said. The CEOs of ExxonMobil and Chevron have warned for months about the depletion of the world's oil stockpiles.

There is room to potentially release another 100 million barrels from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve and for the Europeans to deploy more refined products, Goldwyn said. But neither will be eager to dip into the reserves again, he said.

"If this looks like it's going to be a chronic situation, I think both the U.S and Europeans are going to be reluctant to draw on those reserves just to provide price relief," Goldwyn said.

China is also increasing its crude imports as the situation in the Middle East remains fragile, Staunovo at UBS said. Beijing's decision to dramatically cut its imports earlier this year was one of the major factors keeping prices from shooting even higher during the war.

"Together, these developments are contributing to a decline in oil on water and a tightening physical market," Staunovo said. "This supports our view that oil prices should recover from here."

title: What is the relationship between inflation, interest rates, and economic growth, and what does it mean for the new Federal Reserve chair? - Equitable Growth
summary:

MAY 18, 2026

By: Jacob Robbins

Since regaining the Oval Office in early 2025, President Donald Trump has repeatedly called for lower interest rates 1 and severely criticized former Federal Reserve Board Chair Jerome Powell’s cautious approach to interest rate policy. President Trump’s views culminated in the nomination of former Fed governor Kevin Warsh to replace Powell, explicitly linking his selection to Warsh’s public preference for lower interest rates. 2

Both the president and Warsh have explicitly stated economic theories to support their preferred interest rate policies. President Trump has repeatedly asserted that lower interest rates will lead to higher economic output and thus economic “growth without inflation,” 3 and that there is no meaningful inflation trade-off from easier monetary policy. In support of his claim, he offers two arguments. First, he argues that demand-driven growth, by expanding output, can itself fight inflation. 4 And second, he says that his supply-side economic policies, such as deregulating fossil fuels and implementing high tariffs, will restrain inflation. 5

Warsh, in turn, argues that despite the U.S. economy running at full employment and with inflation above the Fed’s target level of 2 percent, lower interest rates will not lead to higher inflation because of the acceleration of AI technology. In Warsh’s view, the development of AI technologies will rapidly increase economic output through increased productivity, allowing the Fed to cut interest rates aggressively without reigniting inflation. 6

The purpose of this issue brief is to take these economic arguments at face value and see whether they are supported by standard macroeconomic theory or by the available evidence. To preview the conclusion, these statements by President Trump and Warsh are either inconsistent with standard theories or unsupported by factual evidence. A more cynical explanation is that the president’s interest rate demands are politically motivated and that Warsh’s nomination is meant to increase presidential influence over the Federal Reserve.

This is historically dangerous economic terrain. President Trump’s politically motivated attempts to influence the Federal Reserve by weakening its independence falls foul of abundant evidence of the benefits of central bank independence for robust macroeconomic performance and of the significant costs, in terms of inflation and economic output, of past episodes of political pressure on monetary policy.

Let’s begin this issue brief by examining President Trump’s economic reasoning.

President Trump’s statements, taken as a whole, seem to indicate that he does not believe in the existence of any trade-off between inflation and economic output. In contrast, modern macroeconomic theory, well-supported by empirical data, puts this trade-off at the heart of the aggregate supply relationship, wherein high economic activity that approaches or exceeds the capacity to supply goods and services will ultimately raise the demand for workers, oil, and other inputs, which will, in turn, raise prices.

The negative relationship between inflation and unemployment is known as the Phillips curve. An extensive economic literature has studied the slope of the curve, showing that the trade-off exists, 7 even if its magnitude is not always clear and changes over time. Recent economic literature suggests that the slope is particularly large when unemployment is low. 8 That means additional demand is more likely to translate into inflation when the labor market is already tight.

This well-understood relationship helps explain why inflation surged after the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Labor markets were particularly tight, and there were significant supply shocks from the war in Ukraine and other supply-chain disruptions that resulted in inflation rates close to double digits in 2021–2022. Today, the latest jobs report for April 2026 finds that the U.S. unemployment rate held steady at 4.3 percent, closely in line with Federal Reserve projections of the long-run rate of unemployment, suggesting that the inflation costs of higher demand are elevated. In this environment, excessive rate cuts could bring back higher inflation.

The inflationary costs of lower interest rates also are determined by the extent to which expectations of future inflation among consumers and businesses are anchored—that is, to what extent they believe the Fed will be able to achieve its inflation target of 2 percent. 9 During the Great Recession of 2007–2009, well-anchored expectations from 20 years of inflation-targeting success led to fairly small deviations in inflation, despite a massive drop in demand.

In contrast, today, the U.S. and world economies are coming off the largest spike in inflation since the 1980s, a period in which household inflationary expectations became more dispersed and less stable. 10 Another bout of elevated inflation would further reduce the credibility of the central bank’s ability to control price growth, leading to unanchored expectations and spiraling rounds of inflation.

Should President Trump succeed in lowering interest rates and spurring demand, any higher economic output and lower unemployment would be short-lived. That’s because the second form of the Phillips Curve, the “long-run Phillips Curve,” states that the trade-off between inflation and economic output is only available in the short run. 11 Over longer periods, monetary policies that seek to permanently lower the unemployment rate beyond its natural limit will ultimately fail.

The reason for the failure to boost long-run output is that, over time, high inflation will affect the beliefs and expectations of consumers and firms. They will start to bake it into their prices and wage demands. Sustained higher expectations will then cycle back into higher prices, confirming the expectations in a vicious cycle. This was the experience of the U.S. economy in the 1970s and 1980s. 12 In the long run, the Phillips Curve is vertical, meaning that there is no effect of inflation on output but rather that the economy ends up with higher prices but not more real economic activity.

Crucial to the Phillips Curve theory is the notion that unemployment cannot be lowered past its sustainable level, known as the natural rate of unemployment. Estimates of this natural rate are noisy, and they can change over time.

History teaches that inaccurately estimating the natural rate of unemployment has serious consequences. In the 1960s, Federal Reserve forecasts of the natural rate of unemployment were too optimistic, which led to unsustainably loose monetary policy at the time. 13 In contrast, during the 1990s, the Fed’s forecast for natural unemployment may have been too pessimistic, with unemployment consistently low and modest inflation. This is why it is important today for Federal Reserve officials to independently estimate the natural rate of unemployment without undue political pressure.

President Trump also argues that supply-side policies can allow the U.S. economy to grow without higher inflation and therefore that interest rates can be safely cut to support this growth. Standard macroeconomic theory teaches that a decrease in the cost of resources, by increasing aggregate supply, can indeed raise economic output without putting upward pressure on inflation. 14 The implications for the conduct of monetary policy, however, do not straightforwardly call for a decline in interest rates. This is because the appropriate interest rate depends not only on the disinflationary effect of the productivity shock, but also on how persistently that shock raises supply and thus affects the natural real interest rate.

In other words, managing the dynamics of AI innovation requires a calculated decision by a central bank that is carefully taking the pulse of both inflation and output growth.

The two supply-side policies that President Trump emphasizes the most are higher tariffs and the deregulation of the oil and gas industry. 15 The logic that such policies will spur growth without raising inflation is predicated on the argument that they will reduce prices. On the contrary, the latest empirical research shows that a direct result of his recent tariffs has been an increase in prices, contributing to a 0.7 percent higher inflation rate. 16 And while oil and gas prices had moderated early in his second term, they have risen dramatically due to the ongoing war with Iran, with global oil prices at more than $100 a barrel.

Contrary to President Trump’s inflation optimism, the most recent inflation reports show inflation above the Fed’s target of 2 percent. The April 2026 Consumer Price Index report showed 3.8 percent year-over-year inflation, 17 and the March Personal Consumption Expenditures report showed 3.5 percent inflation. 18 As of May 2026, the data do not contain evidence of a supply-side economic expansion.

The new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has offered a different supply-side theory for lower interest rates, centered on the acceleration of artificial intelligence, which he says is “the most productivity enhancing wave of our lifetimes—past, present and future.” 19 In Warsh’s argument, the development of AI technologies will rapidly increase output, allowing the Fed to cut rates aggressively without reigniting inflation.

This reasoning contains a grain of truth: If the promise of AI productivity pays off, there will indeed be reduced inflationary pressure. But that conclusion is premature. General-purpose technologies often take years or decades to diffuse throughout the economy.

So far, aggregate productivity data do not show a dramatic break from recent experience. To paraphrase the late Nobel laureate Robert Solow’s remarks on computer technology, the effects of AI are everywhere except in the data. In the latest data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, year-on-year total factor productivity growth was just 0.8 percent, while labor productivity growth was 2.5 percent. There is no indication in the data of an explosion of productivity that would justify lower interest rates.

President Trump’s theories do not accord with standard economic theory, but they do fit a long historical pattern of presidential pressure on the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates at the expense of long-term monetary stability. This problem of political pressure motivated the introduction of independent central banks, which are not under the direct purview of executive or legislative branches. 20 Independence gives central banks an arm’s-length distance from the executive and legislative branches. These branches set the central bank’s monetary policy objectives but ideally do not interfere directly with the operational conduct of monetary policy itself. 21

Historically, central bank independence has been honored more in the breach than in the observance. Presidents prefer lower interest rates, and they lean on their central bank chairs to achieve their political goals. Noted violations of Fed independence include President Richard Nixon’s pressure on Fed Chair Arthur Burns, as well as President Lyndon B. Johnson’s pressure on Fed Chair William McChesney Martin. This political pressure has been shown to empirically increase inflation with no impact on economic growth. 22

President Trump has repeatedly violated the principle of Fed independence by publicly demanding lower interest rates and initiating politically motivated investigations of Powell and Fed governor Lisa Cook. These actions can only lead to a further deterioration of the Federal Reserve’s credibility, with deleterious consequences for long-term inflation and growth.

Current deregulatory policies under the second Trump administration are not leading to an increase in the supply of basic economic inputs. Tariffs are not spurring a supply-side economic expansion. And while AI has the potential to drive a new wave of economic growth, it is not yet showing up in significant increases in productivity.

Meanwhile inflation remains elevated, in part due to the very policies intended to lower it—tariffs—and to unrelated but no less significant policy choices, such as military action against Iran and the consequent rise in global energy prices and the cost of fossil-fuel based inputs such as fertilizer.

Lower interest rates are politically popular because they can temporarily juice the economy. History demonstrates that the incumbent party’s chances of electoral success are higher when the economy is strong. Yet history also shows that loose monetary policy not anchored to underlying economic conditions can have deep and long-term negative effects on the economy, stunting growth and stoking stubbornly high inflation.

Such a wave of stagflation would have real and significant costs for workers and families, making daily life more expensive while decreasing the availability of jobs and therefore depressing wages. It is that reality that motivated the United States and the rest of the developed world to enshrine the independence of central banks and insulate monetary policy from political pressure.

President Trump and his new Fed Chair Warsh should heed these warnings.

title: OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report: Data Architecture and Research Guide - CASRAI
summary:
A comprehensive researcher guide to the OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report, covering balance models, secondary source production tracking, and JODI-Oil data.

Written and maintained by CASRAI Editorial Board

Published 28 November 2026

The OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) is the flagship statistical publication published by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries Secretariat in Vienna, providing monthly empirical analysis and medium-term projections of global crude oil supply, refined product demand, refining throughputs, and commercial inventory balances. Operating across eleven core analytical sections, the report provides energy economists and academic researchers with authoritative estimates of the global crude oil balance, world economic growth trajectories, and member nation production volumes cross-verified through an independent institutional panel of secondary sources.

The OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report serves as a primary empirical benchmark for global energy market surveillance, macroeconomic planning, and academic research in petroleum economics. Published monthly by the OPEC Secretariat, the publication synthesizes upstream extraction rates, refinery yields, and product demand across global consuming hubs. Within modern energy studies and petroleum engineering research , understanding these figures is essential for constructing supply-demand balances, assessing spare capacity, and calibrating dynamic reservoir extraction strategies against consumption patterns.

The report delivers an assessment structured around eleven standard analytical chapters tracing the petroleum value chain:

The mathematical framework governing the MOMR centers on the “Call on OPEC Crude” identity:

Call on OPEC Crude = World Oil Demand – Non-OPEC Liquids Supply – OPEC Natural Gas Liquids (NGLs) and Non-Conventional Oils

When actual OPEC crude extraction exceeds this calculated call, global markets enter a net stock build, expanding commercial storage inventories. Conversely, when extraction falls below the call, markets experience net stock draws, depleting inventory buffers. Researchers rely on this transparent identity to isolate whether structural deficits or physical surpluses drive price movements.

The OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report is compiled, verified, and published directly by the Secretariat of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries in Vienna, Austria. Within the Secretariat, compilation is coordinated under the Research Division, drawing upon teams across the Petroleum Studies Department, the Data Services Department, and the Environmental Matters Unit. The institutional drafting process follows a monthly cycle during which national statistical submissions, satellite tanker tracking, customs declarations, and proprietary intelligence are synthesized into standardized accounting tables.

The data coverage of the MOMR is global, tracking physical liquids across major producing basins and consuming regions. Unlike administrative surveys capturing only domestic pipeline nominations, the MOMR unifies physical flow accounting across OECD Americas, OECD Europe, OECD Asia-Pacific, Greater China, India, Latin America, the Middle East, and Sub-Saharan Africa. All liquid volumes are harmonized in million barrels per day (mb/d) or thousand barrels per day (tb/d), facilitating direct econometric integration.

The monthly data lifecycle operates through a structured reporting phase wherein preliminary trade declarations and domestic tallies undergo cross-validation before publication. Similar rigorous validation cycles govern sibling commodities and regulatory sectors, such as the weekly and monthly storage audits conducted for domestic natural gas infrastructure in the EIA Natural Gas Storage Report .

A distinctive feature of the OPEC MOMR is its dual-accounting architecture for tracking member nation crude oil production. In every monthly edition, OPEC publishes two parallel statistical tables detailing national extraction rates:

The secondary sources panel serves an essential institutional function. Because member allocations depend on production baselines, relying exclusively on self-reported declarations could introduce reporting discrepancies. Under the Declaration of Cooperation (DoC, or OPEC+), the OPEC Ministerial Conference and the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC) officially utilize secondary source numbers rather than direct communication to audit quota adherence.

The authorized secondary sources panel currently comprises six independent entities:

In March 2022, OPEC replaced the IEA on the panel with Wood Mackenzie and Rystad Energy to expand reliance on commercial asset-level telemetry. The Secretariat averages estimates across these six providers to calculate official secondary source production figures, minimizing outlier distortions. Discrepancies between direct communication and secondary estimates often reflect differing technical boundaries, such as lease condensate inclusion or domestic field blending.

Researchers investigating petroleum markets can access and extract empirical data from the MOMR through OPEC’s digital distribution infrastructure. Access to the full report and historical archives is open to the public without paywalls or subscription fees. To locate and ingest these datasets into quantitative workflows, analysts execute the following standard sequence:

Researchers citing these datasets in peer-reviewed literature should cite the publication month, year, table number, and formal attribution.

While the Monthly Oil Market Report provides high-frequency short-term monitoring, researchers requiring multi-decade historical depth rely on the companion publication: the OPEC Annual Statistical Bulletin (ASB). First published in 1965, the ASB is released annually in mid-year by the OPEC Data Services Department as a statistical almanac for structural, financial, and geological dimensions of the petroleum industry.

The ASB differs from the MOMR in several fundamental analytical dimensions:

Academic researchers cross-reference historical MOMR archives—such as benchmark datasets from the 2022 and 2023 market cycles—against the structural baselines established in the ASB. For downstream processing and manufacturing analysis, linking these crude flow tables with refinery standards provided by organizations like American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers allows chemical engineers to model petrochemical feedstock yields and catalytic cracking economics under shifting crude slate gravities.

Global oil statistics transparency was substantially upgraded through the creation of the Joint Organisations Data Initiative (JODI), an intergovernmental collaboration in which OPEC plays a founding role. Established in 2001 in response to oil price volatility caused by opaque inventory reporting, JODI operates as a joint partnership among eight major international energy organizations: APEC, Eurostat, GECF, IEA, IEF, OLADE, OPEC, and UNSD, coordinated by the IEF Secretariat in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

The primary operational asset of the initiative is the JODI-Oil World Database. JODI-Oil collects monthly physical petroleum data directly from official sovereign government questionnaires across more than 100 participating nations, representing over 90% of global oil supply and demand. Participating countries report on seven critical balance flows (production, imports, exports, bunkers, stock changes, refinery intake, and refinery output) across eight product classifications, including crude oil, natural gas liquids, motor gasoline, aviation fuels, gas/diesel oil, fuel oil, and other petroleum products.

A major contribution of the JODI-Oil Manual is the standardization of international petroleum terminology. Prior to JODI, national agencies defined crude oil and condensate inconsistently. Under harmonized JODI definitions, crude oil is defined as mineral oil of natural origin consisting of hydrocarbons and associated impurities, explicitly including lease condensate extracted at surface lease separators. Commercial stocks measure physical inventories held in refinery tanks, bulk terminals, pipelines, and commercial caverns, excluding oil held in unmined geological formations.

JODI updates its open database around the 18th of each month, releasing full monthly time series extending from January 2002 to one month prior to publication. Researchers can download complete comma-separated value (CSV) packages or execute multi-variable queries via the JODI Data Browser. Combining JODI’s physical customs-level data with the econometric models in the OPEC MOMR enables researchers to isolate discrepancies between governmental declarations and commercial shipping assessments.

To overcome access friction and automate quantitative modeling, researchers frequently access integrated secondary macroeconomic indicators and OPEC pricing indices through external public databases like the St. Louis Federal Reserve FRED Database , which mirrors key historical energy time series into open API feeds.

Global energy market surveillance is anchored by three primary monthly statistical reports: the OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR), the International Energy Agency’s Oil Market Report (OMR), and the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO). The International Energy Forum (IEF) in Riyadh conducts a monthly Trilateral Comparative Analysis, systematically documenting where and why the three agencies diverge.

The dataset table below compares institutional attributes, forecasting parameters, and data distribution formats across these primary global energy intelligence systems. Divergences between these institutions primarily arise from differing statistical definitions of liquids, differing baseline estimations of non-OECD domestic consumption, and varying macroeconomic assumptions regarding global GDP expansion rates.

The OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (MOMR) is the flagship empirical publication published monthly by the OPEC Secretariat in Vienna, Austria. It delivers comprehensive assessments and medium-term forecasts of global crude oil supply, product demand, refining throughputs, tanker freight rates, and commercial inventory balances across OECD and non-OECD regions.

The report contains eleven core analytical chapters, including global macroeconomic forecasts, regional oil demand by product classification, non-OPEC liquids supply projections, OPEC member crude production (reported via both direct communication and secondary sources), refinery crack spreads, maritime shipping metrics, and the definitive balance of supply and demand determining the call on OPEC crude.

The MOMR is essential to energy traders, central banks, and market analysts because its production tables establish the official audit for OPEC+ quota compliance under the Declaration of Cooperation. Revisions to OPEC’s global demand outlook or supply trajectories immediately influence futures pricing across benchmark contracts like Brent and WTI by indicating whether physical markets are shifting toward surplus or deficit.

The complete MOMR is available for free public download on the official OPEC website (opec.org) and through the OPEC Digital Publications repository. Researchers can download the comprehensive monthly monograph in PDF format and retrieve accompanying statistical appendices as clean Microsoft Excel (.xlsx) workbooks containing historical balance sheets and country-level time series.

The MOMR is evaluated alongside the International Energy Agency’s Oil Market Report (IEA OMR) and the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Short-Term Energy Outlook (EIA STEO). While the IEA focuses on consumer OECD emergency stockpiles and the EIA focuses on U.S. domestic supply models, the MOMR provides unique visibility into producer nation extraction, official member declarations, and institutional secondary source audits.

title: Crude Oil Prices: Brent Nears $100 as Middle East Attacks End Three-Week Slide - theopenpress.in
summary:
Global crude oil prices have recovered from their recent slide, with Brent crude climbing back towards $100 a barrel as a fresh wave of attacks on energy facilities and shipping in the Middle East pu…

Published By : Business Desk , The Open Press

Last Updated: November 28, 2026, 15:13 IST

Global crude oil prices have recovered from their recent slide, with Brent crude climbing back towards $100 a barrel as a fresh wave of attacks on energy facilities and shipping in the Middle East put the risk of supply disruptions back at the centre of the market.

Brent crude futures rose to an intraday high not seen since 9 November on Friday, 27 November, before settling at $95.44 a barrel, down 1.2 percent on the day. Despite the late retreat, the international benchmark gained about 3 percent during the week, snapping a three-week losing streak and recording its first weekly advance in November, according to Reuters.

US West Texas Intermediate crude settled at $83.08 a barrel, down 60 cents, or 0.7 percent, from the previous close. There was no settlement on Thursday because of the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States.

The recovery follows a weak spell in which prices slipped below $90 a barrel earlier in the week. Investors had grown more hopeful that military escalation between Washington and Tehran would ease after the US midterm elections, while higher oil flows from the region and a sharp slowdown in global consumption had also weighed on prices, CNN reported.

That mood changed with a fresh series of attacks on oil facilities, tankers and other strategic assets across the Middle East. "Attacks on Middle Eastern energy facilities and tankers have brought supply disruption back into focus," Mark Schaefer, a director at brokerage Liquidity Energy, told Reuters.

Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for an attack on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery on Wednesday. The plant is the kingdom's largest refinery and an important crude export hub.

A projectile struck another refinery in Saudi Arabia's southwestern Jazan region the following day, killing a Nepalese worker and triggering a fire. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said some operations at the facility were temporarily suspended.

The attacks extended beyond energy infrastructure. A suspected Iranian drone strike on a Kuwaiti military facility killed two Italian nationals employed by defence company Rheinmetall Italia, Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said. Kuwait's defence ministry said a Kuwaiti national and a Pakistani national were also injured. Tehran denied responsibility for the attack, according to CNN.

A building housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund in Riyadh was struck for the second time within days, leaving 11 people injured, according to Saudi authorities and an eyewitness cited by CNN.

The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage through which a large share of the world's seaborne crude moves, has become the sharpest source of uncertainty. Around two dozen attacks on ships passing through the waterway were reported in November, according to a CNN analysis of data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre, close to the record 30 incidents reported in October.

Oil flows through the strait stood at just 55 percent of pre-war levels in the week ending 25 November, preliminary data from commodity analytics firm Kpler showed, a sign that security fears are already slowing the movement of crude.

The US military said it had disabled a commercial vessel on Thursday after it attempted to breach Washington's blockade of Iran. An adviser to Iran's supreme leader said Tehran would keep the Strait of Hormuz shut and vowed to break the US embargo, Reuters reported.

"These attacks remind us of the inherent instability of the status quo, as a lasting peace deal between the US and Iran remains elusive," Kathleen Brooks, research director at online brokerage XTB, said in a note cited by CNN.

Market watchers are now asking whether Brent can push past $100 a barrel. "We think Brent can still push above $100 a barrel without another major escalation in the Middle East, but that increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply," ANZ analysts Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes said in a research note, according to Reuters.

The rally still faces headwinds. Expectations of ample global supplies and worries about weaker consumption could limit further gains, while a stronger US dollar and inflation concerns could also weigh on crude.

Traders are now looking to the meeting of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as OPEC+, on 29 November, for clues on production policy in 2027.

The group is expected to keep its existing production targets for the first quarter of 2027, Reuters reported, citing three people familiar with the discussions. OPEC+ has held output steady since September after six consecutive monthly increases.

Iraq is negotiating with OPEC for a higher production ceiling as it looks to expand its energy sector, Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said on Friday. The meeting comes amid broader questions about production capacity and the cohesion of the alliance following the United Arab Emirates' exit from OPEC+.

Why have crude oil prices risen this week?

Brent gained about 3 percent in the week and settled at $95.44 a barrel on Friday after attacks on Saudi refineries, shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and other Gulf targets revived fears of supply disruptions.

How close is Brent to $100 a barrel?

Brent touched an intraday high not seen since 9 November before settling at $95.44. Analysts at ANZ say it can push above $100 without another major escalation, but only with clear evidence of constrained supply.

What happens next for oil markets?

Traders are watching the OPEC+ meeting on 29 November, where the group is expected to hold production targets for the first quarter of 2027, and whether shipping through the Strait of Hormuz recovers.
